|\omega_1|\geq\cdots\geq|\omega_r|\geq0.
\]
The paired columns \(Q_j=(q_{j,1},q_{j,2})\) span a real invariant plane. In exact fitted coordinates \(z_j=Q_j^\top x\), the constrained model gives
\[
\dot z_j=J(\omega_j)z_j,
\]
whose ideal trajectories have constant radius and angular rate \(|\omega_j|\). Churchland et al. construct the same real planes from complex-conjugate eigenvectors of \(M_{\mathrm{skew}}\) and rank them by the magnitudes of the imaginary eigenvalues (Churchland et al. 2012). A real Schur implementation avoids displaying complex coordinates while representing the same invariant planes.
The empirical projection is
\[
Z_j^{(c)}=Q_j^\top X^{(c)}.
\]
Because empirical data only approximately satisfy the constrained fit, these projections need not be circular, constant-radius, periodic, or closed. Ranking by \(|\omega_j|\) prioritizes fitted angular rate, not data variance, held-out fit, biological importance, or statistical reliability. Report those quantities separately.

title: jPCA
text:
From the training trajectories, jPCA learns the PCA subspace, the unconstrained and skew-constrained derivative maps, their invariant rotational planes, fitted angular-rate parameters, and representative coordinates within those planes. It also estimates descriptive fit statistics under the chosen derivative loss.
It does not learn a unique neural state, a probabilistic latent trajectory, a causal transition law, exogenous input, observation map, noise decomposition, autonomous vector field over an unobserved state space, or a mechanism that generates behavior.

title: jPCA
text:
The analyst fixes the feature population, trial and condition definitions, alignment event, time window, bin width, smoother, normalization, across-condition subtraction policy, PCA rank-selection search, derivative estimator, regression loss and regularization, plane-ordering convention, sign/orientation convention, split unit, shuffle family, baseline set, and evaluation metrics.
The original choice of six PCs and a 200-ms movement-related interval was application-specific, not part of a universal definition (Churchland et al. 2012). Searching many windows, ranks, alignments, smoothers, and control families after viewing the final test data converts exploratory flexibility into leakage.

title: jPCA
text:
Time is explicitly ordered through derivative estimation. Adjacent samples are paired only within the same condition or trial trajectory. Equal index spacing is not equal elapsed time unless the sampling grid is regular; irregular sampling requires gap-aware derivatives or a different continuous-time estimation procedure.
The canonical fit pools condition trajectories under one time-invariant matrix. It assumes neither periodic boundary conditions nor repeated cycles. A short arc can score as rotational without completing an oscillation. Event alignment and averaging can synchronize transients, while smoothing can produce phase-shifted, visually coherent curves. Therefore rotational appearance can reflect latency structure or common input rather than autonomous recurrence.

title: jPCA
text:
jPCA uses Euclidean inner products after declared feature scaling and PCA projection. Orthogonality of jPC axes is coordinate- and metric-dependent. The jPC plane is a linear subspace within the retained PCA subspace; it is not a nonlinear manifold, a recovered phase space, or a global tangent plane to an unknown state space.
A skew-symmetric matrix is rotational only with respect to the chosen Euclidean metric. Under a general invertible coordinate change, a skew-symmetric matrix need not remain skew-symmetric. Thus “rotation” is not invariant to arbitrary feature scaling or latent reparameterization, although orthogonal changes within the fixed whitened/Euclidean coordinates preserve the skew property.

title: jPCA
text:
The regression does not require an external behavioral target, but the canonical pipeline is not label-free. Condition identities determine which samples form trajectories; event labels determine alignment; across-condition subtraction uses the condition design; and window or plane selection may use task timing. These are forms of experimental supervision and design dependence.
If behavior, condition identity, or outcome is used to tune rank, window, smoothing, plane, or display, that selection must be nested inside training and validation. A visually compelling post hoc plane is not an unsupervised discovery merely because no class label appears in the least-squares equation.

title: jPCA
text:
PCA uses eigendecomposition or SVD. Both derivative regressions are linear least-squares problems, and the skew-symmetric plane extraction uses a complex eigendecomposition or real Schur decomposition. Numerical choices include rank tolerance, derivative boundary handling, regularization, ordering of nearly equal frequencies, and treatment of zero modes.
There is no posterior inference. Projecting a new processed trajectory uses the training-fitted normalization, PCA basis, and jPCA plane. Recomputing PCA or \(M_{\mathrm{skew}}\) after adding the test trajectory is transductive refitting, not held-out application.

title: jPCA
text:
It provides an explicit, auditable definition of rotation within a variance-dominant linear subspace.
It separates an unrestricted linear derivative fit from the nested skew-symmetric restriction.
Its two-dimensional planes are invariant subspaces of a fitted operator rather than arbitrary hand-selected PC pairs.
It keeps displayed trajectories as linear projections of the data rather than model-smoothed posterior paths (Cunningham and Yu 2014).
It supports direct controls involving derivative prediction, plane occupancy, condition consistency, preprocessing sensitivity, and structured shuffles.
It can reveal phase-offset population patterns that are difficult to see neuron by neuron (Churchland et al. 2012).

title: jPCA
text:
Alignment artifacts: locking trajectories to a common event can synchronize unrelated transients or hide condition-dependent timing.
Condition averaging: smooth mean trajectories can suppress trial variability and manufacture apparent reproducibility that is weak at single-trial level.
Across-condition subtraction: removing the time-varying condition mean changes the data and can create or remove displayed rotations (Lebedev et al. 2019).
Derivative noise: finite differences amplify sampling noise; smoothing can reduce noise while imposing phase and bandwidth structure.
Latency sequences: populations of delayed transient responses can trace rotations even without a recurrent oscillator or autonomous common vector field (Michaels et al. 2016; Lebedev et al. 2019).
Wrong PCA rank: too few PCs can omit structure; too many can expose noise and increase regression flexibility.
Ill-conditioned predictors: weakly occupied directions make \(M\) and its planes unstable.
Short arcs: less than one cycle can look rotational without supporting periodicity or recurrence.
Mixed timescales or regimes: one common time-invariant matrix can average incompatible condition-specific or time-varying relations.
Unmodeled inputs: cue-, sensory-, feedback-, or movement-related drive can be absorbed into a state-only fit.
Pseudo-populations: sequentially recorded neurons do not provide trialwise population covariance and may combine incompatible session timing.
Metric dependence: normalization and feature units change PCA, skew symmetry, and plane ranking.
Plane-selection multiplicity: inspecting many ranks, windows, alignments, smoothers, and planes without nested selection inflates apparent structure.
Shuffle mismatch: a control that destroys covariance, smoothness, latency, or condition balance tests several properties at once and may be too easy to reject.
Interpretive overreach: rotational projection is mistaken for oscillation, mechanism, autonomy, causality, a global vector field, or a unique state space.

Michaels et al. showed that latency-augmented representational simulations can produce rotations, while a covariance-matched condition permutation was more discriminating than an unconstrained shuffle in their reaching analyses (Michaels et al. 2016). Lebedev et al. offered a stronger critical interpretation, arguing that temporal response order and preprocessing can account for visually rotational projections (Lebedev et al. 2019). These sources do not settle every motor-cortex interpretation; together they show that rotations require controls matched to the specific alternative explanation.

title: jPCA
text:
PCA contributes its usual sign and repeated-eigenspace ambiguities. Within a jPCA plane, any rotation of the two displayed axes represents the same oriented plane and the same \(J(\omega)\) block. Simultaneously reflecting one axis changes the displayed handedness and the sign convention for \(\omega\) without changing the unoriented plane. The original implementation selected counterclockwise net rotation and an axis emphasizing preparatory-state spread as display conventions (Churchland et al. 2012).
If two \(|\omega_j|\) values are equal or nearly equal, individual two-dimensional planes can mix within the corresponding higher-dimensional invariant subspace; the combined subspace is more stable than named plane 1 versus plane 2. Zero or weak frequencies do not define a robust rotational plane. Sampling perturbations can also exchange plane order.
The unrestricted map can be nonunique when \(X_-\) is rank deficient. Even with a unique regression coefficient in the chosen coordinates, the fitted state-only equation is not structurally identified as a physical mechanism: unmodeled input, nonlinear dynamics, time variation, and observation mixing can yield the same sampled state–derivative relation. Coordinate conventions choose a representative; they do not supply biological uniqueness.

title: jPCA
text:
Raw condition traces and latency plots: inspect neuron/feature responses, peak times, and condition consistency before projection. This tests whether jPCA is revealing more than a visible sequence of delayed responses.
PCA alone: plot fixed leading PC pairs and report the same held-out split. jPCA should show a more coherent rotational diagnostic than an arbitrary axis alignment, not merely a prettier plot.
Unconstrained linear derivative regression: compare held-out errors for \(\widehat M\) and \(\widehat M_{\mathrm{skew}}\). This is the required nested model comparison.
Symmetric-versus-skew decomposition: fit or score the symmetric expansion/contraction component under the same predictor weighting. A strong skew component should not hide equally important radial dynamics.
Fixed or random planes: within the same training PCA subspace, compare jPCA with prespecified or randomly sampled orthogonal planes using preregistered metrics.
Latency-sequence simulator: generate condition-dependent transient responses with controlled delays but no recurrent autonomous oscillator. This is a targeted negative control motivated by later analyses (Michaels et al. 2016; Lebedev et al. 2019).
Condition-structure shuffles: use a shuffle that preserves declared nuisance statistics, such as neuron-wise temporal smoothness and relevant covariance, while disrupting the condition relationship under test. The covariance-matched permutation of Michaels et al. is one source-specific example rather than a universal null (Michaels et al. 2016).
Observation-space autoregression or input-aware regression: test whether derivative prediction needs the PCA/jPCA representation and whether known task inputs explain structure attributed to autonomous evolution.
LGSSM: provides a probabilistic latent temporal model with process/observation noise and state uncertainty. It solves a different problem; jPCA must not borrow its Gaussian or inferential interpretation.

title: jPCA
text:
Evaluation should be predictive and control-based, not visual alone:

Split independent units: hold out entire trials, sessions, animals, or conditions according to the intended generalization claim. Adjacent bins from one trajectory must not be randomly divided across folds.
Rebuild condition means inside folds: when condition averages are the analysis unit, compute training and held-out averages from disjoint trials. Holding out conditions asks a separate across-condition generalization question.
Fit preprocessing on training data only: normalization, across-condition subtraction, PCA, rank, smoothing hyperparameters, derivative settings, \(M\), \(M_{\mathrm{skew}}\), plane ranking, orientation, and any display window must not use test data.
Score held-out derivatives: apply the training transform and report \[
\lVert D_{\mathrm{test}}-\widehat M X_{-,\mathrm{test}}\rVert_F^2
\quad\text{and}\quad
\lVert D_{\mathrm{test}}-\widehat M_{\mathrm{skew}}X_{-,\mathrm{test}}\rVert_F^2,
\] with an explicitly defined derivative-mean or persistence reference and a held-out \(R^2\) whose denominator is fitted without test leakage.
Separate rate from occupancy: report \(|\omega_j|\), variance/energy occupying each plane, and derivative fit separately. A high fitted rate in a weakly occupied plane is not a dominant data feature.
Quantify rotation: report state–derivative angle, tangential versus radial derivative energy, direction consistency across conditions, radius change, and whether trajectories complete enough arc to support the language used.
Assess stability: compare PCA and jPCA subspaces across bootstrap samples or folds using principal angles after accounting for sign, orientation, ordering, and repeated-frequency ambiguity.
Stress preprocessing: repeat predeclared analyses across plausible alignment, smoothing, normalization, time-window, rank, and across-condition-centering choices.
Use matched controls: evaluate mechanistic, kinematic/representational, latency-sequence, and structured-shuffle alternatives under the same selection and test protocol.
Correct selection multiplicity: hyperparameter and plane selection occur in training/validation; the untouched test set is used once for the final declared comparison.

The original reaching study reported rotations in aligned trial-averaged macaque motor-cortex activity, compared \(M_{\mathrm{skew}}\) with unrestricted \(M\), and used simulated, EMG, and shuffle controls (Churchland et al. 2012). Those empirical findings support that dataset-specific result under the published pipeline; they do not establish universal motor-cortex dynamics or exempt new datasets from independent held-out and matched-null evaluation.

title: jPCA
text:
A future non-executable generation/recovery contract should contain both recoverable rotation and deceptive non-rotational controls.


Choose a six-dimensional continuous-time state with
\[
A=
\operatorname{blockdiag}
\left(
J(2),J(0.7),\operatorname{diag}(-0.4,-0.9)
\right).
\]
For multiple conditions, draw distinct initial states \(x_0^{(c)}\) and generate
\[
x^{(c)}(t)=e^{At}x_0^{(c)}.
\]
Map states to \(p>6\) observed features through a fixed isometric embedding \(H\) with \(H^\top H=I_6\) under the Euclidean metric used by PCA, add declared observation noise, and create repeated trials. Fit all preprocessing and jPCA components using training trials only. The positive recovery target is the image of each latent rotational plane under \(H\), equivalently its representation inside the fitted training PCA coordinates. Evaluate those observed/PCA-space planes by principal angles, angular-rate error, and held-out derivative prediction. Compare with unrestricted regression, PCA pairs, and fixed random planes.
A separate metric-dependence stress test should replace \(H\) by a nonorthogonal full-column-rank mixing matrix. That case is not a nominal positive-recovery failure: it tests the stated fact that arbitrary coordinate changes need not preserve skew-symmetry under the fitted Euclidean metric.




Symmetric decay/expansion: replace \(A\) by a real symmetric matrix with no skew part. jPCA should not receive credit merely for finding an arbitrary plane.
Latency sequence: give each feature a smooth bell-shaped transient with a different peak delay and condition-dependent amplitude, but no shared autonomous state equation. This can produce phase-shifted loops and tests whether visual rotation is mistaken for mechanism.
Input-driven transient: generate \(\dot x=Ax+Bu^{(c)}(t)\) with condition-locked pulses, then fit the misspecified autonomous relation \(\dot x=Mx\). This tests whether common input is absorbed as apparent rotation.
Alignment perturbation: jitter the event time across trials before averaging and compare correct, incorrect, and data-selected alignment.
Condition shuffle: disrupt condition structure while preserving predeclared smoothness and covariance as closely as practical; generate the null independently inside each training fold.

The valid conclusion from successful positive recovery would be limited to recovery under the simulator, representation, loss, and controls. A circle in the latency or input-driven negative control would demonstrate why rotational appearance alone is insufficient. No data, code, figure, or benchmark result is produced in this Method Object.

title: jPCA
text:
jPCA is LDG’s canonical example of a method that combines a static variance baseline, explicit temporal differencing, a constrained linear operator, and a coordinate projection. It is valuable precisely because it forces separation of several claims:

a trajectory is time-indexed;
derivatives are predictable from states in a selected representation;
the best fitted linear relation has a substantial skew component;
a projection displays rotational tendency; and
the biological system is an autonomous oscillator or mechanism.

Only the first four are directly addressed by the bounded method, and each remains conditional on preprocessing and evaluation.






WarningWhat this does NOT imply



A jPCA plane does not prove oscillation, recurrence, a biological mechanism, a global vector field, autonomous dynamics, causal interaction, or a uniquely identified state space. It does not inherit Gaussian SSM assumptions or Kalman inference. Condition averaging, event alignment, smoothing, latency structure, and across-condition subtraction can create, remove, or exaggerate rotational projections.




No modality-specific empirical claim is retained. jPCA could be applied to repeated, aligned movement-feature trajectories, but alignment, condition definition, body-coordinate choice, and averaging would define the result. A rotational projection would not establish a locomotor oscillator or autonomous behavioral state dynamics.



No modality-specific empirical claim is retained. Applying jPCA to aligned saccade or pursuit conditions would require explicit treatment of angular coordinates, event timing, trial dependence, and external visual drive. Input-locked loops would not identify an internal oculomotor mechanism.



No modality-specific empirical claim is retained. Sensor scaling, rereferencing, volume conduction, filtering, phase distortion, trial alignment, and event averaging could dominate derivative relations. A sensor-space jPCA plane would not be a neural source or causal circuit mode.



Churchland et al. applied jPCA to trial-averaged, aligned macaque motor and premotor cortical population responses and reported brief condition-consistent rotational projections within the top six PCs (Churchland et al. 2012). The claim is source- and pipeline-specific. Later work showed that latency-augmented representational simulations can also yield rotations and proposed covariance-matched condition permutations (Michaels et al. 2016), while a critical reanalysis emphasized temporal response sequences and sensitivity to across-condition subtraction (Lebedev et al. 2019). These studies motivate matched alternatives and preprocessing sensitivity analyses rather than a universal interpretation of neural rotations.

title: jPCA
text:
Churchland et al. introduce jPCA, define the PCA-reduced condition–time matrix, adjacent-sample derivative, unrestricted and skew-symmetric fits, complex-eigenvector plane construction, application-specific preprocessing, and the original macaque reaching results and controls (Churchland et al. 2012).
Michaels, Dann, and Scherberger test latency-augmented representational and dynamical simulations and introduce a covariance-matched condition permutation for their motor-cortex comparison (Michaels et al. 2016).
Lebedev et al. reanalyze the Churchland data and code, demonstrate sensitivity to temporal response sequences and across-condition subtraction, and argue for more cautious mechanistic interpretation (Lebedev et al. 2019).

title: jPCA
text: Cunningham and Yu review neural dimensionality reduction and distinguish jPCA-style orthogonal projections from posterior trajectories produced by probabilistic temporal models; they also caution that extracted trajectories reflect the assumptions of the chosen method (Cunningham and Yu 2014).

title: jPCA
text:
Which derivative estimator best balances temporal resolution, phase distortion, and noise without tuning on the final test set?
Which null models preserve enough covariance, smoothness, condition structure, and latency statistics to isolate the scientific claim of interest?
When should rotational structure be scored by held-out derivative prediction, invariant-subspace stability, tangential energy, completed phase, or downstream prediction?
How should known external inputs and feedback be incorporated before interpreting a state-only fit as autonomous?
Which properties of a jPCA plane remain stable across feature scaling, recording subsets, animals, sessions, and alignment choices?
When are single-trial latent methods preferable to condition-averaged projection, and how should their different inferential targets be compared?

title: jPCA
text:
Complete Method schema at L2/review.
Declares condition–time input construction, alignment, averaging, normalization, PCA preprocessing, and derivative estimation.
Defines unrestricted and skew-symmetric least-squares fits without incorrectly equating antisymmetrization with the constrained solution.
Gives complex-eigenplane and real-Schur interpretations, plane ranking, projection, and occupancy/rate distinction.
Separates learned and fixed quantities, temporal assumptions, Euclidean geometry, supervision, and computation.
States sign, orientation, plane, repeated-frequency, PCA, rank-deficiency, and mechanistic non-identifiability boundaries.
Covers alignment, averaging, smoothing, latency, input, conditioning, rank, metric, shuffle, and multiplicity failures.
Includes PCA, raw latency, unrestricted dynamics, symmetric, random-plane, input-aware, LGSSM, and structured-null comparisons.
Gives leakage-safe held-out evaluation and a non-executable positive/negative toy contract.
Explicitly rejects inherited Gaussian-SSM assumptions and oscillation, mechanism, global-vector-field, autonomy, and causality overclaims.
Four retained sources were inspected; bibliographic metadata and DOI or stable identifiers were verified.
Independent mixed review returned PASS with no correction round required.
Stable promotion authorized under the recorded review decision after object-specific PASS and validation.

title: Methods
text: Method Objects organize methods around the problem solved, assumptions, learned and fixed quantities, representations of time and geometry, failure modes, baselines, and evaluation.

title: Methods
text:
Current method library

Principal Component Analysis — canonical static linear Euclidean baseline. (L2, stable)
Factor Analysis — static probabilistic low-rank-plus-diagonal covariance baseline. (L2, stable)
Isomap — graph-shortest-path and classical-MDS geometry baseline. (L2, stable)
Diffusion Maps — affinity-operator and diffusion-distance spectral baseline. (L2, stable)
Demixed Principal Component Analysis — label-dependent marginal reconstruction baseline. (L2, stable)
Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model — probabilistic temporal latent baseline. (L2, stable)
Bounded Autoencoder Baseline — deterministic nonlinear reconstruction baseline. (L2, stable)
Kalman Filtering — online current-state inference for a fixed discrete-time linear-Gaussian state-space model. (L2, stable)
jPCA — PCA-reduced, derivative-fitted skew-symmetric rotational projection method. (L2, stable)
Fixed-Interval Kalman Smoothing — retrospective full-interval state and path inference for a fixed LGSSM. (L2, stable)
Gaussian-Process Factor Analysis — FA observation layer with covariance-prior retrospective latent trajectories. (L2, stable)

Stable status records bounded owner acceptance under the declared evidence and non-implication limits; it is not a claim of universal empirical validity. Objects labeled review have completed the scientific draft and evidence stage but have not yet crossed their object-specific acceptance gate.

title: Factor Analysis
text:
Factor analysis (FA) explains the covariance among \(p\) observed variables using \(q<p\) Gaussian latent factors plus variable-specific residual variation. The unit of analysis in this object is one real-valued observation vector. FA is a probabilistic covariance model, not merely a projection rule: it assigns a likelihood to observations and a posterior distribution to factors under explicit distributional assumptions (Ghahramani and Hinton 1997; Roweis and Ghahramani 1999).
The bounded scope here is exploratory maximum-likelihood Gaussian factor analysis with a diagonal residual covariance whose interior parameter space has \(\psi_j>0\). The zero-uniqueness boundary is excluded from this model but remains relevant because a likelihood supremum can approach it. Confirmatory loading constraints, ordinal or non-Gaussian factor models, mixtures, robust variants, Bayesian priors, and temporal extensions require separate objects.



Let \(x_i\in\mathbb R^p\), \(i=1,\ldots,n\), denote selected complete observation vectors. A reproducible analysis must declare:

the observational unit and whether rows are independent units, repeated measurements, time samples, trials, subjects, or condition summaries;
the variables, units, transformations, exclusion rules, and missing-data policy;
whether the model is fitted to a covariance matrix, a correlation matrix after training-fitted standardization, or the raw observations through the equivalent Gaussian likelihood;
the candidate factor count \(q\) and its selection protocol; and
any loading zeros, equality constraints, rotations, or score conventions introduced after fitting.

The canonical formulation assumes independent and identically distributed observation vectors conditional on common parameters. Treating dependent repeated or temporal samples as independent changes the likelihood and its uncertainty interpretation.



For a chosen \(q\), maximum-likelihood FA estimates:

a mean \(\mu\in\mathbb R^p\);
a loading matrix \(\Lambda\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}\);
diagonal uniqueness covariance \(\Psi=\operatorname{diag}(\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_p)\) with \(\psi_j>0\); and
the model covariance \(C=\Lambda\Lambda^\top+\Psi\).

For each observation it also defines a Gaussian posterior distribution over its latent factor vector. A reported “factor score” is therefore a chosen posterior summary or scoring rule, not an observed quantity and not the same object as a PCA projection score.



FA attributes cross-variable covariance to shared latent factors while reserving a separate residual variance for each observed coordinate. Conditional on the factors, the observed coordinates are independent only because \(\Psi\) is assumed diagonal. Marginally, they can be correlated through \(\Lambda\Lambda^\top\) (Tipping and Bishop 1999, sec. 2.1; Roweis and Ghahramani 1999, sec. 5.2).
This separation is useful when heterogeneous coordinate-wise noise or unique variation is scientifically defensible. It is also restrictive: correlated residuals, unmodeled groups, temporal filtering, and shared artifacts violate the diagonal-uniqueness assumption and may be forced into the factors.



The canonical model is
\[
z_i\sim\mathcal N(0,I_q),\qquad
\epsilon_i\sim\mathcal N(0,\Psi),\qquad
x_i=\mu+\Lambda z_i+\epsilon_i,
\]
with \(z_i\perp\!\!\!\perp\epsilon_i\) and independence across \(i\). Thus
\[
x_i\sim\mathcal N(\mu,C),\qquad C=\Lambda\Lambda^\top+\Psi.
\]
This low-rank-plus-diagonal covariance formulation, together with the need for additional identification conditions beyond choosing a factor count, is part of the classical statistical factor-analysis problem (Anderson and Rubin 1956).
The assumptions are substantive:

the shared structure is linear in the selected observation coordinates;
factors and residuals are Gaussian;
the latent covariance is fixed to \(I_q\) as a scale convention;
residual covariance is diagonal and strictly positive;
one global loading matrix and one global uniqueness matrix apply to all observations; and
the declared sample is represented by independent draws from one stationary marginal distribution.

Diagonal \(\Psi\) makes conditional independence coordinate-system dependent. Rotating the observed axes generally destroys diagonality, whereas component-wise unit changes can be absorbed by corresponding row and uniqueness rescaling (Roweis and Ghahramani 1999, sec. 5.2). Standardizing variables is therefore a modeling choice, not a neutral route to the same answer.



With sample mean \(\bar x\) and divisor-\(n\) sample covariance
\[
S=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)(x_i-\bar x)^\top,
\]
the Gaussian log-likelihood at \(\widehat\mu=\bar x\), up to an additive constant, is
\[
\ell(\Lambda,\Psi)
=-\frac n2\left\{\log|C|+\operatorname{tr}(C^{-1}S)\right\},
\qquad C=\Lambda\Lambda^\top+\Psi.
\]
Unlike ordinary PCA, general FA has no single eigendecomposition giving its maximum-likelihood loading and uniqueness estimates. Numerical optimization or latent-variable algorithms are required (Tipping and Bishop 1999, sec. 2.1).
For fixed parameters, let
\[
M=I_q+\Lambda^\top\Psi^{-1}\Lambda.
\]
Gaussian conditioning gives
\[
z_i\mid x_i\sim\mathcal N\!\left(
M^{-1}\Lambda^\top\Psi^{-1}(x_i-\mu),\ M^{-1}
\right).
\]
The posterior covariance explicitly records uncertainty left after observing \(x_i\); a point score discards part of this information (Ghahramani and Hinton 1997).



Given \(q\), the model class, and preprocessing, fitting returns estimates of \(\mu\) and a candidate decomposition \(\widehat C=\widehat\Lambda
\widehat\Lambda^\top+\widehat\Psi\). The observable covariance distribution is the primary likelihood target; the particular loading–uniqueness decomposition is subject to sampling error, misspecification, boundary behavior, orthogonal equivalence, and any additional identification failures. Fitted parameters also determine model-conditional posterior distributions for factors of observed or new cases.
What is most directly identified by the likelihood is the observable distribution, especially \(C\), not a uniquely oriented set of latent axes. Even recovery of \(C\) does not show that the fitted factors correspond to physical, psychological, or neural causes.



The analyst fixes the observation representation, sample inclusion and dependence treatment, Gaussian linear model class, diagonal residual structure, latent mean zero and covariance \(I_q\), factor count or selection rule, and any structural loading constraints. Training-only centering and scaling must be fixed before evaluating held-out data.
The choice \(\operatorname{Cov}(z)=I_q\) fixes latent scale but not latent orientation. If the latent covariance is instead a free diagonal matrix, scale can be transferred between each factor variance and its loading column, in addition to sign and permutation conventions. If a fully unrestricted latent covariance \(\Phi\) is estimated, any invertible coordinate change \(z'=Az\), \(\Lambda'=\Lambda A^{-1}\), and \(\Phi'=A\Phi A^\top\) preserves the observable covariance. These broader ambiguities require the corresponding broader parameterization; they are not invariances of the canonical \(\operatorname{Cov}(z)=I_q\) model.



Canonical FA is static and order-blind. Permuting observations leaves \(S\) and the likelihood unchanged. If rows are time points, the model does not represent transitions, autocorrelation, process noise, lags, or trajectories; it merely fits their marginal distribution while often overstating effective sample size if dependence is ignored (Roweis and Ghahramani 1999, sec. 5.1).
A discrete-time linear-Gaussian state-space model adds a transition distribution and process noise to a related linear-Gaussian observation layer. That temporal extension is not implicit in FA.



FA posits a linear latent-to-observation map embedded in \(\mathbb R^p\) and a Gaussian covariance ellipsoid \(C\). The diagonal entries of \(\Psi\) define coordinate-specific residual scales, so the privileged observed coordinate system is part of the model. Posterior means shrink observations according to both loadings and uniquenesses; they are not orthogonal Euclidean projections in general.
This is covariance geometry under a chosen representation. It does not establish a nonlinear manifold, recover a Riemannian metric, preserve topology, or determine model-free intrinsic dimension.



Exploratory FA is unsupervised with respect to outcomes and labels: its likelihood uses only the selected observation vectors. Label-dependent variable selection, preprocessing, rank choice, or subgroup construction can nevertheless introduce supervision and leakage at the design level.



Parameter learning maximizes the marginal likelihood after integrating out the latent factors. EM alternates between posterior moments of \(z_i\) and updates of \(\Lambda\) and diagonal \(\Psi\); the diagonal constraint is enforced in the uniqueness update (Ghahramani and Hinton 1997). EM monotonically improves the likelihood under exact steps but can converge slowly, and monotonicity does not imply arrival at a unique global optimum. ECME and direct/quasi-Newton approaches are alternative numerical strategies; Liu and Rubin document an ECME construction for complete and incomplete Gaussian FA and emphasize convergence assessment (Liu and Rubin 1998).
Inference with fitted parameters computes the conditional Gaussian distribution \(p(z_i\mid x_i)\). Parameter learning and factor inference are distinct tasks. Initialization, convergence tolerances, positivity constraints, and multiple starts must be reported because the likelihood is nonconvex in the factorized parameters. Under the strict interior convention \(\psi_j>0\), an optimizer can approach \(\psi_j=0\) so that the likelihood supremum is not attained by an interior MLE; implementations that instead permit \(\psi_j\geq 0\) may report zero as an attained boundary solution.




FA provides an explicit probability model, likelihood, and posterior uncertainty for latent factors.
Diagonal uniquenesses allow heterogeneous residual variances instead of forcing one isotropic noise level.
The model separates shared covariance from coordinate-specific residual variance under clear assumptions.
It is a compact static baseline for later temporal latent models.
Held-out log likelihood and posterior predictive checks are available because the model defines a normalized density.





Correlated residuals: shared artifacts, coupling, spatial leakage, or omitted groups violate diagonal \(\Psi\) and can appear as spurious factors.
Nonlinearity or non-Gaussianity: curved structure, heavy tails, skewness, multimodality, and outliers can distort loadings and uniquenesses.
Wrong factor count: too few factors leave structured residual covariance; too many can overfit, become unstable, or approach boundary uniquenesses.
Heywood or boundary behavior: one or more uniqueness estimates may approach zero. With the strict \(\psi_j>0\) parameter space this can mean an unattained boundary supremum; with a nonnegative implementation it can be an attained boundary solution. Either case signals misspecification, weak identification, or numerical difficulty rather than a scientifically noiseless variable.
Dependence treated as replication: fitting time points, repeated measures, or trials as independent makes likelihood comparisons and uncertainty claims optimistic.
Preprocessing sensitivity: covariance- and correlation-based FA answer different questions; unit changes and standardization alter the decomposition.
Local optimization and slow convergence: different starts can produce different representatives or local solutions, and small likelihood changes can hide incomplete convergence (Liu and Rubin 1998).
Factor-score overinterpretation: posterior means are model-dependent uncertain estimates, not measured states.
Causal naming: labels such as “memory,” “arousal,” or “motor drive” do not turn covariance factors into causes.




For every orthogonal \(Q\in\mathbb R^{q\times q}\),
\[
\Lambda z=(\Lambda Q)(Q^\top z),
\qquad
(\Lambda Q)(\Lambda Q)^\top=\Lambda\Lambda^\top.
\]
Thus the likelihood cannot distinguish orthogonal rotations of the loading matrix. Sign flips and factor permutations are special cases. A post-hoc rotation may choose a more interpretable representative, but it does not create evidence that the selected axes are uniquely present in the data.
With \(\operatorname{Cov}(z)=I_q\), arbitrary factor rescaling is not an invariance: rescaling one loading column without compensating in the fixed latent covariance changes \(C\). Free diagonal latent variances add separate factor-scale ambiguities, whereas a general invertible coordinate ambiguity requires the fully unrestricted latent covariance described above. This distinction prevents “scale ambiguity” from being asserted where the canonical normalization has already fixed it.
Beyond rotational equivalence, uniqueness and loading recovery can be weak or nonunique for some dimensions, factor counts, covariance patterns, and boundary cases; classical identification results therefore impose additional rank or loading-pattern conditions rather than treating rotation as the only possible ambiguity (Anderson and Rubin 1956). Posterior factor scores remain uncertain even when covariance parameters are well estimated. These are statistical identifiability limits, not competing causal mechanisms.




Mean plus diagonal Gaussian (\(q=0\)): estimates no shared factors. FA should improve held-out likelihood or reduce reproducible off-diagonal covariance residuals before shared latent structure is credited.
PCA: finds an orthogonal subspace maximizing variance or minimizing Euclidean reconstruction error. It has no likelihood or variable-specific noise model. FA loadings need not span the PCA subspace, and factor solutions for different \(q\) need not be nested (Tipping and Bishop 1999; Roweis and Ghahramani 1999).
Probabilistic PCA (PPCA): replaces diagonal \(\Psi\) by \(\sigma^2I\). Its maximum-likelihood loading space is the principal subspace, whereas FA’s heterogeneous uniquenesses generally change the fitted loading space (Tipping and Bishop 1999). PPCA is a useful rank-matched test of whether variable-specific residual variance is needed.
Full-covariance Gaussian: can fit an unrestricted covariance but is not a low-parameter latent explanation. Comparing predictive likelihood penalized or validated out of sample tests whether FA’s structure earns its restrictions.
Discrete-time linear-Gaussian state-space model: adds latent evolution, process noise, and temporally conditioned inference. It should be preferred only when sequence structure improves properly blocked prediction or likelihood, not because FA scores look smooth.




Fit preprocessing and parameters on training units only. Evaluation should include:

held-out negative log likelihood under \(\mathcal N(\widehat\mu,\widehat C)\), compared with \(q=0\), rank-matched PPCA, and declared covariance baselines;
residual covariance \(S_{\text{test}}-\widehat C\), especially reproducible off-diagonal structure that contradicts diagonal conditional residuals;
posterior predictive checks for marginal variances, correlations, tails, and subgroup or temporal residual patterns;
rank sensitivity and stability of the fitted common covariance or loading subspace across resamples, with orthogonal alignment before comparing loading representatives; and
convergence diagnostics, positivity of uniquenesses, multiple-start agreement, and sensitivity to scaling and exclusion rules.

Splits must preserve the true dependence unit: hold out entire subjects, sessions, trials, trajectories, or time blocks when observations within them are dependent. Factor recovery cannot be validated by visual separation alone. If known latent variables exist only in simulation, compare posterior estimates after an allowed alignment and separately score covariance recovery. Information criteria may supplement but should not replace held-out and misspecification checks.



An analytic example uses \(p=3\), \(q=1\),
\[
\Lambda=\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\0.5\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\Psi=\operatorname{diag}(0.25,1,4),
\]
which gives
\[
C=\begin{pmatrix}
4.25&2&1\\
2&2&0.5\\
1&0.5&4.25
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

\[
\left(1+\Lambda^\top\Psi^{-1}\Lambda\right)^{-1}=\frac{1}{18.0625},
\]

title: Factor Analysis
text:
Factor analysis (FA) explains the covariance among \(p\) observed variables using \(q<p\) Gaussian latent factors plus variable-specific residual variation. The unit of analysis in this object is one real-valued observation vector. FA is a probabilistic covariance model, not merely a projection rule: it assigns a likelihood to observations and a posterior distribution to factors under explicit distributional assumptions (Ghahramani and Hinton 1997; Roweis and Ghahramani 1999).
The bounded scope here is exploratory maximum-likelihood Gaussian factor analysis with a diagonal residual covariance whose interior parameter space has \(\psi_j>0\). The zero-uniqueness boundary is excluded from this model but remains relevant because a likelihood supremum can approach it. Confirmatory loading constraints, ordinal or non-Gaussian factor models, mixtures, robust variants, Bayesian priors, and temporal extensions require separate objects.

title: Factor Analysis
Factor Analysis
Factor Analysis
text:
FA attributes cross-variable covariance to shared latent factors while reserving a separate residual variance for each observed coordinate. Conditional on the factors, the observed coordinates are independent only because \(\Psi\) is assumed diagonal. Marginally, they can be correlated through \(\Lambda\Lambda^\top\) (Tipping and Bishop 1999, sec. 2.1; Roweis and Ghahramani 1999, sec. 5.2).
This separation is useful when heterogeneous coordinate-wise noise or unique variation is scientifically defensible. It is also restrictive: correlated residuals, unmodeled groups, temporal filtering, and shared artifacts violate the diagonal-uniqueness assumption and may be forced into the factors.

title: Factor Analysis
text:
The canonical model is
\[
z_i\sim\mathcal N(0,I_q),\qquad
\epsilon_i\sim\mathcal N(0,\Psi),\qquad
x_i=\mu+\Lambda z_i+\epsilon_i,
\]
with \(z_i\perp\!\!\!\perp\epsilon_i\) and independence across \(i\). Thus
\[
x_i\sim\mathcal N(\mu,C),\qquad C=\Lambda\Lambda^\top+\Psi.
\]
This low-rank-plus-diagonal covariance formulation, together with the need for additional identification conditions beyond choosing a factor count, is part of the classical statistical factor-analysis problem (Anderson and Rubin 1956).
The assumptions are substantive:

the shared structure is linear in the selected observation coordinates;
factors and residuals are Gaussian;
the latent covariance is fixed to \(I_q\) as a scale convention;
residual covariance is diagonal and strictly positive;
one global loading matrix and one global uniqueness matrix apply to all observations; and
the declared sample is represented by independent draws from one stationary marginal distribution.

Diagonal \(\Psi\) makes conditional independence coordinate-system dependent. Rotating the observed axes generally destroys diagonality, whereas component-wise unit changes can be absorbed by corresponding row and uniqueness rescaling (Roweis and Ghahramani 1999, sec. 5.2). Standardizing variables is therefore a modeling choice, not a neutral route to the same answer.

title: Factor Analysis
text:
With sample mean \(\bar x\) and divisor-\(n\) sample covariance
\[
S=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)(x_i-\bar x)^\top,
\]
the Gaussian log-likelihood at \(\widehat\mu=\bar x\), up to an additive constant, is
\[
\ell(\Lambda,\Psi)
=-\frac n2\left\{\log|C|+\operatorname{tr}(C^{-1}S)\right\},
\qquad C=\Lambda\Lambda^\top+\Psi.
\]
Unlike ordinary PCA, general FA has no single eigendecomposition giving its maximum-likelihood loading and uniqueness estimates. Numerical optimization or latent-variable algorithms are required (Tipping and Bishop 1999, sec. 2.1).
For fixed parameters, let
\[
M=I_q+\Lambda^\top\Psi^{-1}\Lambda.
\]
Gaussian conditioning gives
\[
z_i\mid x_i\sim\mathcal N\!\left(
M^{-1}\Lambda^\top\Psi^{-1}(x_i-\mu),\ M^{-1}
\right).
\]
The posterior covariance explicitly records uncertainty left after observing \(x_i\); a point score discards part of this information (Ghahramani and Hinton 1997).

title: Factor Analysis
text:
Given \(q\), the model class, and preprocessing, fitting returns estimates of \(\mu\) and a candidate decomposition \(\widehat C=\widehat\Lambda
\widehat\Lambda^\top+\widehat\Psi\). The observable covariance distribution is the primary likelihood target; the particular loading–uniqueness decomposition is subject to sampling error, misspecification, boundary behavior, orthogonal equivalence, and any additional identification failures. Fitted parameters also determine model-conditional posterior distributions for factors of observed or new cases.
What is most directly identified by the likelihood is the observable distribution, especially \(C\), not a uniquely oriented set of latent axes. Even recovery of \(C\) does not show that the fitted factors correspond to physical, psychological, or neural causes.

title: Factor Analysis
text:
The analyst fixes the observation representation, sample inclusion and dependence treatment, Gaussian linear model class, diagonal residual structure, latent mean zero and covariance \(I_q\), factor count or selection rule, and any structural loading constraints. Training-only centering and scaling must be fixed before evaluating held-out data.
The choice \(\operatorname{Cov}(z)=I_q\) fixes latent scale but not latent orientation. If the latent covariance is instead a free diagonal matrix, scale can be transferred between each factor variance and its loading column, in addition to sign and permutation conventions. If a fully unrestricted latent covariance \(\Phi\) is estimated, any invertible coordinate change \(z'=Az\), \(\Lambda'=\Lambda A^{-1}\), and \(\Phi'=A\Phi A^\top\) preserves the observable covariance. These broader ambiguities require the corresponding broader parameterization; they are not invariances of the canonical \(\operatorname{Cov}(z)=I_q\) model.

title: Factor Analysis
text:
Canonical FA is static and order-blind. Permuting observations leaves \(S\) and the likelihood unchanged. If rows are time points, the model does not represent transitions, autocorrelation, process noise, lags, or trajectories; it merely fits their marginal distribution while often overstating effective sample size if dependence is ignored (Roweis and Ghahramani 1999, sec. 5.1).
A discrete-time linear-Gaussian state-space model adds a transition distribution and process noise to a related linear-Gaussian observation layer. That temporal extension is not implicit in FA.

title: Factor Analysis
text:
FA posits a linear latent-to-observation map embedded in \(\mathbb R^p\) and a Gaussian covariance ellipsoid \(C\). The diagonal entries of \(\Psi\) define coordinate-specific residual scales, so the privileged observed coordinate system is part of the model. Posterior means shrink observations according to both loadings and uniquenesses; they are not orthogonal Euclidean projections in general.
This is covariance geometry under a chosen representation. It does not establish a nonlinear manifold, recover a Riemannian metric, preserve topology, or determine model-free intrinsic dimension.

title: Factor Analysis
text: Exploratory FA is unsupervised with respect to outcomes and labels: its likelihood uses only the selected observation vectors. Label-dependent variable selection, preprocessing, rank choice, or subgroup construction can nevertheless introduce supervision and leakage at the design level.

title: Factor Analysis
text:
Parameter learning maximizes the marginal likelihood after integrating out the latent factors. EM alternates between posterior moments of \(z_i\) and updates of \(\Lambda\) and diagonal \(\Psi\); the diagonal constraint is enforced in the uniqueness update (Ghahramani and Hinton 1997). EM monotonically improves the likelihood under exact steps but can converge slowly, and monotonicity does not imply arrival at a unique global optimum. ECME and direct/quasi-Newton approaches are alternative numerical strategies; Liu and Rubin document an ECME construction for complete and incomplete Gaussian FA and emphasize convergence assessment (Liu and Rubin 1998).
Inference with fitted parameters computes the conditional Gaussian distribution \(p(z_i\mid x_i)\). Parameter learning and factor inference are distinct tasks. Initialization, convergence tolerances, positivity constraints, and multiple starts must be reported because the likelihood is nonconvex in the factorized parameters. Under the strict interior convention \(\psi_j>0\), an optimizer can approach \(\psi_j=0\) so that the likelihood supremum is not attained by an interior MLE; implementations that instead permit \(\psi_j\geq 0\) may report zero as an attained boundary solution.

title: Factor Analysis
text:
FA provides an explicit probability model, likelihood, and posterior uncertainty for latent factors.
Diagonal uniquenesses allow heterogeneous residual variances instead of forcing one isotropic noise level.
The model separates shared covariance from coordinate-specific residual variance under clear assumptions.
It is a compact static baseline for later temporal latent models.
Held-out log likelihood and posterior predictive checks are available because the model defines a normalized density.

title: Factor Analysis
text:
Correlated residuals: shared artifacts, coupling, spatial leakage, or omitted groups violate diagonal \(\Psi\) and can appear as spurious factors.
Nonlinearity or non-Gaussianity: curved structure, heavy tails, skewness, multimodality, and outliers can distort loadings and uniquenesses.
Wrong factor count: too few factors leave structured residual covariance; too many can overfit, become unstable, or approach boundary uniquenesses.
Heywood or boundary behavior: one or more uniqueness estimates may approach zero. With the strict \(\psi_j>0\) parameter space this can mean an unattained boundary supremum; with a nonnegative implementation it can be an attained boundary solution. Either case signals misspecification, weak identification, or numerical difficulty rather than a scientifically noiseless variable.
Dependence treated as replication: fitting time points, repeated measures, or trials as independent makes likelihood comparisons and uncertainty claims optimistic.
Preprocessing sensitivity: covariance- and correlation-based FA answer different questions; unit changes and standardization alter the decomposition.
Local optimization and slow convergence: different starts can produce different representatives or local solutions, and small likelihood changes can hide incomplete convergence (Liu and Rubin 1998).
Factor-score overinterpretation: posterior means are model-dependent uncertain estimates, not measured states.
Causal naming: labels such as “memory,” “arousal,” or “motor drive” do not turn covariance factors into causes.

title: Factor Analysis
text:
For every orthogonal \(Q\in\mathbb R^{q\times q}\),
\[
\Lambda z=(\Lambda Q)(Q^\top z),
\qquad
(\Lambda Q)(\Lambda Q)^\top=\Lambda\Lambda^\top.
\]

title: Demixed Principal Component Analysis
text:
Demixed principal component analysis (dPCA) constructs supervised linear coordinates that approximately reconstruct declared task-variable marginalizations of multivariate data. It was developed for trial-structured neural population recordings in which activity varies with time and experimentally labeled conditions, while individual variables and ordinary principal components often mix several task dependencies (Brendel et al. 2011; Kobak et al. 2016).
The word demixed names success under a particular label decomposition and reconstruction loss. It does not mean that the resulting components are statistically independent, causally separated, uniquely identified, anatomically localized, or generated by distinct neural modules. The method is a label-dependent linear summary, not blind source separation or a mechanistic model. The bounded formulation here follows the published 2016 analysis of trial-averaged condition means; it is not a trial-level noise-covariance model (Kobak et al. 2016).



Let \(N\) be the number of measured features or neurons, \(T\) the number of aligned time bins, and let \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\) denote declared categorical or discretized task variables. For a balanced full-factorial design, a trial-resolved tensor can be written
\[
\mathcal X\in
\mathbb R^{N\times T\times A_1\times\cdots\times A_m\times K},
\]
where \(K\) is the same number of trials in every condition cell. The fitted input in the bounded formulation here is the trial-averaged condition tensor
\[
\bar{\mathcal X}
\in
\mathbb R^{N\times T\times A_1\times\cdots\times A_m},
\]
flattened into a centered matrix \(X\in\mathbb R^{N\times M}\), with \(M=T\prod_j A_j\). Each condition–time column is given equal weight in the bounded formulation below. The trial-resolved tensor supplies independent repeats for estimating these means and for cross-validation; its individual trial columns do not replace \(X\) in the objective stated below.
A reproducible analysis must declare:

the experimental unit, trial inclusion rules and whether features were recorded simultaneously or assembled as a pseudo-population;
alignment, binning, smoothing, time warping and baseline subtraction;
feature scaling and centering;
the task variables, their coding, level order and which interactions are retained or grouped;
whether all factorial cells exist and how unequal trial counts are handled;
the ranks \(q_\phi\) allocated to each marginalization;
the regularization grid and cross-validation split unit; and
whether projections will be applied to condition means, single trials, or both.

Equal weighting of condition means answers a different question from weighting cells in proportion to their trial counts. Missing cells, correlated labels and unequal noise precision require an explicit model, weighting or rebalancing procedure rather than silent application of balanced formulas (Kobak et al. 2016).



For each declared marginalization group \(\phi\), dPCA returns:

a target matrix \(X_\phi\) with the same shape as \(X\);
a decoder matrix \(D_\phi\in\mathbb R^{q_\phi\times N}\) whose rows define linear projection axes;
an encoder matrix \(F_\phi\in\mathbb R^{N\times q_\phi}\) used to reconstruct the corresponding marginalization;
component scores \(Z_\phi=D_\phi X\); and
an approximate marginal reconstruction \(\widehat X_\phi=F_\phi D_\phi X\).

The combined approximation is
\[
\widehat X=\sum_\phi F_\phi D_\phi X.
\]
Components belonging to different marginalizations are not generally orthogonal, and their scores need not be uncorrelated. The output is deterministic given the fitted data and choices; it is not a posterior distribution over latent variables.



Ordinary PCA chooses one orthogonal subspace to reconstruct all centered variance without using labels. dPCA first decomposes the balanced condition tensor into ANOVA-style marginalizations associated with time, task-variable main effects and interactions. It then solves a separate regularized reduced-rank regression for each marginalization: the full data are projected through a decoder, but the reconstruction target is only the selected label-dependent part of the data (Kobak et al. 2016).
This separates two roles that coincide in ordinary PCA. Decoder rows define low-dimensional readouts \(D_\phi X\); encoder columns map those readouts back toward \(X_\phi\). Allowing encoder and decoder axes to differ avoids forcing all task-associated subspaces to be mutually orthogonal.



The bounded 2016 dPCA formulation is a deterministic supervised approximation method, not a generative probability model. Its operative assumptions are:

declared task labels and their interactions provide scientifically relevant partitions of variation;
condition means can be compared in one common feature space;
linear readouts and linear reconstructions are adequate summaries;
squared Frobenius reconstruction loss and ridge regularization are appropriate criteria;
the factorial marginalization is meaningful under the declared balancing or weighting convention; and
enough independent trials exist to estimate condition means, regularization and held-out behavior.

Earlier dPCA work used an orthogonality-constrained probabilistic formulation, while the canonical reduced-rank formulation removed that constraint because task-related subspaces can be nonorthogonal (Brendel et al. 2011; Kobak et al. 2016). Neither formulation implies that the labeled effects are physical sources or that the data were generated by independent modules.





Let
\[
\Omega=\{t,a_1,\ldots,a_m\}
\]
be the set of indexed variables. For each subset \(S\subseteq\Omega\), let \(\mathcal M_S X\) denote averaging over every variable in \(\Omega\setminus S\) and replicating the resulting values across the averaged indices. Define the full factorial decomposition recursively by
\[
X_S
=
\mathcal M_S X
-
\sum_{R\subsetneq S}X_R.
\]
The empty-set term is the grand mean and is zero after global feature-wise centering. Under a complete balanced factorial design with uniform cell weighting,
\[
X=\sum_{S\subseteq\Omega}X_S,
\]
and distinct terms are orthogonal in the Frobenius inner product, so their squared norms add (Brendel et al. 2011; Kobak et al. 2016).
Interactions are not residual nuisances to be discarded automatically. With stimulus \(s\), decision \(d\) and time \(t\), the complete decomposition contains \(t,s,d,ts,td,sd,tsd\). The canonical neural presentation groups terms such as
\[
X_{\text{stimulus}}=X_s+X_{ts},
\qquad
X_{\text{decision}}=X_d+X_{td},
\]
and
\[
X_{\text{interaction}}=X_{sd}+X_{tsd},
\]
while \(X_t\) is condition-independent time variation. This grouping is an analyst-declared interpretive choice. Different groupings, label codings or averaging measures define different demixing targets.



For each grouped marginalization \(\phi\), choose rank \(q_\phi\) and solve
\[
\min_{F_\phi,D_\phi}
\left\lVert
X_\phi-F_\phi D_\phi X
\right\rVert_F^2
+
\lambda
\left\lVert F_\phi D_\phi\right\rVert_F^2,
\]
subject to
\[
\operatorname{rank}(F_\phi D_\phi)\le q_\phi.
\]

\[

\[

=
X_\phi X^\top
\left(XX^\top+\lambda I\right)^{-1},

\[

\qquad

\[
V_{\mathrm{tot}}=\lVert X\rVert_F^2,
\qquad
V_\phi=\lVert X_\phi\rVert_F^2.

\[
V_{\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_\phi V_\phi
\]

\[

\]

\[

=
\frac{\max_\phi v_\phi(d)}{\sum_\psi v_\psi(d)}.

For each marginalization, dPCA learns a regularized low-rank linear map \(A_\phi=F_\phi D_\phi\), a representative encoder/decoder factorization, ordered component scores and marginal reconstructions. It also yields descriptive variance and demixing summaries under the fixed tensor decomposition.
It does not learn task labels, a causal graph, independent sources, neural modules, a transition law, a latent-state posterior or a unique biological coordinate system.



The analyst fixes the population/features, trials and condition cells, alignment and preprocessing, centering and scaling, label set and coding, factorial averaging measure, interaction grouping, cell weighting or rebalancing, ranks, regularization-selection protocol, cross-validation unit, number of components displayed, and any classifier used for evaluation.
Trial averaging is also fixed. Fitting on condition means emphasizes repeatable label-associated structure but suppresses trial-to-trial variability. Applying decoders to single trials is a separate generalization question.



Time is an indexed task variable in the bounded dPCA formulation. A time marginalization describes mean variation across aligned time bins, while terms such as stimulus–time describe label-dependent temporal profiles. The method does not estimate transitions, derivatives, process noise, a vector field or an evolution law.
Changing bin width, alignment event, smoothing kernel, time warping or analyzed interval changes the marginalizations. Smooth dPCA traces can arise from smoothing and trial averaging; they are not evidence for smooth latent dynamics. Treating adjacent bins from one trial as independent held-out samples causes leakage.



dPCA uses linear projections and Euclidean/Frobenius squared error in the declared feature coordinates. Feature scaling therefore changes the objective and learned axes. Different marginalizations may occupy overlapping, oblique subspaces; the method does not impose or recover a manifold, nonlinear metric, topology or Riemannian geometry.
The encoder and decoder for one component need not point along the same feature-space axis, and decoders from different marginalizations need not be orthogonal. A two-dimensional plot combines selected linear readouts; its visual separation is not a coordinate-free geometric fact.



dPCA is supervised because experimentally supplied labels determine \(X_\phi\) and therefore enter the training loss. Time bins also act as indexed design levels. The method may be unsupervised with respect to a later behavioral outcome only if that outcome was not used in labels, preprocessing, hyperparameter tuning or component selection.
Label correlation and deterministic relations among labels can make marginal effects inseparable or change their interpretation. For example, if a decision is nearly determined by a stimulus, assigning variance separately to stimulus and decision depends on the sampled error trials, coding, balancing and interaction convention. Supervision must not be hidden behind the term “dimensionality reduction.”



The canonical condition-mean objective decomposes into one regularized reduced-rank regression per marginalization. Each can be solved using a stable ridge-regression system and singular value decomposition. This is a deterministic fit rather than posterior inference and does not estimate trial-level noise covariance.
The ridge parameter \(\lambda\) and, when tuned, ranks \(q_\phi\) must be selected using training data only. Kobak et al. used held-out trials to form test pseudo-trials and selected regularization through repeated cross-validation; this supports the principle of trial-level separation, not one universally valid split or parameter grid (Kobak et al. 2016). The reduced-rank objective balances marginal reconstruction with compactness.

Correlated labels: stimulus, choice, reward and outcome may not be separately estimable under the experimental design.
Interaction reassignment: grouping time interactions with main task effects can produce a preferred narrative by construction.
Trial averaging: weak, heterogeneous or trial-specific structure may disappear, while smoothed means can look more reliable than single-trial readouts are.
Pseudo-populations: combining sequentially recorded units prevents estimation of simultaneous noise correlations and may overstate population-level availability.
Overlapping marginal subspaces: no linear axes may cleanly separate the selected effects; forced labeling of components does not repair overlap.
Overfitting: high feature count, few trials, many labels and flexible component selection can fit sampling noise.
Leakage: computing condition means, smoothing parameters, scaling, ranks, regularization or preferred components with held-out trials produces optimistic results.
Scale sensitivity: high-variance neurons or features dominate Frobenius loss unless scaling is scientifically justified.
Nonlinear structure: label dependence may not be representable through low-rank linear readouts.
Outliers and artifacts: variance-based fitting can prioritize abnormal trials or units.
Instability: close singular values, weak marginal variance or small perturbations can rotate the learned subspace.
Interpretive reification: high demixing index or decoding accuracy can be mistaken for independent neural channels, anatomical modules or causes.




Only the low-rank product \(A_\phi=F_\phi D_\phi\) enters the reconstruction. Without normalization, for any invertible \(R\),
\[
F_\phi D_\phi
=
(F_\phi R)(R^{-1}D_\phi),
\]
so encoder and decoder factors are not separately identified. Choosing orthonormal encoder columns and ordering components selects a convention. Individual component signs remain arbitrary, and repeated singular values permit rotations within the corresponding fitted subspace.
Across marginalizations, axes are fitted separately and can be nonorthogonal. Correlated scores do not contradict the algorithm, and apparent visual separation does not establish statistical independence. Changing task coding, interaction grouping, cell weights, rank or regularization changes the estimand rather than revealing another view of one uniquely identified decomposition.
“Demixed” therefore means that a component concentrates variance from one declared marginalization under the fitted loss. It does not mean independent components, causal separation, unique neural modules, anatomical segregation, mechanistic variables or uniquely identified latent causes.




PCA: fit a rank-matched PCA using the same centered and scaled training matrix. PCA provides the strongest ordinary linear reconstruction baseline but ignores labels.
Marginal averages and contrasts: plot or quantify \(X_\phi\) directly without learning a projection. This tests whether the substantive conclusion was already visible in condition means.
Separate PCA per marginalization: fit PCA to each \(X_\phi\). This compresses marginal means but does not by itself provide decoder axes that isolate that marginalization when applied to full or single-trial data.
Simple label decoding: fit a prespecified linear classifier or regressor to raw features or PCA scores. Decoding tests predictability of labels; it does not preserve the geometry or reconstruct the population activity and is not equivalent to demixing.
Mean-only reconstruction: reconstruct each feature by its training mean as a basic error reference.

A dPCA analysis should report whether it improves held-out marginal reconstruction or a separately declared scientific criterion, not merely whether its components look cleaner than PCA.



A leakage-safe evaluation should include:

Trial-level splitting: hold out complete trials, sessions, animals or other independent units as appropriate. Do not split adjacent time bins from the same trial across folds.
Training-only preprocessing: compute centering, scaling, smoothing choices, condition means, marginalizations, interaction groupings, regularization, ranks and component ordering without test observations.
Held-out marginal reconstruction: rebuild held-out pseudo-trials or held-out condition means from independent test trials, then evaluate \[
\left\lVert X^{\mathrm{test}}_\phi-
F^{\mathrm{train}}_\phi D^{\mathrm{train}}_\phi
X^{\mathrm{test}}\right\rVert_F^2
\] with the training definitions applied to those held-out condition estimates. This tests transfer of the mean-based map; it is not a trial-noise likelihood.
Variance accounting: report total and marginal variance, combined reconstruction error, and the contribution of discarded or residual terms. Do not add overlapping nonorthogonal component contributions as though they were independent.
Demixing diagnostics: report the full vector \(v_\phi(d)\) or a confusion matrix, not only the largest marginal label.
Stability: compare subspaces and held-out conclusions across trial resamples, sessions, plausible ranks, regularization values and interaction groupings, using sign/subspace alignment fitted only where appropriate.
Baselines: compare rank-matched PCA, raw marginal averages, separate marginal PCA and simple leakage-safe label decoding.
Nulls: shuffle labels at the independent-trial or experimental-unit level while preserving the declared balance structure.

If decoding is reported, the decoder/component selection and classifier must be refitted inside every training fold. Successful decoding establishes label information under that protocol, not independent representation, causal role or mechanism.



A future non-executable toy model should generate balanced trials for time \(t\), binary stimulus \(s\in\{-1,+1\}\) and binary decision \(d\in\{-1,+1\}\):
\[
x(t,s,d,k)
=
a f_0(t)
+b\,s f_s(t)
+c\,d f_d(t)
+e\,sd f_{sd}(t)
+\varepsilon_k(t),
\]

Evaluation should measure held-out marginal reconstruction, component marginal-variance profiles, subspace recovery up to sign/rotation, and label decoding as a separate criterion.
Two negative controls are required: make \(b\) and \(c\) nearly collinear to demonstrate nonseparable marginal subspaces, and remove or severely unbalance one \((s,d)\) cell to demonstrate confounding and marginalization failure. A label-shuffle null should remove systematic task dependence. This contract creates no code, data or result in this Method Object.



dPCA is LDG’s canonical supervised linear decomposition for separating declared task-variable contributions from ordinary variance maximization. It provides a controlled example of how labels, averaging, loss and experimental design define a representation—and why a useful representation must not be promoted into an independent latent generator or mechanism.






WarningWhat this does NOT imply



A component labeled “stimulus,” “decision,” “reward,” or “time” is label- and loss-dependent. dPCA does not establish statistical independence, causal separation, anatomical segregation, unique neural modules, a latent state, physical dynamics or mechanism. High explained variance, demixing index or decoding accuracy does not strengthen those claims automatically.




No modality-specific empirical claim is retained. Behavioral factors, trial alignment and repeated measurements would have to define a balanced supervised tensor; components would remain label-dependent linear summaries rather than behavioral causes or dynamics.



No modality-specific empirical claim is retained. Event labels, gaze targets and time alignment can supervise a decomposition, but a target-associated component would not identify an oculomotor module or transition law.



No modality-specific empirical claim is retained. Rereferencing, channel scaling, subject/session structure and trial balance would determine the fitted marginalizations; sensor components would not automatically be neural sources.



Kobak et al. introduced the canonical reduced-rank dPCA formulation and reanalyzed four neural population datasets spanning different species, recorded regions and tasks (Kobak et al. 2016). This is primary evidence that the method can summarize those specific trial-structured datasets. It does not establish universal demixed organization, anatomical modules or causal mechanisms in neural populations, and it does not directly validate MEG applications.





Machens develops marginalized covariance constructions for separating declared task-parameter variance and explicitly discusses overlap, nonseparability and the distinction from independent-component assumptions (Machens 2010).
Brendel, Romo and Machens introduce the earlier probabilistic dPCA formulation, including factorial marginalizations and interaction terms (Brendel et al. 2011).
Kobak et al. introduce the canonical encoder/decoder reduced-rank reconstruction objective, regularization, balancing treatment, cross-validation and neural applications used in this object (Kobak et al. 2016).





Izenman provides an inspected authoritative treatment of multivariate reduced-rank regression, rank-constrained coefficient matrices and weighted least-squares formulations (Izenman 2008, chap. 6).

Which weighting estimand is appropriate when condition frequencies are scientifically meaningful but highly unequal?
How should uncertainty in condition means and marginal subspaces be propagated to component plots?
When should interactions remain separate instead of being grouped with time-dependent main effects?

Which conclusions remain stable under alternative label codings, ranks and regularization?

title: Demixed Principal Component Analysis
text:
Demixed principal component analysis (dPCA) constructs supervised linear coordinates that approximately reconstruct declared task-variable marginalizations of multivariate data. It was developed for trial-structured neural population recordings in which activity varies with time and experimentally labeled conditions, while individual variables and ordinary principal components often mix several task dependencies (Brendel et al. 2011; Kobak et al. 2016).
The word demixed names success under a particular label decomposition and reconstruction loss. It does not mean that the resulting components are statistically independent, causally separated, uniquely identified, anatomically localized, or generated by distinct neural modules. The method is a label-dependent linear summary, not blind source separation or a mechanistic model. The bounded formulation here follows the published 2016 analysis of trial-averaged condition means; it is not a trial-level noise-covariance model (Kobak et al. 2016).

title: Demixed Principal Component Analysis
Demixed Principal Component Analysis
text:
For each declared marginalization group \(\phi\), dPCA returns:

a target matrix \(X_\phi\) with the same shape as \(X\);
a decoder matrix \(D_\phi\in\mathbb R^{q_\phi\times N}\) whose rows define linear projection axes;
an encoder matrix \(F_\phi\in\mathbb R^{N\times q_\phi}\) used to reconstruct the corresponding marginalization;
component scores \(Z_\phi=D_\phi X\); and
an approximate marginal reconstruction \(\widehat X_\phi=F_\phi D_\phi X\).

The combined approximation is
\[
\widehat X=\sum_\phi F_\phi D_\phi X.
\]
Components belonging to different marginalizations are not generally orthogonal, and their scores need not be uncorrelated. The output is deterministic given the fitted data and choices; it is not a posterior distribution over latent variables.

title: Demixed Principal Component Analysis
text:
Ordinary PCA chooses one orthogonal subspace to reconstruct all centered variance without using labels. dPCA first decomposes the balanced condition tensor into ANOVA-style marginalizations associated with time, task-variable main effects and interactions. It then solves a separate regularized reduced-rank regression for each marginalization: the full data are projected through a decoder, but the reconstruction target is only the selected label-dependent part of the data (Kobak et al. 2016).
This separates two roles that coincide in ordinary PCA. Decoder rows define low-dimensional readouts \(D_\phi X\); encoder columns map those readouts back toward \(X_\phi\). Allowing encoder and decoder axes to differ avoids forcing all task-associated subspaces to be mutually orthogonal.

\[

=

-
\sum_{R\subsetneq S}X_R.
\]

\[

+
\lambda

\[

\qquad

\]

\[

\]

\[

Two negative controls are required: make \(b\) and \(c\) nearly collinear to demonstrate nonseparable marginal subspaces, and remove or severely unbalance one \((s,d)\) cell to demonstrate confounding and marginalization failure. A label-shuffle null should remove systematic task dependence. This contract creates no code, data or result in this Method Object.

title: Demixed Principal Component Analysis
text:
dPCA is LDG’s canonical supervised linear decomposition for separating declared task-variable contributions from ordinary variance maximization. It provides a controlled example of how labels, averaging, loss and experimental design define a representation—and why a useful representation must not be promoted into an independent latent generator or mechanism.






WarningWhat this does NOT imply



A component labeled “stimulus,” “decision,” “reward,” or “time” is label- and loss-dependent. dPCA does not establish statistical independence, causal separation, anatomical segregation, unique neural modules, a latent state, physical dynamics or mechanism. High explained variance, demixing index or decoding accuracy does not strengthen those claims automatically.




No modality-specific empirical claim is retained. Behavioral factors, trial alignment and repeated measurements would have to define a balanced supervised tensor; components would remain label-dependent linear summaries rather than behavioral causes or dynamics.



No modality-specific empirical claim is retained. Event labels, gaze targets and time alignment can supervise a decomposition, but a target-associated component would not identify an oculomotor module or transition law.



No modality-specific empirical claim is retained. Rereferencing, channel scaling, subject/session structure and trial balance would determine the fitted marginalizations; sensor components would not automatically be neural sources.



Kobak et al. introduced the canonical reduced-rank dPCA formulation and reanalyzed four neural population datasets spanning different species, recorded regions and tasks (Kobak et al. 2016). This is primary evidence that the method can summarize those specific trial-structured datasets. It does not establish universal demixed organization, anatomical modules or causal mechanisms in neural populations, and it does not directly validate MEG applications.
