title: Vector Field
text:
In a Euclidean continuous-time setting, a vector field is a rule that assigns each admissible state an instantaneous change vector, encoding a rate and, when nonzero, a direction.



A state space specifies which state values are admissible, but not how they change. A vector field adds a local evolution rule: at each state, it gives the velocity that a compatible continuous-time trajectory would have there. This makes it possible to distinguish a rule defined across the state space from one realized trajectory or a finite collection of observations.
For an autonomous differential equation, Teschl treats \(\dot{x}=f(x)\) as a vector field and describes its solution curves as tangent to that field at every visited state (Teschl 2012, sec. 6.2). The field is therefore local and instantaneous; finite-time evolution is a different object.



Picture an arrow attached to every admissible state. The arrow at state \(x\) answers a local question: “If the system is at \(x\) under this rule, in what direction and at what instantaneous rate is its state changing?”
One arrow is a vector. The assignment of arrows across the state space is the vector field. Following the arrows over time can produce a trajectory when the evolution is well-defined, but neither a single arrow nor a plotted collection of arrows is itself a trajectory or a complete finite-time evolution.
The arrow is also not a finite jump to the next state. It has rate units—state units per unit time—and describes change at an instant. Over a sufficiently short interval it may support a local approximation, but the system can encounter different arrows as its state changes.



For this Cycle’s core formulation, assume the state space \(\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is open. This is a deliberate scope restriction. For a constrained admissible set, a Euclidean rule can instead be defined on an open neighborhood containing that set, but whether the resulting motion remains admissible requires additional conditions deferred below. On the declared open domain, an autonomous vector field is a map
\[
f:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^n,
\qquad x\mapsto f(x),
\]
where \(f(x)\) is the instantaneous state-change vector assigned at \(x\). A differentiable trajectory \(x(t)\) is compatible with the field when
\[
\dot{x}(t)=f\bigl(x(t)\bigr)
\]
at the times under consideration. This equation states a local relation between the trajectory’s derivative and the field; it does not by itself guarantee that a trajectory exists uniquely or for all time.
The bare concept is the assignment \(x\mapsto f(x)\). Continuity, differentiability, local Lipschitz conditions, and other regularity assumptions are additional properties, not part of that bare assignment. Such assumptions become important when asking whether the field generates unique trajectories or a well-defined flow.


The stable First-Order Autonomous Dynamical System Math Object is the canonical location for the corresponding initial-value problem, regularity ladder, maximal-solution statements, and local-flow construction. Given an initial state \(x_0\) at reference time \(t_0\), it writes the field as the local rule in
\[
\dot{x}=f(x),
\qquad
x(t_0)=x_0.
\]
If the active assumptions give a unique finite-time evolution map \(\phi_\tau\) and the curve \(\tau\mapsto\phi_\tau(x)\) is differentiable at \(\tau=0\), the vector field is its elapsed-time generator:
\[
f(x)
=
\left.\frac{d}{d\tau}\phi_\tau(x)\right|_{\tau=0}.
\]
This relation connects the instantaneous and finite-time descriptions without identifying them. The derivative is taken with respect to elapsed time along the evolution from \(x\); differentiable dependence on the initial state is a stronger property. Neither existence, uniqueness, global continuation, nor joint flow regularity follows from the bare assignment \(x\mapsto f(x)\). Those theorem-level conditions and derivations remain in the Math Object (Teschl 2012, secs. 2.2, 2.6, 6.2).
When explicit time or an external input matters, a model may use
\[
\dot{x}=f(x,u,t).
\]
For each specified input value and time, \(x\mapsto f(x,u,t)\) is a state-dependent velocity assignment; equivalently, the model supplies a family of vector fields indexed by \(u\) and \(t\). The input is not thereby part of the internal state, and its future values may be required to determine later evolution. Åström and Murray use the corresponding state/input separation in continuous-time system descriptions (Åström and Murray 2021, sec. 3.2).
Constrained state spaces with boundaries require separate checks that the assigned change is compatible with admissibility. Boundary conditions, tangent-cone or viability conditions, and vector fields on manifold-valued state spaces are deferred beyond this bounded object. LDG does not import that machinery into the Cycle 1 Euclidean formulation.





\(\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\): the open Euclidean state-space domain used in the core Cycle 1 formulation.
\(x\in\mathcal{X}\): one state value.
\(f\): the vector field, defined across its stated domain.
\(f(x)\in\mathbb{R}^n\): the instantaneous change vector assigned at \(x\).
\(x(t)\): a state trajectory.
\(\dot{x}(t)\): the instantaneous derivative of the trajectory.
\(u\): an optional external input.
\(t\): time; explicit appearance in \(f(x,u,t)\) indicates time-dependent local rules.

The same letter \(f\) is often used for other kinds of maps. Its domain, codomain, and role must therefore be stated.




State Space: supplies the admissible states on which the field is defined.

Assumed background: elementary vectors and single-variable derivatives.
State and Trajectory are related concepts: the field takes a state value as input, while a compatible trajectory has derivative prescribed by the field.
The First-Order Autonomous Dynamical System is the formal companion for existence, uniqueness, continuation, and local-flow results. It is linked as a related object rather than used to replace the conceptual definition here.










Concept
Distinction from vector field




Vector
A vector is one magnitude-and-direction value. A vector field assigns such a vector to every state in its declared domain.


State
A state value \(x\) describes the system at one time. The field value \(f(x)\) describes the instantaneous change assigned at that state; it is not another state value.


Trajectory
A trajectory is one time-parameterized admissible evolution \(x(t)\). A vector field is the local rule defined across states; a compatible differentiable trajectory satisfies \(\dot{x}(t)=f(x(t))\).


Finite displacement
A displacement such as \(x(t+\Delta t)-x(t)\) compares two states over a finite interval. The field value is an instantaneous rate, not that displacement and not generally equal to it.


External input
An input \(u\) is an influence treated as outside the state. It may select or modify the assigned vector through \(f(x,u,t)\) but is not the vector field’s output or automatically a state variable.


Discrete-time update map
An update map sends a current state directly to a later state, for example \(x_{k+1}=F(x_k)\). A vector field assigns an instantaneous rate in continuous time. One formalism should not be silently substituted for the other.


Flow
A flow, where defined, maps initial states across finite elapsed times. The vector field supplies the local instantaneous rule from which such finite-time evolution may be generated.


Fitted velocity field
A fitted field is an estimate constructed from data under modeling and smoothing choices. It may approximate a proposed vector field, but estimation is not part of the definition.






Calling \(f\) a vector field does not by itself imply that:

observed trajectories uniquely determine \(f\) away from, or even along, the sampled states;
a fitted local velocity field is the true physical or biological mechanism;
time-varying data or arrows drawn on a plot establish vector-field structure;
finite differences are exact instantaneous derivatives;
every state in \(\mathcal{X}\) has been observed;
a compatible trajectory exists uniquely or indefinitely from every state;
the field is autonomous, smooth, linear, low-dimensional, or noise-free;
a continuous-time vector field is the natural description of a discrete-time system; or
knowing the local rule automatically supplies its full finite-time evolution.




For an idealized dimensionless pendulum, treat the angle \(\theta\) as an unwrapped real-valued coordinate in this Euclidean example and use the state
\[
x=(\theta,\omega),
\]
where \(\omega\) is angular velocity. On the resulting open coordinate domain \(\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}^2\), consider
\[
f(\theta,\omega)=\bigl(\omega,-\sin\theta\bigr).
\]
At the state \((\theta,\omega)\), the first component says that angle changes instantaneously at rate \(\omega\); the second says that angular velocity changes instantaneously at rate \(-\sin\theta\). Teschl uses this pendulum field as an example of the autonomous vector-field viewpoint (Teschl 2012, sec. 6.2).
The vector \(f(\theta,\omega)\) is one local rate at one state. The vector field is the entire assignment over admissible angle–velocity states. It does not directly give the finite displacement after one second, because the assigned vector generally changes as the pendulum state changes.



Using the population-coordinate convention reviewed by Cunningham and Yu, a proposed neural state can be represented by a vector of population activity at a time (Cunningham and Yu 2014). A neural vector-field model would assign an instantaneous activity-change vector to each admissible population state. The recorded population vectors and their finite differences are observations or estimates; they are not automatically the underlying field.
The same distinction applies to behavior. Local velocity estimates computed from position, pose, or other behavioral variables constitute a vector field only relative to an adequate state description and a continuous-time modeling assumption. Sparse sampling, omitted state variables, input changes, and measurement noise can make different fields consistent with the available trajectories.



Vector fields provide the local-rule layer connecting state-space descriptions to continuous-time dynamics. LDG needs this distinction to ask whether a proposed latent, neural, or behavioral evolution law is supported by data without confusing sampled trajectories, plotted arrows, and mechanism. The concept also prepares the local-versus-finite-time distinction needed for Flow while leaving estimation methods and formal existence theory to later work.




What observations are sufficient to constrain a vector field beyond the sampled trajectories?
How should LDG separate changes in the field from changes in external input or unmeasured state?
When is a continuous-time vector-field description preferable to a discrete-time update rule for sampled data?

These are later modeling and inference questions, not part of this bounded definition.




Vector fields, compatible trajectories, and the pendulum example: (Teschl 2012, sec. 6.2).
State/input-dependent rate notation: (Åström and Murray 2021, sec. 3.2).
Neural population-coordinate convention: (Cunningham and Yu 2014).

Distinguishes vector, state, trajectory, displacement, input, update map, and flow.
States the local derivative relation without claiming universal existence or uniqueness.
Includes explicit inference and visualization non-implications.
Defers constrained-boundary and manifold-valued formulations while using canonical existing relationships.
Has received lightweight conceptual review and incorporated the required L1 corrections.
Links the instantaneous vector-field definition to the stable autonomous-system Math Object without duplicating its theorem-level derivations.

title: Torus
text:
The two-dimensional torus \(T^2\) is the product \(S^1\times S^1\), equivalently a plane with two independent periodic directions.



The torus models systems with two circular variables, such as two phases or two periodic coordinates. Its intrinsic topology is not tied to the familiar doughnut-shaped embedding in \(\mathbb R^3\).



Take a square and identify its left edge with its right edge and its bottom edge with its top edge. Moving off one side returns from the opposite side.



With the product topology and product smooth structure,
\[
T^2=S^1\times S^1
\cong
\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2,
\]
where \(\mathbb Z^2\) acts by coordinatewise integer translations. Quotient coordinates \((t_1,t_2)\pmod{\mathbb Z^2}\) are measured in turns; radian coordinates satisfy \(\theta_i=2\pi t_i\).
It is a compact two-dimensional smooth manifold. The quotient-square, product-of-circles, and embedded doughnut are representations of the same standard topological type under suitable maps.




\(T^2\): two-torus.
\((\theta_1,\theta_2)\): two periodic coordinates.
\(\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2\): quotient representation.




Circle / S¹ supplies each periodic factor. Topology supplies product and quotient constructions.










Concept
Distinction




Doughnut surface
One embedding of a torus; the topology does not require that geometry.


Two-dimensional plane
Locally similar but globally lacks the torus’s periodic identifications.


Limit cycle
One periodic orbit has circle topology; a torus can support two independent phases or quasiperiodic motion.


Product space
The torus is a particular product of two circles.






A toroidal latent claim does not imply a doughnut-shaped point cloud, a flat metric, two identifiable biological oscillators, dense sampling, quasiperiodic dynamics, or a unique embedding.



Two independent clock phases \((\theta_1,\theta_2)\), each taken modulo \(2\pi\), define a point on \(T^2\). Equivalently, \((t_1,t_2)=(\theta_1/2\pi,\theta_2/2\pi)\) is taken modulo \(\mathbb Z^2\). Returning either phase by one full turn leaves the torus point unchanged.



Joint head-direction and rhythmic-phase variables, or two coupled periodic task variables, may motivate toroidal models. Such topology must be compared with simpler circular, planar, and disconnected alternatives.



Torus extends the topology branch from one periodic coordinate to product topology and prepares careful discussion of multi-phase latent structure.




What sampling is required to distinguish a torus from a curved sheet?
How robust are two-hole signatures to noise and missing states?
When does toroidal topology improve prediction?





Sutherland provides the inspected product and quotient topology constructions (Sutherland 2024).
Mrowka’s manifold notes provide product and torus context (Mrowka 2004).





Defines \(T^2\) as a product and quotient.
Separates intrinsic topology from a doughnut embedding.
States empirical and dynamical non-implications.

title: Tangent Space
text:
The tangent space \(T_pM\) is the vector space of first-order directions available on a smooth manifold \(M\) at a point \(p\).



The tangent space is the local linear arena for velocities, derivatives, vector fields, and Riemannian inner products. It approximates first-order behavior at one point; it is not the manifold itself.



At a point on a sphere, the tangent plane contains the instantaneous directions in which a curve on the sphere can move. The sphere leaves that plane at second order.



Let \(M\) be a smooth \(n\)-manifold and \(p\in M\).


Consider smooth curves \(\gamma:(-\epsilon,\epsilon)\to M\) with \(\gamma(0)=p\). Two curves are tangent-equivalent at \(p\) when, in one—and therefore every—chart \((U,x)\) containing \(p\),
\[
\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{0}x(\gamma_1(t))
=
\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{0}x(\gamma_2(t)).
\]
A tangent vector is an equivalence class \([\gamma]\), and the tangent space \(T_pM\) is the set of such classes with vector-space operations induced in coordinates. Mrowka gives the equivalent chart-representative construction (Mrowka 2004, sec. 7.2).



Equivalently, a tangent vector at \(p\) is a linear map
\[
v:C^\infty_p(M)\to\mathbb R
\]
on germs of smooth functions satisfying the Leibniz rule
\[
v(fg)=f(p)v(g)+g(p)v(f).
\]
For a curve representative,
\[
v(f)
=
\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{0}f(\gamma(t)).
\]
The curve-velocity and derivation descriptions define canonically isomorphic tangent spaces (Lee 1997, ch. 2). This Concept states the equivalence but defers its proof.



A chart \(x=(x^1,\ldots,x^n)\) supplies the coordinate basis
\[
\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x^1}\right|_p,
\ldots,
\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x^n}\right|_p,
\]
so every \(v\in T_pM\) has components
\[
v
=
v^i\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\right|_p.
\]
Thus \(\dim T_pM=n\). Under another chart \(y=(y^1,\ldots,y^n)\),
\[
v'^a
=
\frac{\partial y^a}{\partial x^i}(p)v^i,
\]
and
\[
\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\right|_p
=
\frac{\partial y^a}{\partial x^i}(p)
\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial y^a}\right|_p.
\]
The components change, while the intrinsic tangent vector does not.



For a smooth map \(f:M\to N\), the differential at \(p\) is the linear map
\[
df_p:T_pM\to T_{f(p)}N.
\]
Using curve representatives,
\[
df_p([\gamma])=[f\circ\gamma].
\]
Using derivations,
\[
(df_pv)(g)=v(g\circ f).
\]
In charts, the matrix of \(df_p\) is the Jacobian \([\partial f^a/\partial x^i]_p\) (Mrowka 2004, sec. 7.2).



If \(i:M\hookrightarrow\widetilde M\) is a smooth embedding, \(di_p\) identifies \(T_pM\) with a linear subspace of \(T_{i(p)}\widetilde M\). For an embedded manifold in \(\mathbb R^D\), this gives the familiar ambient tangent plane. This represented subspace depends on the embedding, whereas the abstract \(T_pM\) is intrinsic. An arbitrary ambient subspace fitted to data is not automatically the image of an intrinsic tangent space.



The tangent bundle is the disjoint union
\[
TM=\bigsqcup_{p\in M}T_pM
\]
with its compatible smooth bundle structure. A smooth vector field is a smooth section \(X:M\to TM\) satisfying \(X(p)\in T_pM\). Bundle construction proofs and connection theory are deferred.





\(T_pM\): tangent space at \(p\).
\(v\in T_pM\): tangent vector.
\([\gamma]\): equivalence class of curves through \(p\).
\(v(f)\): derivation of a smooth function germ.
\(\partial/\partial x^i|_p\): chart-induced tangent basis.
\(v^i\): tangent-vector components in a chart.
\(df_p:T_pM\to T_{f(p)}N\): differential/pushforward of a smooth map.
\(TM=\bigsqcup_{p\in M}T_pM\): tangent bundle.




Manifold supplies charts and smooth curves. Linear Subspace supplies vector-space language.










Concept
Distinction




Manifold
The nonlinear space of points; \(T_pM\) is one attached local vector space.


Ambient space
An embedding differential represents \(T_pM\) as a subspace of the ambient tangent space; the intrinsic tangent space is not defined by ambient coordinates alone.


Differential / Jacobian
\(df_p\) maps tangent vectors between manifolds. A coordinate Jacobian is its matrix representation, not the intrinsic map itself.


Tangent bundle
The smoothly organized union of all tangent spaces; it is not one vector space because fibers at different points are distinct.


Vector field
Assigns one tangent vector to each point, rather than describing one tangent space.


Local PCA plane
A statistical estimate that may approximate a tangent space under additional sampling and noise assumptions.






A tangent space does not imply global flatness, a canonical identification between different points, a unique ambient orientation, a metric or inner product, accurate estimation from sparse samples, validity far from \(p\), or that local linear dynamics extend globally.



For \(S^1\subset\mathbb R^2\) and \(p=(1,0)\),
\[
T_pS^1=\{(0,a):a\in\mathbb R\}.
\]
This vertical line captures instantaneous motion at \(p\) but not the whole circle.



Local tangent estimates can describe directions of neural or behavioral variation near a state. Their interpretation depends on neighborhood scale and should be compared with simpler local-linear null models.



At L2, Tangent Space connects intrinsic curve/derivation definitions, coordinate representations, differentials, embedded subspaces, vector fields, and later Riemannian geometry without treating local linearization as global structure.




How many samples are needed for reliable tangent estimation?
How should uncertainty in \(T_pM\) propagate to dynamics?
When do tangent estimates vary smoothly across conditions?

Lee provides the inspected curve/derivation equivalence, embedded-submanifold tangent representation, and tangent-bundle context (Lee 1997, ch. 2).
Bundle proofs, connections, and statistical tangent-estimation algorithms are intentionally deferred.

title: State Space
text:
A state space is the set of all state values admitted by a specified state description of a specified system.



A state description says what information is carried forward; a state space says which realized values of that description are possible or allowed. This distinction is necessary before asking how a system changes: evolution moves among admissible state values, not among alternative variable lists.
The state space also fixes the domain in which later claims are interpreted. It determines what counts as one state, which combinations of values are allowed, and which system boundary and resolution are being represented. Terman and Izhikevich give the standard formulation that a state space is the set of possible states, with each state represented as a point (Terman and Izhikevich 2008).



First choose a state description. For an idealized pendulum, that description might contain angle and angular velocity. Then imagine every admissible assignment of those two quantities. Each assignment is one state value, and the collection of all such values is the state space.
This collection is broader than the states observed in one experiment. A recording may visit only a small subset, and finite data contain only sampled measurements. Conversely, not every arbitrary combination of coordinate values need be admissible: physical constraints, logical constraints, or the declared model boundary may exclude some combinations.
A state space is therefore relative to:

the system boundary — which entities and influences are inside the system;
the state description — which future-relevant variables are retained;
the resolution and admissibility constraints — which distinctions and combinations the model treats as meaningful.

A coordinate convention is a separate representational choice. It assigns numerical coordinates to state values in the abstract state space. Different coordinate systems can represent the same underlying state information without changing which abstract states are admissible.



Let a state description specify the structure of a system’s state values and let the declared constraints determine which values are admissible. The state space may be written
\[
\mathcal{X} = \{x : x \text{ is an admissible state value under the specified description and constraints}\}.
\]
When state values are represented by \(n\) coordinates, one may write \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\). The coordinate tuple is a numerical representation of a state value; it is not the abstract state value or state space by itself. Different coordinate systems may represent the same underlying state values, while admissibility constraints determine which represented values belong to \(\mathcal{X}\).
The definition requires a set of possible state values but does not require a particular equation of motion, distance, or visualization. No dimension need yet be specified or justified at L1. In Teschl’s abstract mathematical formulation, an evolution acts on a set denoted \(M\) (Teschl 2012, sec. 6.1); in LDG notation, that set is \(\mathcal{X}\) once its points have been assigned the role of admissible state values.




\(\mathcal{X}\): the state space.
\(x\in\mathcal{X}\): one admissible state value.
\(x(t)\in\mathcal{X}\): the state value assigned at time \(t\).
\(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\): a coordinate representation when the description uses \(n\) coordinates.

A matrix whose rows are recorded samples is not denoted \(\mathcal{X}\) here: it is a dataset drawn from, projected from, or otherwise related to the proposed state space.




State: distinguishes a state description, state value, and state vector.

Assumed background: elementary sets and vector notation.










Concept
Relationship to state space




State description
Specifies what variables or structure constitute a state. The state space contains the admissible values under that description.


State value
One member \(x\in\mathcal{X}\) of the state space. The space is not itself a single state.


State vector / coordinates
A numerical representation of one state value. Coordinate choices do not define the abstract state space and do not by themselves determine which values are admissible. Different coordinates may represent the same underlying state information.


Observation space or measurement range
Contains possible sensor outputs or measured values. It can coincide with the state space under an ideal direct measurement, but it is generally distinct when observations are partial, noisy, or indirect.


Dataset or data matrix
Contains finitely many recorded values. It samples or represents observed data; it is not automatically the set of all admissible states.


Trajectory
A time-parameterized admissible evolution through state values in the state space. The space contains possible states; a trajectory records one system evolution through them.


Parameter space
Contains alternative parameter values indexing models or evolution rules. Parameters and states have different modeling roles even when both are represented by vectors.


Latent space
A coordinate domain introduced for unobserved or inferred variables. It is a state space only if its values are assigned an adequate state role for the specified evolution.


Phase space
Often used as a synonym for state space in dynamical-systems contexts. Usage varies by field, so LDG requires the intended state description and admissible values to be stated rather than relying on the label alone.






Calling a set a state space does not by itself imply that:

every admissible state has been observed or can be observed;
recorded samples cover the space densely or without bias;
every coordinate is a direct measurement;
the space is identical to a data matrix, point cloud, or plotted projection;
all coordinate combinations are admissible;
the representation is unique, minimal, low-dimensional, or Euclidean;
a particular distance, geometry, or neighborhood relation has been justified;
a rule of evolution, trajectory, or causal mechanism has been identified; or
the model-defined space is the complete physical state space of the real system.




For the pendulum description
\[
x=(\text{angle},\;\text{angular velocity}),
\]
one state value is one particular pendulum condition specified by angle and angular velocity. The abstract state space is the set of all such conditions admitted by the chosen pendulum description and its physical assumptions.
Choosing radians rather than degrees, selecting an angular-velocity unit, or using another equivalent numerical encoding changes the coordinate representation, not the underlying set of admissible pendulum states.
A table containing 1,000 camera samples is not that state space. It is a finite collection of observations. Even if angle and angular velocity are estimated from every frame, the resulting 1,000 state estimates show only the values sampled during that recording, not all admissible pendulum states.



For \(D\) recorded neurons, population activity is often represented by \(D\) firing-rate coordinates; each time point is then a point in the corresponding population-coordinate domain (Cunningham and Yu 2014). The finite set of recorded population vectors is data, not automatically the full neural state space. Calling the coordinate domain a neural state space additionally commits the analysis to treating those population variables as a state description for a declared system and time scale.
Likewise, a pose-estimation matrix or collection of behavioral features is not automatically a behavioral state space. The proposed space must specify which feature combinations are admissible and why the features constitute state rather than partial observations. A lower-dimensional latent representation remains model- and criterion-dependent; its visualization alone does not establish a unique underlying state space.



LDG will repeatedly compare recorded variables, latent coordinates, and proposed dynamical descriptions. State-space language keeps three objects separate: the state description, the set of admissible state values, and the finite data used to study them. This separation is required before trajectories or initial conditions can be defined consistently and before later work can make defensible claims about latent structure.




What empirical evidence would show that a proposed state space excludes state values needed for prediction?
Which apparent constraints reflect the system and which reflect sampling or measurement limits?
When two coordinate systems represent the same future-relevant information, what makes one scientifically preferable?

These are model- and dataset-specific follow-ups, not reasons to enlarge the L1 definition.




General state-space definition and pendulum example: (Terman and Izhikevich 2008).
Abstract set acted on by a dynamical system: (Teschl 2012, sec. 6.1).
Neural population-coordinate usage: (Cunningham and Yu 2014).

Distinguishes descriptions, values, vectors, observations, and datasets.
Separates the abstract set of admissible states from its coordinate representations.
Includes non-implications and a minimal example without importing later formalism.

title: Stability
text:
Stability describes whether specified small perturbations of a dynamical object produce evolutions that remain close under a declared time direction and notion of closeness.



“Stable” is incomplete unless the object, perturbation, time horizon, and comparison criterion are stated. At this stage LDG focuses on forward Lyapunov stability of a fixed point and distinguishes it from asymptotic return.



Balance a ball in a bowl and nudge it slightly. If it stays near the bottom, the equilibrium is stable. If it also returns toward the bottom, it is asymptotically stable. A ball balanced on a hilltop is a fixed point but not stable.



Let \(x^\ast\) be a fixed point of a forward evolution on a state space \(\mathcal X\). In neighborhood form, \(x^\ast\) is Lyapunov stable when, for every neighborhood \(U\) of \(x^\ast\), there exists a neighborhood \(V\subseteq U\) such that every trajectory starting in \(V\) is supported for all \(t\ge0\) and remains in \(U\) for all \(t\ge0\).
On a metric state space \((\mathcal X,d)\) this becomes
\[
\forall\varepsilon>0\;\exists\delta>0\;\forall x_0\in\mathcal X:
\quad

\[

\le

\qquad t\ge0.
\]

The bounded definitions perturb the initial state while holding the evolution rule, parameters, inputs, state description, and metric fixed. Concept
Distinction




Fixed point
Fixedness concerns the unperturbed state; stability concerns nearby initial states.


Attraction

title: Process Noise
text:
Process noise is stochastic variability or unresolved disturbance entering the state-transition model and therefore changing the latent state trajectory.



Process noise represents uncertainty in evolution, not merely uncertainty in measurement. It changes predictions for future state even if observations were perfect.



Two systems starting from the same state can diverge because the transition itself receives different disturbances.



In a probabilistic state-space model, process noise is the stochasticity in the transition kernel
\[
Q_k(x,u,A)
=
\Pr(X_{k+1}\in A\mid X_k=x,u_k=u).
\]
It changes the conditional distribution of the next state even when the present state and declared input are fixed. A deterministic transition is the special case in which \(Q_k\) is a Dirac measure.


A common representation is
\[
X_{k+1}=F_k(X_k,u_k;\theta_x)+w_k,
\]
with a conditional disturbance law
\[
w_k\mid X_k=x,u_k=u
\sim
p_w(\,\cdot\mid x,u,k).
\]
When the required moments are finite, define the conditional mean and covariance
\[
m_k(x,u)=\mathbb E[w_k\mid x,u],
\]
\[
\Sigma^w_k(x,u)
=
\mathbb E\left[
(w_k-m_k)(w_k-m_k)^\top
\mid x,u
\right].
\]
Using \(m_k=0\) and a constant matrix \(\Sigma^w_k(x,u)=Q\) states that the first two conditional moments are zero and constant across state, input, and time. It does not make the full conditional law state independent or time homogeneous; higher moments or distributional shape may still vary. Kalman’s primary formulation uses independent zero-mean Gaussian random excitation with a specified covariance as one important special case (Kalman 1960).



The following properties are distinct and must be stated separately:

Gaussian: each declared joint distribution is Gaussian.
White/uncorrelated across time: cross-time covariance vanishes for unequal times.
Independent across time: the random vectors are probabilistically independent, which is stronger than uncorrelatedness outside the Gaussian case.
Identically distributed: the conditional law does not change with \(k\).
iid across time: combines independence across time with identical distribution.
Uncorrelated components: off-diagonal covariance entries vanish.
Independent components: the joint law factorizes across components; zero off-diagonal covariance does not imply this outside a suitable jointly Gaussian assumption.
Independent of state, input, parameters, and initial condition: a separate collection of assumptions, not implied by the label process noise.

Colored process noise has temporal dependence. Cross-component covariance allows coordinated disturbances across state variables. Both can be scientifically meaningful rather than defects.



Additive state-independent noise is not the general case. A model may use
\[
X_{k+1}
=
F_k(X_k,u_k)
+
L_k(X_k,u_k)\,\varepsilon_k,
\]
where the disturbance amplitude or orientation depends on state or input. If
\[
\mathbb E[\varepsilon_k\mid x,u]=0,
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_k\mid x,u)=\Sigma_\varepsilon,
\]
then the resulting conditional transition covariance is
\[
\Sigma^w_k(x,u)=L_k(x,u)\,\Sigma_\varepsilon\,L_k(x,u)^\top.
\]
Independence of \(\varepsilon_k\) from \((x,u)\) is sufficient for these conditional assumptions but is not necessary.



A continuous-time diffusion may be written schematically as
\[
dX_t=f(t,X_t,u_t)\,dt+L(t,X_t,u_t)\,dW_t.
\]
The Brownian increment \(dW_t\) and diffusion matrix \(L\) define continuous-time stochastic forcing. They are not ordinary finite-variance functions that can be substituted directly for a discrete \(w_k\). The exact SDE determines its transition law independently of any numerical integration scheme.
A numerical discrete approximation does depend on the scheme. For an Euler–Maruyama step with locally fixed \(L\),
\[
w_k\approx L(t_k,X_k,u_k)\sqrt{\Delta t}\,\xi_k,
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(w_k\mid X_k,u_k)\approx LL^\top\Delta t,
\]
with \(\xi_k\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\) under the stated approximation. SDE existence, stochastic calculus, exact transition laws, and discretization-error theory are outside this Concept.





\(Q_k(x,u,A)\): transition probability kernel.
\(w_k\): additive process-disturbance realization.
\(m_k(x,u)\): conditional process-noise mean.
\(\Sigma^w_k(x,u)\): conditional process-noise covariance matrix, distinct from the transition kernel \(Q_k(x,u,A)\).
\(L_k(x,u)\): state/input-dependent disturbance loading.
\(W_t\): Brownian motion in a continuous-time diffusion model.
\(F_k\): deterministic part of the transition rule.




State-Space Model supplies the transition equation where process noise enters.










Concept
Distinction




Observation noise
Perturbs measurements conditional on state; process noise perturbs state evolution.


Input
A declared external argument or intervention under the chosen boundary. An unknown deterministic input is not automatically process noise.


Parameter uncertainty
Uncertainty about a fixed rule specification; it is not a new random transition disturbance unless the model is reformulated.


Model error
Broader structural misspecification that need not be adequately represented by any random transition kernel.


Residual
A discrepancy after fitting that can mix process noise, observation noise, unknown inputs, numerical error, and misspecification.


Initial-state uncertainty
Uncertainty at the starting time rather than new disturbance during transitions.






Process noise does not imply zero mean, independence, whiteness, identical distribution, Gaussianity, additivity, state independence, physical randomness, or that model misspecification has been solved. Increasing or tuning \(Q\) can absorb residual variation and improve predictive calibration without identifying its physical cause or proving that the variability is irreducibly stochastic.



For
\[
X_{k+1}=X_k+w_k,
\qquad
Y_k=X_k,
\]
the observations are perfect but the evolution is uncertain. If \(X_0\) is treated as fixed and \(w_k\sim\mathcal N(0,Q)\) are independent across time and independent of \(X_0\), then
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X_k\mid X_0)=kQ.
\]
Repeated runs from the same \(X_0\) therefore separate because transition uncertainty accumulates. Replacing the independent, identical-law assumption with positively correlated disturbances changes this growth law even when each one-step variance is still \(Q\).
For a multiplicative contrast, \(X_{k+1}=aX_k+\sigma X_k\varepsilon_k\) has state-dependent disturbance scale; it cannot be represented by one constant additive covariance without approximation.



Trial-to-trial latent variability may be modeled as process noise, variable initial state, unknown input, or model error. These explanations are not interchangeable and should be compared.



At L2, Process Noise locates stochasticity in the transition kernel and makes its conditional moments, dependence structure, and continuous/discrete interpretation explicit. It separates variability in latent evolution from measurement variability, unknown input, initial uncertainty, and model error.

How can process noise be distinguished from initial-condition variation?
Which covariance structures are identifiable?

Åström and Murray provide the inspected modern linear-Gaussian process-disturbance/measurement-noise special case (Åström and Murray 2021, sec. 8.4). Section numbering was checked against the inspected 24 July 2020 electronic second-edition manuscript corresponding to the published edition.
Filtering equations, covariance propagation proofs, stochastic calculus, and SDE discretization theory are intentionally deferred.

title: Observation Noise
text:
Observation noise is stochastic variability in measurements conditional on the modeled latent state and observation mapping.



Observation noise can make identical latent states produce different data without changing the underlying trajectory. Confusing it with process noise changes inference, prediction, and scientific interpretation.



The system may be in the same state, but the sensor reports slightly different values each time.



In a probabilistic observation model, observation noise or measurement variability is encoded in the conditional observation kernel
\[
K_{k,\theta_y}(x,u,B)
=
\Pr(Y_k\in B\mid X_k=x,u_k=u,\theta_y),
\qquad B\in\Sigma_{\mathcal Y}.
\]
It changes the distribution of measurements while conditioning on the same modeled state and declared input. A deterministic observation map is the special case in which \(K_k\) is a Dirac measure.


A common representation is
\[
Y_k=G_k(X_k,u_k;\theta_y)+v_k,
\]
with
\[
v_k\mid X_k=x,u_k=u
\sim
p_v(\,\cdot\mid x,u,k).
\]
When the required moments exist, define
\[
m^v_k(x,u)=\mathbb E[v_k\mid x,u],
\]
\[
\Sigma^v_k(x,u)
=
\operatorname{Cov}(v_k\mid x,u).
\]
The familiar fixed-law model
\[
v_k\mid X_k,u_k\sim\mathcal N(0,R)
\]
adds zero mean, Gaussianity, constant covariance, and conditional independence from state and input. These are optional assumptions, not the definition of observation noise. Tipping and Bishop’s PPCA model uses an isotropic Gaussian observation error as one special case (Tipping and Bishop 1999, secs. 2.1, 3.1).



The following properties are separate:

Unbiased/zero conditional mean: \(m^v_k(x,u)=0\).
Homoscedastic: the conditional covariance does not vary with state, input, or time.
Heteroscedastic: \(\Sigma^v_k(x,u)\) varies with state, input, or time.
Uncorrelated channels: off-diagonal conditional covariance entries vanish.
Independent channels: the conditional joint law factorizes across channels; this is stronger than zero covariance outside a suitable Gaussian assumption.
White/temporally uncorrelated: under a declared conditioning path, \(\operatorname{Cov}(v_k,v_\ell\mid X_{0:T},u_{0:T},\theta_y)=0\) for \(k\ne\ell\).
Independent across time: under the same conditioning convention, the conditional joint law factorizes across times; this is stronger than uncorrelatedness outside the Gaussian case.
iid: under the same conditioning convention, combines independence across time with an identical conditional distribution.

A diagonal covariance supports conditional channel independence only under additional distributional assumptions such as joint Gaussianity. Tipping and Bishop make channel independence a consequence of their diagonal Gaussian error model, not covariance diagonality alone (Tipping and Bishop 1999, sec. 2.1).



If a sensor has temporal memory, the observation may depend on latent history,
\[
p(y_k\mid x_{0:k},y_{0:k-1},\theta_y),
\]
rather than only on \(x_k\). Separately, a colored stochastic error sequence can correlate measurements across time even without deterministic sensor filtering. These are distinct mechanisms, but either can invalidate the usual product \(\prod_k p(y_k\mid x_k)\) unless sensor memory or correlated noise is explicitly represented in the state or observation model.









NoteEstablished Statistical Background



Many observations do not have a natural additive-error representation. Examples include
\[
Y_k\mid X_k=x
\sim
\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda(x))
\]
for counts and
\[
Y_k\mid X_k=x
\sim
\operatorname{Categorical}(\pi(x))
\]
for labels. Their variability is specified directly by the conditional observation law. Treating such data as Gaussian additive noise can change support, variance structure, and scientific interpretation.







\(K_{k,\theta_y}(x,u,B)\): conditional observation probability kernel.
\(v_k\): additive observation-noise realization.
\(m^v_k(x,u)\): conditional observation-noise mean.
\(\Sigma^v_k(x,u)\): conditional observation-noise covariance.
\(R\): constant covariance in a common Gaussian special case.
\(G_k\): deterministic part of an additive observation mapping.




Observation Model supplies the measurement relation where this noise enters.










Concept
Distinction




Process noise
Changes latent evolution; observation noise changes data conditional on state.


Residual
A fitted discrepancy that may contain observation noise, process noise, calibration error, preprocessing artifacts, missing predictors, and misspecification.


Calibration uncertainty
Uncertainty in sensor parameters or mapping; it can be modeled hierarchically and is not automatically a new measurement realization.


Preprocessing
Deterministic or stochastic transformations applied to recorded data; they alter the effective observation model rather than simply adding \(v_k\).


Missingness / censoring
Selection or truncation of observations; it requires a missingness or censoring model when informative.


Sampling variability
Variation across sampled datasets or events; it is not necessarily conditional measurement noise.


Observation model
Includes the mapping and distribution, not only its noise component.






Observation noise does not imply zero mean, whiteness, independence, identical distribution, Gaussianity, additivity, homoscedasticity, unbiasedness, or state independence. Labeling residuals as noise does not prove they lack structure. Fitting or increasing a covariance \(R\) can absorb discrepancies and improve predictive calibration without identifying a physical sensor mechanism or separating noise from misspecification.



For
\[
X_{k+1}=X_k,
\qquad
Y_k=X_k+v_k,
\qquad
v_k\mid X_k\sim\mathcal N(0,R),
\]
the latent state is constant while repeated measurements vary. Averaging reduces variance only under assumptions about independence or temporal correlation; it does not alter the state dynamics.
For a count observation,
\[
Y_k\mid X_k=x\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(e^x),
\]
so \(\operatorname{Var}(Y_k\mid x)=\mathbb E[Y_k\mid x]=e^x\). The measurement variability is heteroscedastic and encoded by the count likelihood rather than an additive constant-variance Gaussian term.



Sensor noise, spike-count variability, motion artifacts, and annotation errors may enter observation models differently. Treating all unexplained variance as independent observation noise can hide structured neural or behavioral signals.



At L2, Observation Noise locates stochastic variability in the conditional measurement law and makes its moment, dependence, support, and memory assumptions explicit. It protects latent-dynamics claims from being driven by measurement variability and prepares deconvolution and state-space inference questions.

How should heteroscedastic or count-valued observations be modeled?
What calibration data constrain \(R\)?

Noise estimation, filtering, calibration estimation, missing-data inference, and generalized-observation algorithms are intentionally deferred.

title: Metric
text:
A metric is a function assigning a nonnegative distance to each pair of points while satisfying identity, symmetry, and the triangle inequality.



Claims about proximity, neighborhoods, trajectory error, clustering, stability, and geometry depend on a notion of distance. Coordinates alone do not determine which metric is scientifically meaningful.



A metric turns “near” and “far” into declared mathematical relations. Different metrics on the same set can produce different neighborhoods and nearest neighbors.



For a set \(X\), a metric is a function
\[
d:X\times X\to[0,\infty)
\]
such that for all \(x,y,z\in X\):
\[
d(x,y)=0\iff x=y,
\]
\[
d(x,y)=d(y,x),
\]
\[
d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z).
\]
These are identity of indiscernibles, symmetry, and the triangle inequality. Nonnegativity is encoded in the codomain. Sutherland states the same metric axioms and the induced topology (Sutherland 2024).


The open ball of radius \(r>0\) around \(x\) is
\[
B_r^d(x)=\{y\in X:d(x,y)<r\}.
\]
Open balls form a basis for the topology induced by \(d\). A sequence converges to \(x\) exactly when
\[
d(x_n,x)\to0.
\]
It is Cauchy when
\[
\forall\varepsilon>0\;\exists N\;\forall m,n\ge N:
\quad d(x_m,x_n)<\varepsilon.
\]
The metric space is complete when every Cauchy sequence converges to a point in \(X\). Completeness depends on the metric, not only on the underlying topology.



On a vector space, every norm induces the translation-invariant metric
\[
d(x,y)=\|x-y\|.
\]
An inner product induces the norm \(\|x\|=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}\) and therefore a metric. Not every norm comes from an inner product, and not every metric comes from a norm.
Squared Euclidean distance,
\[
d_2^2(x,y)=\|x-y\|_2^2,
\]
is generally not a metric because it can violate the triangle inequality. On \(\mathbb R\), for example, \(d_2^2(0,2)=4>1+1=d_2^2(0,1)+d_2^2(1,2)\).



Two metrics are topologically equivalent when they induce the same open sets. They then have the same convergent sequences and continuous maps, but need not have the same Cauchy sequences, completeness, numerical distances, nearest neighbors, or convergence rates.
They are bi-Lipschitz equivalent when there exist constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\) such that
\[
c\,d_1(x,y)
\le
d_2(x,y)
\le
C\,d_1(x,y)
\]
for all \(x,y\). Bi-Lipschitz equivalence is quantitative: it preserves Cauchy behavior and completeness and controls distortion of distances up to constants. It is stronger than topological equivalence.



If \((X_1,d_1)\) and \((X_2,d_2)\) are metric spaces, examples on \(X_1\times X_2\) include
\[
d_{\max}((x_1,x_2),(y_1,y_2))
=
\max\{d_1(x_1,y_1),d_2(x_2,y_2)\},
\]
and
\[
d_2((x_1,x_2),(y_1,y_2))
=
\sqrt{d_1(x_1,y_1)^2+d_2(x_2,y_2)^2}.
\]
For \(x,y\in\mathbb R^D\) and weights \(w_i>0\),
\[
d_w(x,y)
=
\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{D}w_i(x_i-y_i)^2}
\]
is a metric. Zero weights produce only a pseudometric on the full coordinate space because distinct points can have zero distance. Negative weights do not define a real positive metric.
Rescaling coordinates and then applying ordinary Euclidean distance changes the metric unless the metric is transformed consistently. Coordinate invariance is therefore a property to demonstrate, not an automatic consequence of using coordinates.



A Riemannian Metric assigns inner products to tangent spaces and induces curve lengths and a point-to-point distance by taking an infimum over path lengths. The tensor field and the induced metric-space distance are related but are not the same mathematical object (Lee 1997, chs. 3, 6).





\((X,d)\): metric space.
\(d(x,y)\): distance.
\(B_r^d(x)=\{y:d(x,y)<r\}\): open metric ball.
\(x_n\to x\): metric convergence, equivalent to \(d(x_n,x)\to0\).
\(d_1,d_2\): alternative metrics on the same set.
\(c,C\): bi-Lipschitz lower and upper distortion constants.
\(d_w\): weighted Euclidean metric with strictly positive weights.




State Space supplies the set of states whose pairwise distances may be defined. The related Topology object supplies broader open-set language; here the topology is induced directly by metric balls.










Concept
Distinction




Norm
Measures vector magnitude and induces a metric by \(d(x,y)=\|x-y\|\). Not every metric comes from a norm.


Similarity
Need not satisfy metric axioms and often increases rather than decreases with resemblance.


Divergence / loss
Can be asymmetric or fail the triangle inequality while remaining useful for optimization or statistical comparison.


Squared distance
Often used as a loss but may fail the triangle inequality and therefore not be a metric.


Learned distance
A fitted function that must still be checked against metric axioms and evaluated for generalization and scientific relevance.


Riemannian metric
A smoothly varying inner product on tangent spaces that induces curve lengths and distance.


Graph distance
Shortest-path length is a finite metric on a connected graph (or within each connected component); disconnected pairs otherwise have infinite extended distance.






A metric does not imply Euclidean geometry, smoothness, completeness, a unique scientific choice, coordinate invariance, causal similarity, or that nearest points share mechanism. Intrinsic-dimension estimates, neighborhood graphs, and local geometric summaries can change with the selected metric and scale. Topological equivalence does not imply equal nearest neighbors, Cauchy behavior, completeness, or quantitative rates.



On \(\mathbb R^2\),
\[
d_E(x,y)=\sqrt{(x_1-y_1)^2+(x_2-y_2)^2}
\]
and
\[
d_M(x,y)=|x_1-y_1|+|x_2-y_2|
\]
are both metrics and induce the standard topology, but their balls are circular and diamond-shaped and their numerical distances differ. The weighted metric
\[
d_w(x,y)=\sqrt{100(x_1-y_1)^2+(x_2-y_2)^2}
\]
makes differences in the first coordinate ten times more costly. A nearest-neighbor or trajectory-error analysis can therefore change solely because of the declared metric.



Distances between neural states or behaviors often depend on scaling, covariance, temporal alignment, and noise. Metric choice should be justified rather than inherited silently from plotting coordinates.



At L2, Metric supplies the explicit notions of topology, convergence, completeness, quantitative equivalence, and coordinate weighting needed for stability, geometry, neighbors, and trajectory comparisons. It makes metric dependence a reviewable scientific assumption rather than a plotting default.




Which metric is invariant to nuisance transformations?
How should uncertainty alter distance comparisons?
When should learned metrics be preferred to simple baselines?





Sutherland provides the inspected metric axioms and induced-topology definitions (Sutherland 2024). LDG uses the standard all-pairs Cauchy definition rather than the adjacent-pair shorthand appearing in those brief notes.
Lee develops lengths and metric distance induced by Riemannian structure (Lee 1997, ch. 6).
Metric-learning algorithms, completion constructions, and equivalence proofs are intentionally deferred.





States all metric axioms.
Separates metric, norm, similarity, and Riemannian metric.
States scientific metric-choice limitations.
Defines open balls, induced topology, convergence, Cauchy sequences, and completeness.
Separates general, norm-induced, inner-product-induced, and squared distances.
Distinguishes topological and bi-Lipschitz metric equivalence.
Gives valid product and positive-weight metrics and states pseudometric failures.
Separates metrics from similarities, divergences, learned distances, and Riemannian tensors.
States scientific metric dependence of neighbors, stability, dimension, trajectories, and geometry.

d_E(x,y)=\sqrt{(x_1-y_1)^2+(x_2-y_2)^2}
\]
and
\[
d_M(x,y)=|x_1-y_1|+|x_2-y_2|
\]
are both metrics and induce the standard topology, but their balls are circular and diamond-shaped and their numerical distances differ. The weighted metric
\[
d_w(x,y)=\sqrt{100(x_1-y_1)^2+(x_2-y_2)^2}
\]
makes differences in the first coordinate ten times more costly. A nearest-neighbor or trajectory-error analysis can therefore change solely because of the declared metric.

title: Linear Subspace
text:
A linear subspace is a subset of a vector space that contains zero and is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.



Linear subspaces formalize directions of variation that can be combined linearly. They underlie PCA-style representations, linear dynamical modes, tangent-space approximations, and simple baselines for nonlinear geometry.



A plane through the origin in \(\mathbb R^3\) is a subspace: adding two vectors in the plane or scaling either one keeps the result in the plane.



For a vector space \(V\), a subset \(U\subseteq V\) is a subspace when
\[
0\in U,\qquad u+v\in U,\qquad au\in U
\]
for all \(u,v\in U\) and scalars \(a\). A basis of \(U\) is a linearly independent spanning set; when \(U\) is finite-dimensional, the number of vectors in any basis is \(\dim U\). Axler gives these definitions and closure tests (Axler 2024, secs. 1C, 2C).




\(V\): ambient vector space.
\(U\le V\): linear subspace.
\(\operatorname{span}\{v_1,\ldots,v_d\}\): subspace generated by vectors.
\(\dim U\): subspace dimension.




Ambient Dimension provides the surrounding representation.
Assumed background: vector addition and scalar multiplication.










Concept
Distinction




Affine subspace
A translated subspace that need not contain the origin.


Manifold
Can be curved and need not be closed under linear combinations.


Tangent space
A linear space attached locally to a smooth object, not necessarily the object itself.


Principal-component subspace
A data-estimated subspace selected by a variance criterion.






A fitted linear subspace does not imply a unique representation, mechanistic axes, globally linear dynamics, manifold structure, or that residual variation is noise.



\[
U=\{(x,y,0):x,y\in\mathbb R\}\subset\mathbb R^3
\]
is a two-dimensional subspace. The parallel plane \(z=1\) is affine but not linear because it does not contain zero.



Population activity is often approximated by linear subspaces. Such models should be compared with raw-space baselines and nonlinear alternatives without treating variance-explaining axes as mechanisms.



Linear Subspace supplies the simplest geometric baseline and a prerequisite for tangent-space and linear-dynamics discussions.




Which subspace features are stable across trials and sessions?
How should affine offsets be handled?
When does a nonlinear model outperform a matched linear subspace?





Axler provides the inspected authoritative definitions of subspace, basis, and dimension (Axler 2024).





States the closure conditions.
Separates linear, affine, manifold, and tangent-space concepts.
Includes a minimal coordinate example.

title: Limit Cycle
text:
A limit cycle is an isolated periodic orbit of a continuous-time dynamical system, with its stability behavior qualified separately.



Limit cycles model self-sustained oscillation: the system repeats a closed orbit without requiring the state to remain fixed. They must be distinguished from a sinusoidal-looking observation, a forced periodic response, and a family of non-isolated periodic orbits.
Terminology varies. Some sources use “limit cycle” specifically for an attracting periodic orbit. LDG adopts the broader isolated-periodic-orbit convention and always qualifies its stability; Teschl discusses attracting periodic orbits under the limit-cycle label (Teschl 2012, sec. 7.3).



Imagine trajectories spiraling toward the same closed loop. Once on the loop, the state continues moving and returns after each period. The loop, not any one point on it, is the recurring dynamical object.



Let \(\phi_t\) be a two-sided flow and let \(x_0\) be a regular point. The trajectory through \(x_0\) is periodic when there exists \(T>0\) such that
\[
\phi_T(x_0)=x_0,
\qquad
\phi_{t+T}(x_0)=\phi_t(x_0).
\]
The fundamental period \(T_0\) is the least positive return time. The corresponding periodic orbit is the invariant set
\[
\Gamma
=
\{\phi_t(x_0):0\le t<T_0\}.
\]
All points on \(\Gamma\) describe the same orbit with different phase origins. Teschl distinguishes this regular positive-period orbit from a fixed orbit, whose state does not move (Teschl 2012, sec. 6.3).


LDG convention: a limit cycle is an isolated regular periodic orbit. Isolation means there is a neighborhood of \(\Gamma\) containing no other periodic orbit. This convention includes attracting, repelling, semistable, and more general transverse behaviors; each must be qualified separately. Some sources, including portions of Teschl, use “limit cycle” more narrowly for an attracting periodic orbit (Teschl 2012, sec. 7.3).



The cycle is orbitally attracting when its basin
\[
B^+(\Gamma)
=
\{x:[0,\infty)\subseteq I_x,\ d(\phi_t(x),\Gamma)\to0\}
\]
contains a neighborhood of \(\Gamma\). Equivalently, every sufficiently nearby state has a forward-complete trajectory and
\[
\lim_{t\to\infty}d(\phi_t(x),\Gamma)=0.
\]
This is convergence to the orbit as a set, not synchronization to the reference point \(x_0\) or to one prescribed phase. Motion tangent to the cycle supplies a neutral phase direction; attraction concerns transverse deviations.
The cycle is orbitally Lyapunov stable when every neighborhood of \(\Gamma\) contains a smaller neighborhood whose forward trajectories remain in the larger one. It is asymptotically orbitally stable when it is both orbitally stable and attracting. A repelling cycle attracts in backward time. A semistable cycle can attract from one side and repel from another.






TipLDG Synthesis



In dimensions above two, the transverse return dynamics can contain both contracting and expanding directions, so attracting, repelling, and semistable are not an exhaustive taxonomy. Full hyperbolic and Floquet classifications are deferred.


Under the adopted Attractor convention, an attracting periodic orbit is an attractor: it is closed and invariant, has a neighborhood basin, and the flow restricted to the orbit is transitive. A non-attracting isolated periodic orbit remains a limit cycle under the broader LDG convention but is not thereby an attractor.



Choose a local codimension-one section \(\Sigma\) transverse to the vector field near \(p\in\Gamma\). When nearby trajectories return to the section, the Poincaré map has the form
\[
P_\Sigma(y)=\phi_{\tau(y)}(y),
\]
where \(\tau(y)\) is the local first-return time. The cycle intersects \(\Sigma\) at a fixed point of \(P_\Sigma\), and nearby return-map fixed points correspond locally to nearby periodic orbits under the stated construction. This reduces a local orbital question to a fixed-point question on the transverse section (Teschl 2012, secs. 6.4, 10.2). Existence of the section/return time, derivative criteria, Floquet multipliers, and stability proofs are deferred.



A periodic response to an external periodic input is not automatically an autonomous limit cycle of the original state variables. It may be a forced response whose timing is locked to the input. One can sometimes create an autonomous augmented system by adding the forcing phase as a state, but that changes the state space and the dynamical claim.





\(\Gamma\): the closed periodic orbit as a set.
\(x_0\): one reference point on the orbit.
\(T_0>0\): the least positive or fundamental period.
\(\Sigma\): local transverse Poincaré section.
\(P_\Sigma\): local return map.
\(\tau(y)\): local return time to \(\Sigma\).
\(I_x\): supported elapsed-time interval through \(x\).
\(B^+(\Gamma)\): forward basin of the periodic orbit.
\(\phi_t\): the flow.
\(d(\phi_t(x),\Gamma)\): distance of a nearby trajectory from the orbit.




Trajectory defines one time-indexed evolution. Attractor distinguishes attracting cycles from periodic orbits with other behavior. Flow supplies the evolution and supported-time structure.
Assumed background: local transverse sections. Their existence and smoothness proofs are deferred.










Concept
Distinction




Periodic orbit
Every limit cycle is periodic under the LDG convention, but isolation is additionally required.


Non-isolated periodic family
A center can contain a continuum of concentric periodic orbits; none is a limit cycle under the isolation-based LDG convention.


Attractor
An orbitally attracting limit cycle satisfies the adopted attractor convention; isolation alone does not.


Orbital stability
Controls distance to the orbit as a set. It does not require convergence to one reference phase.


Poincaré-map fixed point
Represents the periodic orbit on a transverse section; it is not a fixed state of the continuous flow.


Fixed point
A fixed point is constant. A limit cycle contains continuing motion and has positive period.


Forced oscillation
Periodicity caused by an external periodic input need not be an autonomous limit cycle.


Oscillatory observation
A measured scalar can oscillate while the underlying state is not on a limit cycle, and a limit cycle can project to a non-sinusoidal signal.






A limit cycle does not imply:

sinusoidal motion or a circular orbit;
attraction unless stability is specified;
that every nearby trajectory shares or converges to the same phase;
that a periodic-looking finite trace is generated autonomously;
that observed frequency alone identifies the state-space orbit;
absence of noise, inputs, transient dynamics, or multiple cycles;
that a spectral peak or autocorrelation peak identifies a closed state-space orbit;
that a closed projected curve is closed in the complete state space; or
that a periodic forced response persists without the forcing signal.




In polar coordinates,
\[
\dot r=r(1-r),\qquad \dot\theta=1,
\]
the orbit \(\Gamma=\{r=1\}\) has fundamental period \(2\pi\). For every initial condition with \(r_0>0\),
\[
r(t)\to1,
\]
so the distance to \(\Gamma\) tends to zero. The limiting phase depends on the initial phase and elapsed time; attraction does not select one point of the cycle. The origin is a separate fixed point.
If instead a measured signal oscillates because an external sinusoidal input drives a non-oscillatory system, the observation can be periodic without an autonomous limit cycle in the original state space.



Limit-cycle hypotheses can describe rhythmic neural population activity, locomotor patterns, or repetitive movements. They require a state-space recurrence claim, not only a spectral peak or repeated peaks in one measured channel.



At L2, Limit Cycle gives LDG a typed bridge among periodic trajectories, invariant orbits, transverse attraction, attractors, and Poincaré fixed points. It prevents phase neutrality, frequency-domain evidence, or forced periodic responses from being overinterpreted as autonomous state-space dynamics.




How can one distinguish a noisy limit cycle from a driven oscillator?
Which coordinates preserve phase and amplitude interpretations?
What interventions reveal attraction toward the orbit?





Teschl defines periodic points, fundamental periods, periodic orbits, and the Poincaré return map (Teschl 2012, secs. 6.3–6.4).
Teschl discusses isolated and attracting periodic orbits under limit-cycle terminology (Teschl 2012, sec. 7.3).
Floquet, return-map derivative, and orbital-stability theorems are intentionally deferred.

States the LDG terminology convention.
Separates periodicity from attraction and external forcing.
Includes a minimal attracting-cycle example.

Defines orbital attraction through distance to the orbit and preserves phase neutrality.
Separates attracting, repelling, semistable, and mixed transverse behavior.

title: Latent Trajectory
text:
A latent trajectory is a time-indexed latent random element or one realized path of that element, distinguished from the observations and from any point summary used to estimate it.



Latent-trajectory language is used for several different objects: a latent process specified by a model, its posterior distribution after observing data, a posterior draw, and a plotted point estimate. Keeping these objects separate prevents a smooth estimate from being mistaken for a uniquely recovered state evolution or for evidence of a dynamical mechanism.



An observation sequence can support many hidden paths. A model assigns relative probability to those paths, and inference updates that distribution using data. Plotting one posterior mean or one maximum-a-posteriori path suppresses this uncertainty and may also hide latent-coordinate symmetries.



Let \((\mathcal Z,\Sigma_{\mathcal Z})\) be a latent space and let \(I=\{0,\ldots,T\}\) in discrete time. A latent trajectory random element is a measurable map
\[
Z_{0:T}:\Omega\to\mathcal Z^{T+1}.
\]
One realization is a path \(z_{0:T}=(z_0,\ldots,z_T)\). In continuous time, one must declare a path space \(\mathcal P(I,\mathcal Z)\)—for example, continuous or càdlàg paths with a specified measurable structure—and write \(Z:\Omega\to\mathcal P(I,\mathcal Z)\). Temporal indexing does not by itself make \(Z_t\) a sufficient dynamical state or specify a transition law.
Assuming an appropriate regular conditional distribution exists, given observations \(Y_{0:T}=y_{0:T}\) and a generative model, the inferential target is generally a conditional probability measure over complete paths,
\[
\Pi(A\mid y_{0:T})
=
\Pr(Z_{0:T}\in A\mid Y_{0:T}=y_{0:T}),
\qquad A\in\Sigma_{\mathcal Z}^{\otimes(T+1)},
\]
or a conditional density \(p(z_{0:T}\mid y_{0:T})\) when a suitable reference measure exists. This posterior law is not identical to any single plotted path.


Under the first-order state-space assumptions declared in State-Space Model, a path law may factor through an initial law and transition kernels,
\[
p(z_{0:T},y_{0:T})
=
p(z_0)
\prod_{k=0}^{T-1}p(z_{k+1}\mid z_k)
\prod_{k=0}^{T}p(y_k\mid z_k).
\]
The factorization is a model assumption, not a consequence of the term “latent trajectory.” Common inferential objects include:

filtering distribution: \(p(z_k\mid y_{0:k})\), using observations available through time \(k\);
fixed-interval smoothing distribution: \(p(z_{0:T}\mid y_{0:T})\), or its marginal \(p(z_k\mid y_{0:T})\), using later observations as well;
posterior sample: a random draw \(\tilde z_{0:T}\sim p(z_{0:T}\mid y_{0:T})\);
joint MAP path: when a declared path density and maximizer exist, a value \(\hat z^{\mathrm{MAP}}_{0:T}\in\arg\max p(z_{0:T}\mid y_{0:T})\);
marginal MAP sequence: independently selected maximizers of \(p(z_k\mid y_{0:T})\), which need not equal a joint MAP path or form a supported transition sequence;
posterior mean path: \(\hat z^{\mathrm{mean}}_k=\mathbb E[Z_k\mid y_{0:T}]\), when \(\mathcal Z\) is represented in a vector space and the expectation exists.

Kalman distinguishes filtering, smoothing, and prediction by whether the target time is equal to, earlier than, or later than the last observation time, and treats an estimate as a function of a conditional distribution and a loss (Kalman 1960). Consequently, the posterior mean is tied to squared-error loss in declared coordinates; it is not a representation-free definition of “the recovered trajectory.” A MAP value based on a density can also depend on the reference measure and coordinate parameterization.
Point summaries are not automatically admissible realized paths. Pointwise marginal means or modes can leave a discrete or nonlinear state space, violate hard path constraints, or combine features that never co-occur in a posterior draw. Even when a summary lies in the path space, it need not be typical under the posterior or satisfy an unforced deterministic evolution law. Exact posterior samples respect the modeled posterior support, but that only establishes compatibility with the fitted model.



Let \(h:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal Z'\) be a bimeasurable bijection and define \(Z'_k=h(Z_k)\). The transformed path law is the pushforward under the componentwise path map \(h^{0:T}\). Preserving the same observable model requires every affected component to transform consistently:
\[
\mu'=h_\#\mu,
\]
\[
Q'_k(z',A')
=
Q_k\!\left(h^{-1}(z'),h^{-1}(A')\right),
\]
\[
G'_k(z',B)
=
G_k\!\left(h^{-1}(z'),B\right).
\]
For deterministic dynamics \(z_{k+1}=f_k(z_k)\), this gives \(f'_k=h\circ f_k\circ h^{-1}\). The posterior over transformed paths must likewise be the pushforward \((h^{0:T})_\#\Pi\). Transforming only the reported trajectory, without the latent law, transition model, and observation model, generally changes the generative specification rather than merely changing coordinates.
Coordinate-wise trajectory errors such as Euclidean RMSE are therefore meaningful only after declaring coordinates, units, metric, time correspondence, and any permitted alignment. If a known group \(G\) generates an observational symmetry, evaluation may instead target an orbit or equivalence class, for example
\[
\inf_{g\in G}
\frac{1}{T+1}\sum_{k=0}^{T}
d_{\mathcal Z}\!\left(z_k^\star,g\cdot\hat z_k\right)^2,
\]
with the group, metric, fitting data, and held-out use of the alignment stated. Observable predictions or other identifiable functions can also be compared when latent coordinates themselves are not identified. In PPCA, for example, the loading matrix and latent coordinate frame have an orthogonal-rotation ambiguity (Tipping and Bishop 1999, sec. 3.2). This exact symmetry does not license arbitrary nonlinear alignment for every latent model.









TipLDG Operational Synthesis



The following protocol connects the posterior, identifiability, and state-space distinctions above into a bounded evaluation design. It is a proposed LDG practice, not a theorem attributed to the inspected sources.


In simulations or other settings with declared latent ground truth \(z_{0:T}^\star\), evaluation should report more than one visually aligned path:

state or trajectory error: use a declared metric and, when necessary, a justified symmetry/alignment convention;
temporal generalization: evaluate held-out times, trials, initial conditions, or parameter conditions rather than only the fitted sequence;
uncertainty coverage: across repeated data sets, check whether marginal state regions or simultaneous path regions contain the appropriately aligned ground truth at their advertised rates, and do not conflate these two coverage targets;
calibration or scoring: compare posterior or predictive distributions with proper scoring rules or repeated-simulation calibration, not only the width of one interval;
model comparison: test against a simpler static or weak-dynamics baseline to determine whether a transition model improves held-out prediction or recovery.

If alignment is estimated from the same ground truth used for scoring, that dependence and any resulting optimism must be reported. Coverage is a repeated-procedure property under a declared data-generating process; one visually plausible credible band is not a calibration result. Simulated ground truth establishes recovery only relative to the simulator and declared equivalence convention, not unique physical or biological truth.

Concept
Distinction




Observed trajectory
A path constructed directly from measured variables. It can be input to latent inference but is not the hidden path itself.


Deterministic embedding path

A stronger modeling role in which each latent value is treated as a state adequate for the specified evolution and system boundary.

A rule assigning local change or transition distributions across supported states. One inferred path does not determine such a rule away from visited states.


Flow
A compatible family of finite-time evolution maps over supported initial states. One latent trajectory is only one orbit/path under a flow, when such a flow exists.

Determines whether latent paths, parameters, or only equivalence classes/functions are uniquely constrained by the observable law.

Let the latent state space be \(\mathcal Z=\{-1,+1\}\) and suppose the posterior assigns probability \(1/2\) to the constant path \((-1,\ldots,-1)\) and probability \(1/2\) to \((+1,\ldots,+1)\). \[
z_{k+1}=Az_k+w_k,
\qquad
y_k=Cz_k+v_k,
\]
filtering and smoothing return conditional distributions over states or paths, not only one line.
