title: Latent Trajectory
text: A latent trajectory is a time-indexed latent random element or one realized path of that element, distinguished from the observations and from any point summary used to estimate it.

title: Latent Trajectory
text: Latent-trajectory language is used for several different objects: a latent process specified by a model, its posterior distribution after observing data, a posterior draw, and a plotted point estimate. Keeping these objects separate prevents a smooth estimate from being mistaken for a uniquely recovered state evolution or for evidence of a dynamical mechanism.

title: Latent Trajectory
text: An observation sequence can support many hidden paths. A model assigns relative probability to those paths, and inference updates that distribution using data. Plotting one posterior mean or one maximum-a-posteriori path suppresses this uncertainty and may also hide latent-coordinate symmetries.

title: Latent Trajectory
text:
Let \((\mathcal Z,\Sigma_{\mathcal Z})\) be a latent space and let \(I=\{0,\ldots,T\}\) in discrete time. A latent trajectory random element is a measurable map
\[
Z_{0:T}:\Omega\to\mathcal Z^{T+1}.
\]
One realization is a path \(z_{0:T}=(z_0,\ldots,z_T)\). In continuous time, one must declare a path space \(\mathcal P(I,\mathcal Z)\)—for example, continuous or càdlàg paths with a specified measurable structure—and write \(Z:\Omega\to\mathcal P(I,\mathcal Z)\). Temporal indexing does not by itself make \(Z_t\) a sufficient dynamical state or specify a transition law.
Assuming an appropriate regular conditional distribution exists, given observations \(Y_{0:T}=y_{0:T}\) and a generative model, the inferential target is generally a conditional probability measure over complete paths,
\[
\Pi(A\mid y_{0:T})
=
\Pr(Z_{0:T}\in A\mid Y_{0:T}=y_{0:T}),
\qquad A\in\Sigma_{\mathcal Z}^{\otimes(T+1)},
\]
or a conditional density \(p(z_{0:T}\mid y_{0:T})\) when a suitable reference measure exists. This posterior law is not identical to any single plotted path.


Under the first-order state-space assumptions declared in State-Space Model, a path law may factor through an initial law and transition kernels,
\[
p(z_{0:T},y_{0:T})
=
p(z_0)
\prod_{k=0}^{T-1}p(z_{k+1}\mid z_k)
\prod_{k=0}^{T}p(y_k\mid z_k).
\]
The factorization is a model assumption, not a consequence of the term “latent trajectory.” Common inferential objects include:

filtering distribution: \(p(z_k\mid y_{0:k})\), using observations available through time \(k\);
fixed-interval smoothing distribution: \(p(z_{0:T}\mid y_{0:T})\), or its marginal \(p(z_k\mid y_{0:T})\), using later observations as well;
posterior sample: a random draw \(\tilde z_{0:T}\sim p(z_{0:T}\mid y_{0:T})\);
joint MAP path: when a declared path density and maximizer exist, a value \(\hat z^{\mathrm{MAP}}_{0:T}\in\arg\max p(z_{0:T}\mid y_{0:T})\);
marginal MAP sequence: independently selected maximizers of \(p(z_k\mid y_{0:T})\), which need not equal a joint MAP path or form a supported transition sequence;
posterior mean path: \(\hat z^{\mathrm{mean}}_k=\mathbb E[Z_k\mid y_{0:T}]\), when \(\mathcal Z\) is represented in a vector space and the expectation exists.

Kalman distinguishes filtering, smoothing, and prediction by whether the target time is equal to, earlier than, or later than the last observation time, and treats an estimate as a function of a conditional distribution and a loss (Kalman 1960). Consequently, the posterior mean is tied to squared-error loss in declared coordinates; it is not a representation-free definition of “the recovered trajectory.” A MAP value based on a density can also depend on the reference measure and coordinate parameterization.
Point summaries are not automatically admissible realized paths. Pointwise marginal means or modes can leave a discrete or nonlinear state space, violate hard path constraints, or combine features that never co-occur in a posterior draw. Even when a summary lies in the path space, it need not be typical under the posterior or satisfy an unforced deterministic evolution law. Exact posterior samples respect the modeled posterior support, but that only establishes compatibility with the fitted model.



Let \(h:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal Z'\) be a bimeasurable bijection and define \(Z'_k=h(Z_k)\). The transformed path law is the pushforward under the componentwise path map \(h^{0:T}\). Preserving the same observable model requires every affected component to transform consistently:
\[
\mu'=h_\#\mu,
\]
\[
Q'_k(z',A')
=
Q_k\!\left(h^{-1}(z'),h^{-1}(A')\right),
\]
\[
G'_k(z',B)
=
G_k\!\left(h^{-1}(z'),B\right).
\]
For deterministic dynamics \(z_{k+1}=f_k(z_k)\), this gives \(f'_k=h\circ f_k\circ h^{-1}\). The posterior over transformed paths must likewise be the pushforward \((h^{0:T})_\#\Pi\). Transforming only the reported trajectory, without the latent law, transition model, and observation model, generally changes the generative specification rather than merely changing coordinates.
Coordinate-wise trajectory errors such as Euclidean RMSE are therefore meaningful only after declaring coordinates, units, metric, time correspondence, and any permitted alignment. If a known group \(G\) generates an observational symmetry, evaluation may instead target an orbit or equivalence class, for example
\[
\inf_{g\in G}
\frac{1}{T+1}\sum_{k=0}^{T}
d_{\mathcal Z}\!\left(z_k^\star,g\cdot\hat z_k\right)^2,
\]
with the group, metric, fitting data, and held-out use of the alignment stated. Observable predictions or other identifiable functions can also be compared when latent coordinates themselves are not identified. In PPCA, for example, the loading matrix and latent coordinate frame have an orthogonal-rotation ambiguity (Tipping and Bishop 1999, sec. 3.2). This exact symmetry does not license arbitrary nonlinear alignment for every latent model.









TipLDG Operational Synthesis



The following protocol connects the posterior, identifiability, and state-space distinctions above into a bounded evaluation design. It is a proposed LDG practice, not a theorem attributed to the inspected sources.


In simulations or other settings with declared latent ground truth \(z_{0:T}^\star\), evaluation should report more than one visually aligned path:

state or trajectory error: use a declared metric and, when necessary, a justified symmetry/alignment convention;
temporal generalization: evaluate held-out times, trials, initial conditions, or parameter conditions rather than only the fitted sequence;
uncertainty coverage: across repeated data sets, check whether marginal state regions or simultaneous path regions contain the appropriately aligned ground truth at their advertised rates, and do not conflate these two coverage targets;
calibration or scoring: compare posterior or predictive distributions with proper scoring rules or repeated-simulation calibration, not only the width of one interval;
model comparison: test against a simpler static or weak-dynamics baseline to determine whether a transition model improves held-out prediction or recovery.

If alignment is estimated from the same ground truth used for scoring, that dependence and any resulting optimism must be reported. Coverage is a repeated-procedure property under a declared data-generating process; one visually plausible credible band is not a calibration result. Simulated ground truth establishes recovery only relative to the simulator and declared equivalence convention, not unique physical or biological truth.

title: Intrinsic Dimension
text:
Intrinsic dimension is the number of independent coordinates or degrees of freedom assigned to an object under a specified structural model, scale, and criterion.



Intrinsic dimension can be smaller than ambient dimension, but it is not a model-free property of a finite noisy dataset. Different estimators, scales, noise models, and tolerances can yield different answers.



Points near a curve in a high-dimensional recording space may vary mainly along one direction at a coarse scale, while fine-scale noise occupies many directions.



For a smooth \(d\)-dimensional manifold represented in \(\mathbb R^D\), \(d\) is its manifold dimension and \(D\) its ambient dimension. More generally, “intrinsic dimension” may refer to manifold dimension, local dimension, effective linear rank, or another declared complexity criterion.
LDG therefore requires every estimate \(\widehat d\) to state the model class, neighborhood or scale, estimator, and noise assumptions. Levina and Bickel demonstrate an estimator whose behavior depends on neighborhoods and on data lying near rather than exactly on a manifold (Levina and Bickel 2004).




\(D\): ambient dimension.
\(d\): claimed intrinsic dimension.
\(\widehat d\): estimated dimension.
scale or neighborhood size: the resolution at which dimension is assessed.




Ambient Dimension supplies the surrounding representation against which an intrinsic claim is compared.










Concept
Distinction




Rank
Exact linear dimension of a matrix or subspace; intrinsic dimension can be nonlinear or scale-dependent.


Latent dimension
Number of variables in a chosen latent model; it may be selected rather than identified as intrinsic truth.


Manifold dimension
A specific mathematical dimension when manifold assumptions hold.


Variance explained
A criterion for approximation, not a universal definition of dimension.






A low intrinsic-dimension estimate does not prove a manifold, identify unique latent variables, establish mechanism, remain constant across scales, or justify a particular nonlinear embedding.



Noiseless points on a line in \(\mathbb R^{10}\) have a one-dimensional linear structure. Adding small isotropic noise can make fine-scale estimates approach ten while coarse-scale estimates remain near one.



Neural dimensionality depends on trial conditions, preprocessing, temporal scale, model class, and criterion. Reported dimension should therefore be treated as an operational estimate.



Intrinsic Dimension enforces one of LDG’s central prohibitions: dimensionality is model- and criterion-dependent, and reduction is not proof of geometry.

How should uncertainty and heterogeneity in local dimension be reported?
What null models reveal spurious low-dimensional estimates?





Levina and Bickel provide an inspected primary intrinsic-dimension estimator and discuss scale and near-manifold behavior (Levina and Bickel 2004).





Defines dimension relative to model, scale, and criterion.
Separates rank, latent dimension, and manifold dimension.
States that low estimated dimension does not prove a manifold.

title: Initial Condition
text:
An initial condition assigns a specified state value to a specified reference time for the evolution being considered.



An evolution rule does not by itself say which realized evolution is under discussion. An initial condition supplies the state value from which the description is started, anchored at a reference time. It therefore connects a general state description to a particular trajectory or set of possible trajectories.
“Initial” is relative to the problem, not necessarily to the physical beginning of the system. A researcher may choose the start of a trial, stimulus onset, movement onset, or any other declared reference time. The same state value can serve as an initial condition for one analysis and as an intermediate state in another.



Suppose a pendulum model is ready to describe how angle and angular velocity change. To continue the model from time \(t_0\), one must specify the pendulum’s state there. Saying “the angle is zero” is generally insufficient because different angular velocities lead to different subsequent motions. Saying “at \(t_0\), angle is zero and angular velocity is one” assigns a complete state value and therefore supplies an initial condition for that state description.
The initial condition is not an extra kind of physical quantity. It is a state value placed in a particular role: the value used to anchor an evolution problem at a reference time.



Let \(\mathcal{X}\) be the state space and let \(t_0\) be the chosen reference time. An initial condition has the form
\[
x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x_0\in\mathcal{X}.
\]
Here \(x_0\) is an admissible state value. The equation is a condition imposed on a trajectory \(x(t)\): any trajectory considered for the problem must pass through \(x_0\) at \(t_0\). Teschl uses this standard form when defining an initial value problem (Teschl 2012, sec. 2.2).
The condition constrains a trajectory only together with a specified evolution rule, parameters, and any required future input values or prescription after \(t_0\). At L1, no universal existence or uniqueness claim is made: depending on the description and assumptions, a condition and rule may admit one trajectory, several, or none over the requested time interval.




\(t_0\): the reference time selected for the problem.
\(\mathcal{X}\): the state space.
\(x_0\in\mathcal{X}\): the assigned initial state value.
\(x(t_0)=x_0\): the initial-condition statement.
\(x(t)\): a trajectory satisfying the condition when such a trajectory is defined.

The subscript zero marks the reference role; it does not require the clock time to be numerically zero.




State: distinguishes state values from observations and parameters.
State Space: supplies the admissible values from which \(x_0\) is chosen.
Trajectory: supplies the time-indexed object constrained at \(t_0\).

Assumed background: elementary function notation.










Concept
Distinction from initial condition




State value
Any realized condition of the system at a time. It becomes an initial condition when assigned to the chosen reference time for an evolution problem.


Trajectory
A time-parameterized admissible evolution of states. The initial condition constrains its value at one reference time but is not the entire trajectory.


Parameter
A parameter indexes or specifies the evolution rule and is held fixed under the declared description. The initial state is initialized and propagated by that rule. A constant unknown can be moved into an augmented state only by explicitly changing the model’s role assignments.


Observation at the reference time
A measurement \(y(t_0)\) may be noisy, partial, or indirect. It is evidence about \(x_0\), not automatically the initial condition itself.


First recorded sample
The first available datum may occur after the modeled interval begins, may omit state variables, or may be an observation. It is not automatically a complete initial condition.


External input
A future input may influence the subsequent trajectory but is not generally contained in \(x_0\). The model must separately specify any input information it requires.


Boundary condition
A boundary condition is a broader constraint that may be imposed at another time or location. An initial condition specifically assigns state information at a chosen reference time.


Reset or trial onset
An experimental event can define \(t_0\), but it does not guarantee that the system’s state is known, identical across trials, or independent of earlier history.






Calling \(x(t_0)=x_0\) an initial condition does not by itself imply that:

\(t_0\) is the time when the physical system began to exist;
\(x_0\) was directly or exactly measured;
the first data row is a complete state value;
the same nominal experimental condition produces the same \(x_0\) on every trial;
the evolution rule and parameters are known;
a trajectory exists for all later times or is unique;
changing \(x_0\) while changing parameters or inputs isolates an initial-condition effect; or
differences in later behavior are caused solely by differences in the initial condition.




For the pendulum state \(x=(\text{angle},\text{angular velocity})\), choose a reference time \(t_0\) and assign
\[
x(t_0)=(0,1).
\]
This says that at \(t_0\) the pendulum is at zero angle with angular velocity one in the chosen units. The pair is the initial state value; \(t_0\) is part of the condition. Pendulum length and damping remain parameters of the declared model, while applied torque after \(t_0\) is an external input if the model includes one.
A camera measurement reporting angle near zero is not sufficient to establish this initial condition because angular velocity is missing and the measured angle is uncertain. Estimating the full state at \(t_0\) produces an estimated initial condition, which should not be silently treated as exact.



In neural dynamics, a population activity vector at a declared event time may be modeled as an initial condition for subsequent population evolution. Cunningham and Yu summarize motor-cortical work in which preparatory population activity is interpreted as setting the initial state for movement-period dynamics (Cunningham and Yu 2014). This is a model interpretation of recorded activity, not proof that the vector is the complete physical neural state or that later differences are caused only by that initial value.
For behavior, position alone at trial onset may not be an adequate initial condition when velocity, posture, context, or internal task state affects subsequent behavior. LDG should distinguish the experimental alignment event, the measurements available there, and the state value actually assigned to the model.



Many LDG questions compare time courses across trials, conditions, subjects, or modalities. title: Initial Condition
text: An initial condition assigns a specified state value to a specified reference time for the evolution being considered.

title: Initial Condition
text:
An evolution rule does not by itself say which realized evolution is under discussion. An initial condition supplies the state value from which the description is started, anchored at a reference time. It therefore connects a general state description to a particular trajectory or set of possible trajectories.
“Initial” is relative to the problem, not necessarily to the physical beginning of the system. A researcher may choose the start of a trial, stimulus onset, movement onset, or any other declared reference time. The same state value can serve as an initial condition for one analysis and as an intermediate state in another.

title: Initial Condition
text:
Suppose a pendulum model is ready to describe how angle and angular velocity change. To continue the model from time \(t_0\), one must specify the pendulum’s state there. Saying “the angle is zero” is generally insufficient because different angular velocities lead to different subsequent motions. Saying “at \(t_0\), angle is zero and angular velocity is one” assigns a complete state value and therefore supplies an initial condition for that state description.
The initial condition is not an extra kind of physical quantity. It is a state value placed in a particular role: the value used to anchor an evolution problem at a reference time.

title: Initial Condition
text:
Let \(\mathcal{X}\) be the state space and let \(t_0\) be the chosen reference time. An initial condition has the form
\[
x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x_0\in\mathcal{X}.
\]
Here \(x_0\) is an admissible state value. The equation is a condition imposed on a trajectory \(x(t)\): any trajectory considered for the problem must pass through \(x_0\) at \(t_0\). Teschl uses this standard form when defining an initial value problem (Teschl 2012, sec. 2.2).
The condition constrains a trajectory only together with a specified evolution rule, parameters, and any required future input values or prescription after \(t_0\). At L1, no universal existence or uniqueness claim is made: depending on the description and assumptions, a condition and rule may admit one trajectory, several, or none over the requested time interval.

title: Initial Condition
text:
\(t_0\): the reference time selected for the problem.
\(\mathcal{X}\): the state space.
\(x_0\in\mathcal{X}\): the assigned initial state value.
\(x(t_0)=x_0\): the initial-condition statement.
\(x(t)\): a trajectory satisfying the condition when such a trajectory is defined.

The subscript zero marks the reference role; it does not require the clock time to be numerically zero.

title: Initial Condition
text:
State: distinguishes state values from observations and parameters.
State Space: supplies the admissible values from which \(x_0\) is chosen.
Trajectory: supplies the time-indexed object constrained at \(t_0\).

Assumed background: elementary function notation.

title: Initial Condition
text:
Concept
Distinction from initial condition




State value
Any realized condition of the system at a time. It becomes an initial condition when assigned to the chosen reference time for an evolution problem.


Trajectory
A time-parameterized admissible evolution of states. The initial condition constrains its value at one reference time but is not the entire trajectory.


Parameter
A parameter indexes or specifies the evolution rule and is held fixed under the declared description. The initial state is initialized and propagated by that rule. A constant unknown can be moved into an augmented state only by explicitly changing the model’s role assignments.


Observation at the reference time
A measurement \(y(t_0)\) may be noisy, partial, or indirect. It is evidence about \(x_0\), not automatically the initial condition itself.


First recorded sample
The first available datum may occur after the modeled interval begins, may omit state variables, or may be an observation. It is not automatically a complete initial condition.


External input
A future input may influence the subsequent trajectory but is not generally contained in \(x_0\). The model must separately specify any input information it requires.


Boundary condition
A boundary condition is a broader constraint that may be imposed at another time or location. An initial condition specifically assigns state information at a chosen reference time.


Reset or trial onset
An experimental event can define \(t_0\), but it does not guarantee that the system’s state is known, identical across trials, or independent of earlier history.

title: Initial Condition
Initial Condition
text:
For the pendulum state \(x=(\text{angle},\text{angular velocity})\), choose a reference time \(t_0\) and assign
\[
x(t_0)=(0,1).
\]
This says that at \(t_0\) the pendulum is at zero angle with angular velocity one in the chosen units. The pair is the initial state value; \(t_0\) is part of the condition. Pendulum length and damping remain parameters of the declared model, while applied torque after \(t_0\) is an external input if the model includes one.
A camera measurement reporting angle near zero is not sufficient to establish this initial condition because angular velocity is missing and the measured angle is uncertain. Estimating the full state at \(t_0\) produces an estimated initial condition, which should not be silently treated as exact.

title: Initial Condition
text:
In neural dynamics, a population activity vector at a declared event time may be modeled as an initial condition for subsequent population evolution. Cunningham and Yu summarize motor-cortical work in which preparatory population activity is interpreted as setting the initial state for movement-period dynamics (Cunningham and Yu 2014). This is a model interpretation of recorded activity, not proof that the vector is the complete physical neural state or that later differences are caused only by that initial value.
For behavior, position alone at trial onset may not be an adequate initial condition when velocity, posture, context, or internal task state affects subsequent behavior. LDG should distinguish the experimental alignment event, the measurements available there, and the state value actually assigned to the model.

title: Identifiability
text:
Identifiability asks whether distinct model specifications can produce the same distribution of observable data under the stated experimental design.



If several parameters or latent representations are observationally equivalent, unlimited data from the same design cannot select a unique one without added constraints. Optimization quality cannot repair structural non-identifiability.



Imagine two different internal descriptions that make exactly the same predictions for every observation the experiment can collect. The data cannot tell them apart.



Let \(\Theta\) be a model-specification space and let \(\mathcal P(\mathcal Y)\) denote probability laws on the observable sample space under a fixed experimental design. The model induces a parameterization map
\[
\Psi:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal Y),
\qquad
\Psi(\theta)=P_\theta.
\]
Rothenberg frames identification through this mapping from structural parameters to observable distributions (Rothenberg 1971).


The parameterization is globally (strictly) identifiable when
\[
P_{\theta_1}=P_{\theta_2}
\Longrightarrow
\theta_1=\theta_2.
\]
It is locally identifiable at \(\theta\) when there is a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\theta\) such that
\[
\Psi^{-1}(P_\theta)\cap U=\{\theta\}.
\]
Local identifiability excludes indistinguishable parameters arbitrarily near \(\theta\) but permits observationally equivalent parameters elsewhere.
A finite-dimensional parametric model is generically identifiable under a declared convention when identifiability holds outside a specified exceptional subset, commonly a lower-dimensional algebraic set or a set of measure zero. The meaning of “generic,” the reference measure/geometry, and any remaining finite symmetry must be stated. Generic identifiability does not make the exceptional parameters impossible or empirically detectable. Allman, Matias, and Rhodes use this notion for latent-structure models and explicitly allow label permutations (Allman et al. 2009).



Define
\[
\theta_1\sim\theta_2
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
P_{\theta_1}=P_{\theta_2}.
\]
This is an equivalence relation. When exact parameter recovery is impossible or scientifically unnecessary, the identifiable target may be the equivalence class \([\theta]\in\Theta/{\sim}\) or an identifiable function \(\psi(\theta)\) satisfying
\[
P_{\theta_1}=P_{\theta_2}
\Longrightarrow
\psi(\theta_1)=\psi(\theta_2).
\]
A known symmetry group \(G\) may generate part of the equivalence: \(g\cdot\theta\) and \(\theta\) produce the same observable law. Identifiability up to \(G\) means the observational fiber equals the declared group orbit, not that the original coordinates are uniquely recovered.



Structural identifiability asks the idealized infinite-information question using exact observable distributions and the declared model/design.






TipLDG Operational Synthesis



LDG uses practical identifiability for finite-data weakness caused by limited experimental coverage, weak sensitivity, ill-conditioning, broad posterior uncertainty, or large estimator variance. Optimization failure is a separate computational difficulty: it can prevent recovery even when a well-conditioned identifiable target exists. A structurally identifiable model can be practically difficult; a structurally non-identifiable parameter cannot be made unique by a better optimizer or more data from the same unchanged design.





Symmetries must be derived from the specific model:

In finite mixtures and discrete hidden-state models, permuting latent labels can leave the observable distribution unchanged; Allman, Matias, and Rhodes call this label swapping and formulate identifiability up to permutation (Allman et al. 2009).
In PPCA with \(z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\), replacing \(W\) by \(WR\) and \(z\) by \(R^\top z\) for orthogonal \(R\) preserves the latent prior and observable covariance. Thus \(W\) and the latent coordinate frame are non-identifiable under right-orthogonal transformations (Tipping and Bishop 1999, sec. 3.2). Describing the full model as identifiable “up to rotation” additionally requires conditions excluding further degeneracies.
General scalings or invertible transformations preserve the observable law only when the observation map, latent law, transition model, and other affected components are transformed consistently. They are not universal symmetries.






\(\theta\): model specification or parameter.
\(P_\theta\): induced observable-data distribution.
\(\Psi:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal Y)\): parameterization map.
\(\Psi^{-1}(P_\theta)\): observational fiber.
\(\theta_1\sim\theta_2\): observational equivalence.
\([\theta]\in\Theta/{\sim}\): identifiable equivalence-class target.
\(\psi(\theta)\): identifiable function when constant on observational fibers.
\(G\cdot\theta\): orbit of a declared symmetry group.




Latent Variable and Observation Model supply the hidden quantities and observable mapping whose uniqueness is questioned.










Concept
Distinction




Estimability / practical identifiability
Concerns finite-data precision, conditioning, posterior concentration, or an estimator; structural identifiability is a property of the idealized model plus design.


Observability
In control theory, concerns recovering state from outputs over time; related but not synonymous.


Interpretability
A scientific meaning assigned to a model component; an identifiable parameter can still be hard to interpret.


Predictive accuracy
Equivalent models predict the same observable law by definition, and non-equivalent misspecified models can still have similar finite-sample prediction. Prediction does not identify internal parameters.


Causal identification
Targets interventional or counterfactual quantities under a causal model and identifying assumptions. Some targets are identifiable from sufficiently strong observational assumptions, while others require interventional data or design; statistical parameter identifiability alone is not causal identification.


Label or coordinate convention
Can choose one representative from an equivalence class for reporting or computation without making it scientifically identified.






Identifiability does not imply easy estimation, good conditioning, low variance, correct model class, observability of every realized state, causal interpretation, or mechanistic truth. Generic identifiability does not guarantee the fitted parameter is outside the exceptional set. Non-identifiability does not imply useless prediction, but it limits which internal claims can be unique.





Let
\[
z\sim\mathcal N(0,I),
\qquad
y=Wz+\varepsilon,
\qquad
\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2I).
\]
For any orthogonal matrix \(R\), define \(z'=R^\top z\) and \(W'=WR\). Then \(z'\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\) and
\[
W'z'=Wz,
\]
so the observable distribution is unchanged. The loading matrix \(W\) and latent coordinate frame are therefore not identified under this orthogonal action. The observable covariance \(WW^\top+\sigma^2I\) is determined by the PPCA law; identification of the loading subspace requires the relevant rank and eigenvalue-separation conditions and is not asserted here without them.



In a two-component mixture, exchanging component labels and all label-indexed parameters leaves the mixture distribution unchanged. One can identify the unordered pair of components under suitable conditions, but not a privileged numerical label without an external convention.
These are exact model symmetries. An arbitrary scaling or nonlinear transform is not observationally equivalent unless every affected model component is transformed consistently.




Latent neural coordinates, dynamical matrices, and observation mappings can trade off while fitting the same recordings. Claims should state what is identifiable—predictions, subspaces, equivalence classes, or individual parameters.



At L2, Identifiability provides a typed map from model specifications to observable laws and clarifies when the scientific target is a parameter, an identifiable function, or an equivalence class. It is the principal guardrail against equating a fitted latent representation with a unique biological mechanism.




Which interventions break important equivalences?
What transformations preserve the scientific claim?
Which parameters are only practically, rather than structurally, weakly determined?





Rothenberg provides the inspected primary parametric identification framework and local-identification perspective (Rothenberg 1971).
Allman, Matias, and Rhodes provide an inspected primary treatment of strict and generic identifiability, exceptional sets, and latent-label permutations (Allman et al. 2009).
Tipping and Bishop provide the inspected PPCA rotation symmetry (Tipping and Bishop 1999, sec. 3.2).
Information-matrix/rank tests, algebraic identifiability proofs, experimental-design optimization, and estimator theory are intentionally deferred.

title: Flow
text:
A flow is a finite-time evolution family that, where well-defined, maps each initial state in its domain to the state reached after an elapsed time under one shared autonomous continuous-time rule.



A vector field gives a local instantaneous rule, while a flow describes its accumulated effect over finite time across possible initial states. Fixing one initial state in a flow yields one trajectory; considering all supported initial states yields a consistent family of trajectories generated by the same dynamics.
This distinction prevents a collection of observed curves from being mistaken for a flow. A flow is not merely a dataset of trajectories: its time-evolution maps must act consistently on states and compose across successive time intervals. Teschl defines the flow of an autonomous differential equation by collecting its integral curves into one map (Teschl 2012, sec. 6.2).
The stable First-Order Autonomous Dynamical System Math Object is the canonical location for the existence, uniqueness, maximal-continuation, and regularity results that justify such maps. This Concept retains only the notation and distinctions needed to interpret finite-time evolution without duplicating those theorem-level derivations.



Imagine the vector field as an arrow attached to every state. The flow answers a finite-time question: “Starting from this state, where does the shared rule carry the system after elapsed time \(\tau\)?”
There are two useful ways to hold part of the flow fixed:

Fix an initial state \(x_0\): varying elapsed time \(\tau\) traces one trajectory.
Fix an elapsed time \(\tau\): the map \(\phi_\tau\) moves every supported initial state to its state after that duration.

A flow is the coherent collection of these finite-time maps, not any unrelated collection of before-and-after pairs.



Consider an autonomous Euclidean system
\[
\dot{x}=f(x),\qquad x\in\mathcal{X}.
\]
Suppose the active assumptions provide a unique maximal solution through each supported initial state. For \(x\in\mathcal{X}\), let \(I_x\) be the maximal elapsed-time interval containing \(0\) for the solution through \(x\), and define the supported domain
\[
W
=
\{(\tau,x)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathcal{X}:\tau\in I_x\}.
\]
The joint finite-time evolution map is
\[
\Phi:W\rightarrow\mathcal{X},
\qquad
\Phi(\tau,x)=\phi_\tau(x),
\]
where \(\phi_\tau(x)\) is the state reached after elapsed time \(\tau\) from \(x\). For fixed \(\tau\), the corresponding state map has the typed domain
\[
\operatorname{dom}(\phi_\tau)
=
\{x\in\mathcal{X}:(\tau,x)\in W\}.
\]
The supported set need not be all of \(\mathbb{R}\times\mathcal{X}\), and \(\operatorname{dom}(\phi_\tau)\) need not equal \(\mathcal{X}\). The evolution family satisfies
\[
\phi_0(x)=x,
\]
and the composition law only where the required evolutions are supported. Explicitly, if \(s\in I_x\) and \(\tau\in I_{\phi_s(x)}\), then \(s+\tau\in I_x\) and
\[
\phi_{\tau+s}(x)=\phi_\tau\bigl(\phi_s(x)\bigr).
\]
The first relation says that zero elapsed time leaves the state unchanged. The second says that evolving for \(s\) and then for \(\tau\) agrees with evolving once for the combined elapsed time. It is not a claim that every map is defined on all states or all elapsed times (Teschl 2012, sec. 6.2).
Local existence and uniqueness support this single-valued local finite-time evolution. Under the stronger condition \(f\in C^1\), the stable Math Object states that \(W\) is open and \(\Phi\) is jointly \(C^1\) in elapsed time and initial state; under the adopted LDG convention, this jointly regular map is the generated local flow. The regularity theorem and its derivation remain in the Math Object.
For an initial condition \(x(t_0)=x_0\), the associated trajectory can be written
\[
x(t)=\phi_{t-t_0}(x_0)
\]
when \(t-t_0\in I_{x_0}\), equivalently when \((t-t_0,x_0)\in W\). Here \(t\) is absolute clock time, whereas \(\tau=t-t_0\) is elapsed time from the initial condition.
When the active ODE assumptions make each curve \(\tau\mapsto\phi_\tau(x)\) differentiable in elapsed time, it satisfies
\[
\frac{d}{d\tau}\phi_\tau(x)
=
f\bigl(\phi_\tau(x)\bigr),
\]
and its derivative at zero recovers the vector field:
\[
f(x)=\left.\frac{d}{d\tau}\phi_\tau(x)\right|_{\tau=0}.
\]
This derivative is along one trajectory with respect to elapsed time. It does not by itself assert differentiability with respect to the initial state \(x\); joint initial-state regularity is the stronger local-flow conclusion above. These relations express the local-versus-finite-time distinction and are not an existence or uniqueness proof.
For a two-sided smooth local flow, reverse elapsed time supplies a local inverse: \(\phi_{-\tau}\) reverses \(\phi_\tau\) on the corresponding supported domains. This does not make \(\phi_\tau\) a globally defined bijection \(\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{X}\) for every \(\tau\) (Teschl 2012, sec. 6.2).
The one-parameter notation \(\phi_\tau\) is most natural for autonomous dynamics. Semiflows restricted to nonnegative elapsed time, explicitly time-dependent systems, and input-driven evolution are outside this bounded L2 Concept rather than silently treated as the same structure.




\(\mathcal{X}\): the state space.
\(f\): the autonomous vector field or local instantaneous rule.
\(x_0\in\mathcal{X}\): an initial state value.
\(t_0\): the reference time of the initial condition.
\(t\): absolute clock time along a trajectory.
\(\tau\): elapsed flow time.
\(I_x\): the maximal elapsed-time interval containing \(0\) for the solution through \(x\).
\(W\): the supported elapsed-time/state pairs \((\tau,x)\) with \(\tau\in I_x\).
\(\Phi(\tau,x)=\phi_\tau(x)\): the joint local finite-time evolution map on \(W\); jointly \(C^1\) under the stated stronger flow condition.
\(\phi_\tau\): the finite-time state map on the states for which elapsed time \(\tau\) is defined; its domain may depend on \(\tau\) for a local flow.
\(\operatorname{dom}(\phi_\tau)=\{x\in\mathcal{X}:(\tau,x)\in W\}\): the supported states for one fixed elapsed time.
\(\phi_\tau(x_0)\): the state reached from \(x_0\) after elapsed time \(\tau\).
\(x(t)=\phi_{t-t_0}(x_0)\): the trajectory associated with one initial condition.

The symbol \(\phi\) is conventional. A source may use \(\Phi\), \(T_t\), or another symbol; the defining role and composition property matter more than the letter.




State Space: supplies the admissible initial and later states.
Trajectory: supplies the time-parameterized evolution obtained by fixing one initial state.
Initial Condition: supplies \(x(t_0)=x_0\).
Vector Field: supplies the local instantaneous rule in this Cycle’s continuous-time setting.

Assumed background: elementary functions, composition of functions, and derivatives.

The First-Order Autonomous Dynamical System is the formal companion for unique maximal solutions, supported domains, and flow regularity. It is linked as a related object rather than used to replace the conceptual definition here.










Concept
Distinction from flow




Vector field
Assigns a local instantaneous change vector \(f(x)\) to each state. A flow gives finite-time evolution \(\phi_\tau(x)\) across states and elapsed times where that evolution is defined.


Trajectory
Fixing \(x_0\) and varying elapsed time gives a trajectory \(\tau\mapsto\phi_\tau(x_0)\); with reference time \(t_0\), this is \(x(t)=\phi_{t-t_0}(x_0)\). One trajectory is one member of the family organized by the flow.


Initial condition
Selects the starting state and reference time for one trajectory. The flow specifies how all supported initial states evolve over elapsed time.


Orbit
The visited-state set of one trajectory with time labels discarded. A flow contains finite-time maps across initial states and retains more information than any one orbit.


Single finite-time map
One map \(\phi_\tau\) advances states by one chosen duration. The flow is the compatible family over elapsed times, including the identity and composition relations.


Discrete-time update rule
A map such as \(F(x)\) advances a state by one discrete step, and its iterates define discrete evolution. It is not automatically a continuous-time flow or the time-one map of one.


Collection of observed trajectories
A dataset may contain separate time courses with noise, different inputs, or different dynamics. It represents one shared flow only if a common state-evolution family is justified.


State transition estimate
An estimated mapping from data depends on model and inference choices. It may estimate part of a flow, but estimation is not part of the definition.






Calling an evolution family a flow does not by itself imply that:

any arbitrary collection of trajectories comes from one shared flow;
similar-looking trajectories have identical vector fields or finite-time dynamics;
one observed trajectory determines the maps \(\phi_\tau\) for other initial states;
finite noisy observations identify a unique flow;
a visualization of curves establishes a dynamical mechanism;
the flow is defined for every state or for all positive and negative times;
every fixed-time map is a globally defined bijection \(\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{X}\), even though a two-sided smooth local flow has reverse-time local inverses on corresponding supported domains;
every vector field automatically generates a unique global flow; or
an input-driven or explicitly time-dependent system has the same one-parameter flow structure.




Consider the one-dimensional autonomous rule
\[
\dot{x}=1,
\qquad \mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}.
\]
The vector field assigns the same instantaneous rate \(f(x)=1\) at every state. Its flow is
\[
\phi_\tau(x_0)=x_0+\tau.
\]
For a fixed elapsed time \(\tau\), \(\phi_\tau\) shifts every initial state by \(\tau\). For an initial condition \(x(t_0)=x_0\), the trajectory is \(x(t)=x_0+(t-t_0)\). The maps compose because
\[
\phi_\tau\bigl(\phi_\sigma(x_0)\bigr)=x_0+\sigma+\tau=\phi_{\tau+\sigma}(x_0).
\]
This example separates the objects without adding advanced theory: \(f\) is the local rate, \(\{\phi_\tau\}\) is the finite-time evolution family, and \(t\mapsto\phi_{t-t_0}(x_0)\) is one trajectory in absolute clock time.



Using a population-activity vector as a proposed neural state gives a coordinate setting in which trajectories can be described (Cunningham and Yu 2014). A neural flow claim is stronger: it proposes that population states across supported initial conditions evolve according to one coherent finite-time family. Similar-looking trial trajectories or a pooled trajectory plot do not establish that shared family, especially when inputs, task conditions, or unmeasured state differ.
For behavior, a set of movement traces is likewise not automatically evidence for one behavioral flow. The traces may reflect different control inputs, parameters, state definitions, or measurement processes. Inferring a shared flow from such data is a methodological problem that requires assumptions and evaluation beyond this Concept Object.



At L2, Flow connects the stable Vector Field Concept to the reusable autonomous-system formalism without collapsing the instantaneous rule, one trajectory, an orbit, and the supported family of finite-time maps into one object. This distinction is essential before later recovery tasks can ask whether observed neural or behavioral trajectories support shared dynamics.

When should an input-dependent or explicitly time-dependent evolution be represented with notation other than a one-parameter autonomous flow?

These are later inference and modeling questions outside this bounded L2 scope.

title: Flow
text: A flow is a finite-time evolution family that, where well-defined, maps each initial state in its domain to the state reached after an elapsed time under one shared autonomous continuous-time rule.

title: Flow
text:
A vector field gives a local instantaneous rule, while a flow describes its accumulated effect over finite time across possible initial states. Fixing one initial state in a flow yields one trajectory; considering all supported initial states yields a consistent family of trajectories generated by the same dynamics.
This distinction prevents a collection of observed curves from being mistaken for a flow. A flow is not merely a dataset of trajectories: its time-evolution maps must act consistently on states and compose across successive time intervals. Teschl defines the flow of an autonomous differential equation by collecting its integral curves into one map (Teschl 2012, sec. 6.2).
The stable First-Order Autonomous Dynamical System Math Object is the canonical location for the existence, uniqueness, maximal-continuation, and regularity results that justify such maps. This Concept retains only the notation and distinctions needed to interpret finite-time evolution without duplicating those theorem-level derivations.

title: Flow
text:
Imagine the vector field as an arrow attached to every state. The flow answers a finite-time question: “Starting from this state, where does the shared rule carry the system after elapsed time \(\tau\)?”
There are two useful ways to hold part of the flow fixed:

Fix an initial state \(x_0\): varying elapsed time \(\tau\) traces one trajectory.
Fix an elapsed time \(\tau\): the map \(\phi_\tau\) moves every supported initial state to its state after that duration.

A flow is the coherent collection of these finite-time maps, not any unrelated collection of before-and-after pairs.

title: Flow
text:
Consider an autonomous Euclidean system
\[
\dot{x}=f(x),\qquad x\in\mathcal{X}.
\]
Suppose the active assumptions provide a unique maximal solution through each supported initial state. For \(x\in\mathcal{X}\), let \(I_x\) be the maximal elapsed-time interval containing \(0\) for the solution through \(x\), and define the supported domain
\[
W
=
\{(\tau,x)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathcal{X}:\tau\in I_x\}.
\]
The joint finite-time evolution map is
\[
\Phi:W\rightarrow\mathcal{X},
\qquad
\Phi(\tau,x)=\phi_\tau(x),
\]
where \(\phi_\tau(x)\) is the state reached after elapsed time \(\tau\) from \(x\). For fixed \(\tau\), the corresponding state map has the typed domain
\[
\operatorname{dom}(\phi_\tau)
=
\{x\in\mathcal{X}:(\tau,x)\in W\}.
\]
The supported set need not be all of \(\mathbb{R}\times\mathcal{X}\), and \(\operatorname{dom}(\phi_\tau)\) need not equal \(\mathcal{X}\). The evolution family satisfies
\[
\phi_0(x)=x,
\]
and the composition law only where the required evolutions are supported. Explicitly, if \(s\in I_x\) and \(\tau\in I_{\phi_s(x)}\), then \(s+\tau\in I_x\) and
\[
\phi_{\tau+s}(x)=\phi_\tau\bigl(\phi_s(x)\bigr).
\]
The first relation says that zero elapsed time leaves the state unchanged. The second says that evolving for \(s\) and then for \(\tau\) agrees with evolving once for the combined elapsed time. It is not a claim that every map is defined on all states or all elapsed times (Teschl 2012, sec. 6.2).
Local existence and uniqueness support this single-valued local finite-time evolution. Under the stronger condition \(f\in C^1\), the stable Math Object states that \(W\) is open and \(\Phi\) is jointly \(C^1\) in elapsed time and initial state; under the adopted LDG convention, this jointly regular map is the generated local flow. The regularity theorem and its derivation remain in the Math Object.
For an initial condition \(x(t_0)=x_0\), the associated trajectory can be written
\[
x(t)=\phi_{t-t_0}(x_0)
\]
when \(t-t_0\in I_{x_0}\), equivalently when \((t-t_0,x_0)\in W\). Here \(t\) is absolute clock time, whereas \(\tau=t-t_0\) is elapsed time from the initial condition.
When the active ODE assumptions make each curve \(\tau\mapsto\phi_\tau(x)\) differentiable in elapsed time, it satisfies
\[
\frac{d}{d\tau}\phi_\tau(x)
=
f\bigl(\phi_\tau(x)\bigr),
\]
and its derivative at zero recovers the vector field:
\[
f(x)=\left.\frac{d}{d\tau}\phi_\tau(x)\right|_{\tau=0}.
\]
This derivative is along one trajectory with respect to elapsed time. It does not by itself assert differentiability with respect to the initial state \(x\); joint initial-state regularity is the stronger local-flow conclusion above. These relations express the local-versus-finite-time distinction and are not an existence or uniqueness proof.
For a two-sided smooth local flow, reverse elapsed time supplies a local inverse: \(\phi_{-\tau}\) reverses \(\phi_\tau\) on the corresponding supported domains. This does not make \(\phi_\tau\) a globally defined bijection \(\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{X}\) for every \(\tau\) (Teschl 2012, sec. 6.2).
The one-parameter notation \(\phi_\tau\) is most natural for autonomous dynamics. Semiflows restricted to nonnegative elapsed time, explicitly time-dependent systems, and input-driven evolution are outside this bounded L2 Concept rather than silently treated as the same structure.

title: Flow
text:
\(\mathcal{X}\): the state space.
\(f\): the autonomous vector field or local instantaneous rule.
\(x_0\in\mathcal{X}\): an initial state value.
\(t_0\): the reference time of the initial condition.
\(t\): absolute clock time along a trajectory.
\(\tau\): elapsed flow time.
\(I_x\): the maximal elapsed-time interval containing \(0\) for the solution through \(x\).
\(W\): the supported elapsed-time/state pairs \((\tau,x)\) with \(\tau\in I_x\).
\(\Phi(\tau,x)=\phi_\tau(x)\): the joint local finite-time evolution map on \(W\); jointly \(C^1\) under the stated stronger flow condition.
\(\phi_\tau\): the finite-time state map on the states for which elapsed time \(\tau\) is defined; its domain may depend on \(\tau\) for a local flow.
\(\operatorname{dom}(\phi_\tau)=\{x\in\mathcal{X}:(\tau,x)\in W\}\): the supported states for one fixed elapsed time.
\(\phi_\tau(x_0)\): the state reached from \(x_0\) after elapsed time \(\tau\).
\(x(t)=\phi_{t-t_0}(x_0)\): the trajectory associated with one initial condition.

The symbol \(\phi\) is conventional. A source may use \(\Phi\), \(T_t\), or another symbol; the defining role and composition property matter more than the letter.

title: Embedding
text:
An embedding is an injective map that represents one space inside another while preserving the declared structure strongly enough that the original object can be recovered from its image.



Embedding language distinguishes a faithful representation of an object from a projection or visualization that may collapse distinct points or distort relevant structure.



A circle can be placed in the plane without self-identifying points. Mapping the same circle onto a line with overlaps would not faithfully embed it.



At the topological level, a map \(e:X\to Y\) is an embedding when it is injective and gives a homeomorphism between \(X\) and its image \(e(X)\) with the subspace topology. Smooth embeddings add smoothness and an injective derivative.
This L1 object uses only the representation principle; full topology and differential conditions belong to later objects. Whitney’s classical work establishes broad smooth embedding results for differentiable manifolds (Whitney 1936).




\(X\): source space.
\(Y\): ambient target space.
\(e:X\hookrightarrow Y\): embedding.
\(e(X)\): embedded image.




State Space supplies the source object whose states may be represented. Ambient Dimension supplies the target-space coordinate count.
Assumed background: functions, injectivity, and elementary continuity.










Concept
Distinction




Projection
May collapse distinct points and need not preserve the source structure.


Dimensionality reduction
An algorithmic goal; its output is not automatically a mathematical embedding.


Feature map
Any map to features; injectivity or structural preservation may be absent.


Manifold
A type of space that may be embedded; an embedding does not prove the data form a manifold.






An embedding does not imply isometry, low distortion under a chosen metric, unique coordinates, causal or mechanistic meaning, a manifold source, or successful recovery from finite noisy samples.



The map
\[
e(\theta)=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)
\]
represents the abstract circle in \(\mathbb R^2\) when \(\theta\) is understood modulo \(2\pi\). The coordinate image has ambient dimension two but one intrinsic circular degree of freedom.



Learned low-dimensional coordinates are often called embeddings. LDG requires specifying whether “embedding” is only an algorithmic label or a supported claim of injective structural preservation.



Embedding prepares precise manifold and topology language while preventing nonlinear visualization from being treated as evidence by itself.




Which structure should a scientific embedding preserve?
How can injectivity be assessed from finite samples?
What distortions matter for dynamics and behavior?





Whitney provides the inspected classical primary source for smooth manifold embedding results (Whitney 1936).





Defines injective structure-preserving representation.
Separates embedding from projection, features, and dimensionality reduction.
States that embedding does not prove a manifold or mechanism.

title: Deconvolution
text:
Deconvolution is the inverse problem of estimating an unknown input, source, or kernel from observations modeled as a convolution, usually in the presence of noise and incomplete information.



Convolution can smooth or suppress components of a signal. Recovering what preceded that filtering is often unstable: small observation errors can produce large changes in a naive inverse.



If a sensor blurs a sharp event with a known response kernel, deconvolution tries to infer the event that could have produced the blurred measurement. Multiple sources may fit nearly equally well once noise is present.



Let \(\mathcal U\) be a source space, \(\mathcal K\) a kernel space, and \(\mathcal Y\) an observation space. For a fixed kernel \(k\), define the convolution operator
\[
K_k:\mathcal U\to\mathcal Y,
\qquad
K_k u=k*u.
\]
The observed data follow a forward model such as
\[
y=K_k u+v,
\]
where \(v\) is observation noise under a declared observation law. Known-kernel deconvolution estimates \(u\) with \(k\) fixed. Blind deconvolution estimates both \(u\) and \(k\) and therefore has additional scaling, shift, boundary, and factorization ambiguities. Blind recovery is not identifiable without constraints that restrict these equivalences.


If \(K_k u_1=K_k u_2\), then the data cannot distinguish \(u_1\) and \(u_2\). Equivalently, their difference lies in the null space,
\[
u_1-u_2\in\ker K_k.
\]
Even when the null space is trivial, small singular values or nearly suppressed frequency components can make the inverse ill-conditioned: small perturbations in \(y\) produce large changes in a naive recovered source. Injectivity, stable inversion, and numerical conditioning are separate properties.



Under transform and boundary conditions for which convolution becomes multiplication,
\[
\widehat y(\omega)
=
\widehat k(\omega)\widehat u(\omega)
+
\widehat v(\omega).
\]
The formal inverse
\[
\widehat u(\omega)
=
\frac{\widehat y(\omega)}{\widehat k(\omega)}
\]
is defined only where \(\widehat k(\omega)\ne0\). If \(|\widehat k(\omega)|\) is small, the noise term is amplified by \(1/|\widehat k(\omega)|\). Zeros erase those components under the stated model. Finite windows, sampling, aliasing, padding, and circular-versus-linear convolution further change the implemented operator, so transform division is not a universal exact inverse.



A common regularized estimator is
\[
\widehat u_\lambda
\in
\arg\min_{u\in\mathcal U}
\left\{
\mathcal D(K_k u,y)
+
\lambda\mathcal R(u)
\right\},
\]
where \(\mathcal D\) is a data-fit or negative-log-likelihood term and \(\mathcal R\) encodes assumptions such as smoothness, sparsity, nonnegativity, or bounded variation. Regularization can stabilize inversion but introduces bias toward the preferred solution class. Different penalties or priors can select different sources that fit the data similarly.
A probabilistic formulation combines an observation likelihood and prior,
\[
p(u\mid y,k)
\propto
p(y\mid K_k u)\,p(u).
\]
A posterior or MAP estimate is conditional on those choices; it is not assumption-free recovery.
For blind deconvolution one may optimize over \((u,k)\),
\[
\min_{u,k}
\mathcal D(K_k u,y)
+
\lambda_u\mathcal R_u(u)
+
\lambda_k\mathcal R_k(k),
\]
but scale and shift conventions, kernel normalization/support, positivity, and other identifiability constraints must be declared.



A small forward residual \(\|K_k\widehat u-y\|\) checks consistency with the observation but does not prove source recovery. In a toy model with known ground truth, evaluation should separately report source error, event/support recovery, timing error, kernel error when estimated, and sensitivity to noise, sampling, boundaries, and regularization. Without ground truth, held-out forward prediction, calibration, interventions, or multiple observation channels provide indirect evidence only and cannot establish a unique source.
Richardson’s inspected paper supplies a primary convolutional image-restoration example, demonstrates sensitivity to noise and boundaries, and describes an iterative approximation without a general convergence proof (Richardson 1972). The general inverse-operator and regularization framing above is established inverse-problem background, not attributed solely to that algorithm.





\(\mathcal U,\mathcal K,\mathcal Y\): source, kernel, and observation spaces.
\(K_k:\mathcal U\to\mathcal Y\): convolution forward operator for kernel \(k\).
\(y\): observed convolved signal.
\(u\): unknown source or input.
\(k\): known or estimated kernel.
\(v\): observation noise.
\(\widehat u\): recovered source estimate.
\(\ker K_k\): source perturbations invisible to the forward operator.
\(\mathcal D\): data-fit or negative-log-likelihood term.
\(\mathcal R\): regularizer or prior penalty.
\(\lambda\): regularization strength.




Convolution supplies the forward operator. Observation Noise supplies the measurement uncertainty that makes inversion fragile.










Concept
Distinction




Inverse filtering
A direct inverse construction; deconvolution is the broader inverse problem and may require regularization or probabilistic inference.


Blind deconvolution
Both source and kernel are unknown, adding scale, shift, boundary, and factorization ambiguities that require explicit constraints.


Denoising
Removes or models noise without necessarily undoing a convolution operator.


Source separation
Separates multiple contributing sources; it is not automatically a convolution inverse.


Causal/mechanistic recovery
Claims a physical generator or cause. Mathematical recovery under a forward model does not establish this interpretation.


System identification
Estimates a system or kernel; deconvolution may instead assume the kernel and estimate the input.






Deconvolution does not imply exact recovery, a unique or stable inverse, a correct known kernel, identifiable blind factors, separation of signal from structured noise, unbiased regularization, or recovery of a biological cause from a measurement trace. A low forward residual can coexist with large source error.



Let the discrete kernel be \(k=(1/2,1/2)\), so
\[
y_n=\frac{u_n+u_{n-1}}{2}+v_n.
\]
For the alternating component \(u_n=(-1)^n\), the noiseless convolution is zero because adjacent values cancel. That component lies in the null space under an infinite/periodic idealization and cannot be recovered from \(y\). Components near that alternating frequency are strongly attenuated, so division amplifies noise.
A smoothness-regularized estimate can suppress the amplified component and improve stability, but it may also erase a true sharp event. Source error and forward fit must therefore be evaluated separately.



Examples include estimating neural events from calcium fluorescence or latent neural activity from a hemodynamic response. Recovery quality depends on kernel validity, sampling, noise, and prior assumptions.



At L2, Deconvolution provides a typed inverse-operator baseline with explicit identifiability, conditioning, regularization, and evaluation limits before recovered time courses are interpreted as latent states, dynamics, or mechanisms.




Which regularizers reflect defensible scientific assumptions?
When must kernel uncertainty be modeled jointly?
How should recovery be evaluated against known ground truth?





Richardson gives an inspected primary convolutional degradation and iterative restoration example, including noise and boundary effects (Richardson 1972).

title: Deconvolution
text: Deconvolution is the inverse problem of estimating an unknown input, source, or kernel from observations modeled as a convolution, usually in the presence of noise and incomplete information.

title: Deconvolution
text: Convolution can smooth or suppress components of a signal. Recovering what preceded that filtering is often unstable: small observation errors can produce large changes in a naive inverse.

title: Deconvolution
text: If a sensor blurs a sharp event with a known response kernel, deconvolution tries to infer the event that could have produced the blurred measurement. Multiple sources may fit nearly equally well once noise is present.

title: Deconvolution
text:
Let \(\mathcal U\) be a source space, \(\mathcal K\) a kernel space, and \(\mathcal Y\) an observation space. For a fixed kernel \(k\), define the convolution operator
\[
K_k:\mathcal U\to\mathcal Y,
\qquad
K_k u=k*u.
\]
The observed data follow a forward model such as
\[
y=K_k u+v,
\]
where \(v\) is observation noise under a declared observation law. Known-kernel deconvolution estimates \(u\) with \(k\) fixed. Blind deconvolution estimates both \(u\) and \(k\) and therefore has additional scaling, shift, boundary, and factorization ambiguities. Blind recovery is not identifiable without constraints that restrict these equivalences.


If \(K_k u_1=K_k u_2\), then the data cannot distinguish \(u_1\) and \(u_2\). Equivalently, their difference lies in the null space,
\[
u_1-u_2\in\ker K_k.
\]
Even when the null space is trivial, small singular values or nearly suppressed frequency components can make the inverse ill-conditioned: small perturbations in \(y\) produce large changes in a naive recovered source. Injectivity, stable inversion, and numerical conditioning are separate properties.



Under transform and boundary conditions for which convolution becomes multiplication,
\[
\widehat y(\omega)
=
\widehat k(\omega)\widehat u(\omega)
+
\widehat v(\omega).
\]
The formal inverse
\[
\widehat u(\omega)
=
\frac{\widehat y(\omega)}{\widehat k(\omega)}
\]
is defined only where \(\widehat k(\omega)\ne0\). If \(|\widehat k(\omega)|\) is small, the noise term is amplified by \(1/|\widehat k(\omega)|\). Zeros erase those components under the stated model. Finite windows, sampling, aliasing, padding, and circular-versus-linear convolution further change the implemented operator, so transform division is not a universal exact inverse.



A common regularized estimator is
\[
\widehat u_\lambda
\in
\arg\min_{u\in\mathcal U}
\left\{
\mathcal D(K_k u,y)
+
\lambda\mathcal R(u)
\right\},
\]
where \(\mathcal D\) is a data-fit or negative-log-likelihood term and \(\mathcal R\) encodes assumptions such as smoothness, sparsity, nonnegativity, or bounded variation. Regularization can stabilize inversion but introduces bias toward the preferred solution class. Different penalties or priors can select different sources that fit the data similarly.
A probabilistic formulation combines an observation likelihood and prior,
\[
p(u\mid y,k)
\propto
p(y\mid K_k u)\,p(u).
\]
A posterior or MAP estimate is conditional on those choices; it is not assumption-free recovery.
For blind deconvolution one may optimize over \((u,k)\),
\[
\min_{u,k}
\mathcal D(K_k u,y)
+
\lambda_u\mathcal R_u(u)
+
\lambda_k\mathcal R_k(k),
\]
but scale and shift conventions, kernel normalization/support, positivity, and other identifiability constraints must be declared.



A small forward residual \(\|K_k\widehat u-y\|\) checks consistency with the observation but does not prove source recovery. In a toy model with known ground truth, evaluation should separately report source error, event/support recovery, timing error, kernel error when estimated, and sensitivity to noise, sampling, boundaries, and regularization. Without ground truth, held-out forward prediction, calibration, interventions, or multiple observation channels provide indirect evidence only and cannot establish a unique source.
Richardson’s inspected paper supplies a primary convolutional image-restoration example, demonstrates sensitivity to noise and boundaries, and describes an iterative approximation without a general convergence proof (Richardson 1972). The general inverse-operator and regularization framing above is established inverse-problem background, not attributed solely to that algorithm.

text:
Concept
Distinction




Inverse filtering
A direct inverse construction; deconvolution is the broader inverse problem and may require regularization or probabilistic inference.


Blind deconvolution
Both source and kernel are unknown, adding scale, shift, boundary, and factorization ambiguities that require explicit constraints.


Denoising
Removes or models noise without necessarily undoing a convolution operator.

title: Deconvolution
text: Deconvolution does not imply exact recovery, a unique or stable inverse, a correct known kernel, identifiable blind factors, separation of signal from structured noise, unbiased regularization, or recovery of a biological cause from a measurement trace. A low forward residual can coexist with large source error.

title: Deconvolution
text:
Let the discrete kernel be \(k=(1/2,1/2)\), so
\[
y_n=\frac{u_n+u_{n-1}}{2}+v_n.
\]
For the alternating component \(u_n=(-1)^n\), the noiseless convolution is zero because adjacent values cancel. That component lies in the null space under an infinite/periodic idealization and cannot be recovered from \(y\). Components near that alternating frequency are strongly attenuated, so division amplifies noise.
A smoothness-regularized estimate can suppress the amplified component and improve stability, but it may also erase a true sharp event. Source error and forward fit must therefore be evaluated separately.

text: Examples include estimating neural events from calcium fluorescence or latent neural activity from a hemodynamic response. Recovery quality depends on kernel validity, sampling, noise, and prior assumptions.

title: Convolution
text:
Convolution combines a signal with a shifted kernel by summing or integrating lag-weighted contributions to produce an output.



Convolution is the canonical input-output operation for linear time-invariant filters. It provides a fixed-kernel baseline against which latent state dynamics can be compared.



At each output time, align the kernel with the input history, multiply overlapping values, and add them. The kernel determines which lags matter and with what sign.



For scalar functions \(k,u:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\), continuous convolution is
\[
(k*u)(t)
=
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}k(\tau)u(t-\tau)\,d\tau,
\]
at times for which the integral exists. A common sufficient condition is \(k\in L^1(\mathbb R)\) with bounded \(u\); other \(L^p\) conditions are possible and must be declared. Compact support is useful only together with sufficient local integrability or boundedness; support alone does not guarantee the integral exists.
For sequences \(k=(k_m)\) and \(u=(u_m)\),
\[
(k*u)_n
=
\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}k_m u_{n-m},
\]
when the series converges. Absolute summability of one sequence together with boundedness of the other is one sufficient condition; finite-support sequences give a finite sum.


For scalar functions or sequences, when all required integrals/sums exist and rearrangement is justified,
\[
k*u=u*k,
\]
\[
(k_1*k_2)*u=k_1*(k_2*u),
\]
and convolution is distributive and linear in each argument. These identities require compatible domains and convergence conditions. Matrix multiplication is not commutative, so analogous matrix-valued operations must retain order.



For input \(u(t)\in\mathbb R^m\), output \(y(t)\in\mathbb R^q\), and kernel \(H(\tau)\in\mathbb R^{q\times m}\),
\[
y(t)
=
\int H(\tau)u(t-\tau)\,d\tau
\]
is dimensionally well typed. Each output channel is a sum of convolutions of input channels with the corresponding scalar kernel entries. The expression \(u*H\) is not generally an interchangeable commutative form because vector/matrix multiplication order and dimensions matter.



For a causal LTI system initialized at \(t_0\) with zero initial state and no direct feedthrough, the output has the zero-state response
\[
y_{\mathrm{zs}}(t)
=
\int_{t_0}^{t}H(t-s)u(s)\,ds
=
\int_{0}^{t-t_0}H(\tau)u(t-\tau)\,d\tau.
\]
Causality is represented by \(H(\tau)=0\) for \(\tau<0\). The full state-space output can additionally contain an initial-condition response and direct feedthrough:
\[
y(t)
=
Ce^{A(t-t_0)}x(t_0)
+
\int_{t_0}^{t}Ce^{A(t-s)}Bu(s)\,ds
+
Du(t).
\]
Thus \(H(\tau)=Ce^{A\tau}B\) for \(\tau>0\) gives the ordinary zero-state kernel. The term \(Du(t)\) must be kept separate or represented by a generalized impulse contribution \(D\delta(\tau)\); it is not an ordinary function-valued lag kernel (Åström and Murray 2021, sec. 6.3).









NoteEstablished Mathematical / Computational Background



Under one common convention, cross-correlation is
\[
(r_{ku})(t)=\int \overline{k(\tau)}u(\tau+t)\,d\tau,
\]
so it compares shifted alignment rather than applying the same reversal convention as convolution. Conventions vary, especially for complex signals, and must be stated.
Finite recorded arrays require boundary choices such as zero padding, periodic extension, reflection, truncation, or reporting only valid overlaps. Circular convolution produced by a discrete Fourier transform is not the same as linear convolution unless padding and indexing are chosen accordingly. FFT multiplication is an implementation of convolution under stated transform/boundary conventions, not the definition of convolution.







\(k\): scalar kernel or impulse response.
\(H(\tau)\in\mathbb R^{q\times m}\): matrix-valued kernel.
\(u(t)\in\mathbb R^m\): input signal.
\(y(t)\in\mathbb R^q\): convolved output.
\(y_{\mathrm{zs}}\): zero-state response.
\(\tau\) or \(m\): lag variable.




Kernel defines the lag-dependent weighting function.










Concept
Distinction




Correlation
Compares shifted alignment under a declared conjugation/reversal convention; it is not automatically the same operation as convolution.


Circular convolution
Uses periodic indexing, as in an unpadded DFT implementation. Linear convolution requires appropriate padding or another boundary convention.


FFT multiplication
A computational method under transform and boundary assumptions, not the mathematical definition.


Filtering
A broader operation; LTI filtering is represented by convolution.


Kernel
The weighting function; convolution is the operation using it.


State-space response
May include initial-state response and direct feedthrough in addition to the zero-state convolution term.


Smoothing
One possible effect of particular kernels. Convolution kernels can also differentiate, delay, oscillate, or amplify.






Convolution does not imply causality, finite memory, invertibility, a known kernel, smoothing, stable dynamics, a particular boundary convention, linear biological mechanism, or that all time dependence is captured by a fixed filter. Algebraic identities do not apply when the relevant sums/integrals diverge or dimensions are incompatible.



With discrete kernel \(k=(1/2,1/2)\),
\[
y_n=\tfrac12u_n+\tfrac12u_{n-1},
\]
so the output averages the current and previous inputs. This smoothing loses some rapidly varying information.



Convolution appears in temporal receptive fields, sensor responses, smoothing, and hemodynamic models. Predictive success of a convolutional model does not establish hidden recurrent dynamics.



At L2, Convolution gives LDG explicit existence, dimensional, algebraic, causal, initial-condition, and direct-feedthrough boundaries for the fixed-kernel alternative before deconvolution or more complex latent temporal models.

title: Attractor
text:
An attractor is an invariant dynamical set toward which states from a surrounding basin approach under the specified forward evolution, with any additional minimality or transitivity convention stated explicitly.



Attractors organize long-time behavior across many initial conditions. They may be fixed points, periodic orbits, or more complicated invariant sets. The term is also used inconsistently, so LDG must specify the adopted convention rather than label any frequently visited region an attractor.



An attractor is not merely a place where trajectories are often seen. It is a set that the dynamics preserves and toward which a nontrivial collection of nearby initial states evolves.



Let \((\mathcal X,d)\) be a metric state space and let \(I_x\) be the supported elapsed-time interval through \(x\). For a nonempty closed set \(\Lambda\subseteq\mathcal X\), define its forward basin (or forward stable set in Teschl’s terminology) by
\[
B^+(\Lambda)
=
\left\{
x\in\mathcal X:
[0,\infty)\subseteq I_x
\text{ and }
\lim_{t\to\infty}d(\phi_t(x),\Lambda)=0
\right\},
\]
where
\[
d(x,\Lambda)=\inf_{z\in\Lambda}d(x,z).
\]
The support condition prevents finite-time termination from being mistaken for long-time attraction. Convergence is to the set: it does not require convergence to one point, one phase, or a specified rate.
A set \(\Lambda\) is attracting when it is invariant and \(B^+(\Lambda)\) contains a neighborhood of \(\Lambda\). This is local attraction unless \(B^+(\Lambda)\) equals the declared full forward domain.


LDG follows Teschl’s convention for this object: under a complete two-sided flow, an attractor is a nonempty closed invariant attracting set that is also topologically transitive. Topological transitivity means that for any nonempty relatively open \(U,V\subseteq\Lambda\), there exists \(t\in\mathbb R\) such that
\[
\phi_t(U)\cap V\ne\varnothing.
\]
This added condition excludes attracting supersets that decompose into dynamically separate invariant pieces. It is one established convention, not the unique definition used throughout dynamics. Forward semiflows, stochastic systems, random attractors, and input-driven systems require separately declared variants (Teschl 2012, sec. 8.1).



A trapping region \(E\) is an open connected set with compact closure such that
\[
\phi_t(\overline E)\subset E,
\qquad t>0.
\]
Under Teschl’s complete-flow assumptions,
\[
\Lambda_E
=
\omega^+(E)
=
\bigcap_{t\ge0}\phi_t(\overline E)
\]
is a nonempty compact connected invariant attracting set (Teschl 2012, sec. 8.1). This is a sufficient construction of an attracting set, not a necessary characterization and not, by itself, proof of topological transitivity. The omega-limit and trapping-region proofs remain deferred.



Attraction and Lyapunov stability are different predicates. A point or set can be Lyapunov stable without attracting a neighborhood, and convergence toward a set does not by itself establish Lyapunov stability. When both properties are required, they must be checked separately using the Stability definitions.





\(\Lambda\): the candidate invariant set.
\(d(x,\Lambda)=\inf_{z\in\Lambda}d(x,z)\): distance from a point to the set.
\(I_x\): supported elapsed-time interval through \(x\).
\(B^+(\Lambda)\) or \(W^+(\Lambda)\): forward basin/stable set of \(\Lambda\).
\(E\): trapping region with compact closure.
\(\omega^+(E)\): forward omega-limit set of \(E\).
\(\phi_t\): forward evolution; a complete two-sided flow is required for the adopted transitivity convention.
\(t\to\infty\): the long-time limit in scope.




Stability supplies perturbation and closeness distinctions. Flow supplies finite-time evolution and supported domains across initial states. Metric supplies the distance-to-set construction.










Concept
Distinction




Attracting set
Has an invariant set with a neighborhood basin. Under the adopted convention it becomes an attractor only after topological transitivity is also established.


Lyapunov-stable object
Stability means nearby trajectories remain close; attraction concerns convergence toward a set. Either property can require separate verification.


Limit cycle
An attracting periodic orbit can be an attractor, but attractors need not be periodic.


Basin
The basin is the set of initial states approaching the attractor, not the attractor itself.


Frequently visited region
High occupancy can arise from sampling, noise, slow motion, or external input without invariance, a neighborhood basin, forward support, or transitivity.


Trapping-region limit set
A sufficient construction of a compact connected attracting set; it is not automatically transitive and therefore not automatically an attractor under the adopted convention.






An attractor does not imply:

that every initial state approaches it;
a unique attractor or basin;
a fixed point rather than a periodic or more complex set;
robustness to parameter changes or stochastic forcing;
that an empirical density peak is an attractor;
that finite trajectories identify the full basin;
that one trajectory approaching \(\Lambda\) establishes attraction from a neighborhood;
that recurrence, slow motion, clustering, decoding, low reconstruction error, or a density peak establishes invariance or transitivity;
that attraction implies Lyapunov stability or robustness to perturbations; or
that attraction explains the biological mechanism producing the data.




For \(\dot x=-x\), \(\Lambda=\{0\}\) is invariant and
\[
x(t)=x_0e^{-t}\longrightarrow0
\]
for every \(x_0\in\mathbb R\). Thus \(B^+(\Lambda)=\mathbb R\), and the singleton is topologically transitive, so it is a point attractor under the adopted convention.
By contrast, for \(\dot x=0\), every singleton is Lyapunov stable, but the basin of \(\{p\}\) is only \(\{p\}\) and does not contain a neighborhood in \(\mathbb R\); it is not an attractor. An attracting periodic orbit supplies a non-point example, but a repelling or merely isolated periodic orbit does not.



Attractor language is used for persistent activity, categorical decisions, memories, and recurring population states. A defensible claim requires evidence for an invariant model set and attraction from perturbed initial states, not only clustering, decoding, or repeated visitation.



At L2, Attractor provides an explicit basin, support condition, distance-to-set convergence, selected transitivity convention, and trapping-region construction. It preserves LDG’s prohibition against treating visualization, occupancy, recurrence, or one convergent trace as dynamical evidence.
