title: Bounded Autoencoder Baseline
text:
A bounded autoencoder learns a deterministic feed-forward map from an observation to a fixed-width bottleneck and back to the observation space. Its purpose in LDG is modest: test whether a prespecified finite nonlinear encoder–decoder architecture improves held-out reconstruction over linear baselines under the same preprocessing and loss.
The bounded method excludes variational autoencoders, stochastic latent-variable models, recurrent or sequence autoencoders, dynamical autoencoders, contrastive objectives, denoising training, sparse or contractive penalties, and broad generative-model claims. Those are related families with different objectives and assumptions, not silent extensions of this baseline.



Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^p\) be observations. The data definition must state whether a row is a trial, subject, session, time point, condition average, trajectory window or another unit. Fit training preprocessing parameters only on the training split. With training mean \(\mu\) and a declared nonsingular diagonal scaling matrix \(S\), define
\[
u_i=S^{-1}(x_i-\mu).
\]
A reproducible bounded autoencoder must declare before test evaluation:

the training, validation and test split units;
missing-data and exclusion policies;
centering, scaling and any feature transforms;
bottleneck width \(d<p\);
the exact finite encoder and decoder layer widths;
activation functions, output activation and the presence or absence of biases;
the absence of skip connections that bypass the bottleneck;
parameter initialization, optimizer, learning-rate schedule and batch size;
maximum epochs, validation metric, early-stopping rule and checkpoint selection;
weight decay or other permitted ordinary training regularization; and
the number of random initializations and model-selection rule.

The core loss is mean squared reconstruction error in the transformed coordinates. If features require another loss because of their support or scientific meaning, that defines another bounded variant and must be compared separately rather than called the same MSE baseline.



For a fitted parameter pair \((\hat\theta,\hat\phi)\), the method returns:

an encoder \[
f_{\hat\theta}:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^d;
\]
a bottleneck code \[
z=f_{\hat\theta}(u);
\]
a decoder \[
g_{\hat\phi}:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^p;
\]
a transformed-coordinate reconstruction \[
\widehat u=g_{\hat\phi}(f_{\hat\theta}(u));
\]
and an original-unit reconstruction \[
\widehat x=\mu+S\widehat u.
\]

The code \(z\) is a learned deterministic feature vector. Calling it “latent” describes its internal unobserved role in the network; it does not make it a posterior latent variable, unique hidden cause or dynamical state.



Train the composition
\[
h_{\theta,\phi}=g_\phi\circ f_\theta
\]
to approximate the identity map on the training distribution while forcing all information through an undercomplete bottleneck. Auto-associative networks and nonlinear principal-component constructions use this identity-target arrangement to learn compact internal representations (Bourlard and Kamp 1988; Kramer 1991).
Compression alone does not guarantee useful structure. A sufficiently expressive encoder and decoder can memorize a finite training set even through a narrow code, and an overcomplete or bypassed architecture can learn an identity map without meaningful reduction. Capacity, validation and explicit baselines are therefore part of the scientific method, not merely implementation details (Goodfellow et al. 2016, chap. 14).



This autoencoder is not a probabilistic generative model. It specifies no prior \(p(z)\), observation likelihood \(p(x\mid z)\), posterior, observation-noise covariance or sampling procedure. Its assumptions are approximation and training choices:

the fixed network class contains a useful encoder–decoder composition;
MSE in the transformed feature coordinates reflects the reconstruction errors that matter;
the training and evaluation samples represent the intended deployment distributions;
the bottleneck and finite architecture constrain the fit enough to generalize;
the optimizer and initialization can find a useful solution; and
validation-based stopping and hyperparameter selection control overfitting adequately for the declared sample size.

A nonlinear autoencoder can fit a curved reconstruction map, but that fit is not evidence that the data-generating support is a smooth manifold or that the bottleneck is an intrinsic coordinate chart.





For a fixed feed-forward architecture with \(L_e\) encoder layers and \(L_d\) decoder layers, write schematically
\[
f_\theta(u)
=
\rho_{L_e}\!\left(
W^{(e)}_{L_e}
\rho_{L_e-1}(\cdots \rho_1(W^{(e)}_1u+b^{(e)}_1)\cdots)
+b^{(e)}_{L_e}
\right),
\]
and similarly
\[
g_\phi(z)
=
\eta_{L_d}\!\left(
W^{(d)}_{L_d}
\eta_{L_d-1}(\cdots \eta_1(W^{(d)}_1z+b^{(d)}_1)\cdots)
+b^{(d)}_{L_d}
\right).
\]
The bottleneck output dimension is exactly \(d\). Hidden activation functions and the output activation are fixed architecture choices. For unconstrained real-valued standardized features, a linear output layer is the ordinary MSE choice; bounded output activations change the representable range and should match declared preprocessing.



Let \(I_{\mathrm{tr}}\) index training observations. The bounded objective is
\[
\widehat R_{\mathrm{tr}}(\theta,\phi)
=
\frac{1}{|I_{\mathrm{tr}}|}
\sum_{i\in I_{\mathrm{tr}}}
\left\lVert
u_i-g_\phi(f_\theta(u_i))
\right\rVert_2^2
+
\lambda_e\Omega_e(\theta)
+
\lambda_d\Omega_d(\phi),
\]
where ordinary weight decay may be used through declared penalties \(\Omega_e,\Omega_d\); setting both coefficients to zero is allowed. Sparsity, denoising, contractive, adversarial, contrastive or probabilistic terms are outside this bounded objective.
Training returns an optimizer-dependent candidate rather than a guaranteed global minimizer. Validation loss selects the epoch and any architecture, bottleneck, regularization or optimization hyperparameters. The untouched test set is used once for final comparison.



If the encoder and decoder are linear, biases are handled consistently with centering, the bottleneck has width \(d\), and squared reconstruction error is optimized globally, the composite rank-\(d\) map recovers the principal PCA subspace under the ordinary centered equal-weight Euclidean formulation. The individual encoder and decoder matrices need not equal the PCA loading matrix and are not unique; it is the reconstructed subspace or composite map that has the PCA relationship (Bourlard and Kamp 1988; Baldi and Hornik 1989).
Nonlinear activations remove this closed-form equivalence and introduce nonconvex optimization. A nonlinear autoencoder should therefore be compared both with analytic PCA and with an architecture-matched linear autoencoder. Failure of the trained linear network to approach PCA performance is an implementation or optimization warning, not evidence against PCA.




The training procedure learns all declared encoder and decoder weights and biases, producing a composite reconstruction map and bottleneck codes for supplied observations. If validation selects among candidates, it also selects one epoch, seed or hyperparameter configuration under the declared rule.
It does not learn a probability distribution, intrinsic dimension, transition model, vector field, causal graph, physical measurement process or unique latent coordinate system.



The analyst fixes the observation and feature definitions, preprocessing family, split units, architecture search space or single architecture, bottleneck candidates, activations, loss, regularization family, optimizer family, seed count, training budget, early-stopping rule, selection metric and baselines. Validation may choose only among these predeclared candidates.
Parameter count is part of the method. Comparing a high-capacity nonlinear network with a linear baseline without reporting capacity and training budget confounds nonlinearity with flexibility and optimization effort.



The bounded autoencoder is order-blind. Permuting observation rows leaves the empirical objective unchanged, apart from stochastic minibatch order. If rows are time samples, the network sees a collection of feature vectors but no temporal succession, lag, derivative or transition relation.
Time may be encoded inside each input vector, for example through a fixed window, but then the autoencoder reconstructs that engineered window. It still does not learn dynamics. Recurrent, temporal-convolutional, predictive and sequence-to-sequence autoencoders are explicitly outside scope.



MSE imposes Euclidean squared reconstruction geometry after the declared scaling \(S\). Changing feature units or weights changes which discrepancies dominate. The decoder image
\[
\{g_{\hat\phi}(z):z\in\mathbb R^d\}
\]
can be curved, folded, self-intersecting or poorly constrained away from training codes. Neither low reconstruction error nor smooth interpolation proves that this image is a manifold, that the encoder is injective, or that Euclidean distance in code space corresponds to a scientifically meaningful metric.
The term “embedding” should therefore be used only as an algorithmic label unless injectivity and structural preservation are independently supported. A bottleneck map can send distinct observations to the same code and compensate only imperfectly through reconstruction.



No external class or behavioral label enters the core objective. The identity reconstruction target supplies a training target, so the method is often described as unsupervised or self-supervised depending on convention. Label-guided architecture selection, outcome-based component selection or downstream-task tuning adds supervision and must occur inside a leakage-safe validation protocol.
The absence of labels does not make the learned representation objective-free: MSE, architecture, preprocessing, bottleneck and sampling distribution provide strong inductive biases.



Training uses gradient-based empirical-risk minimization with a declared optimizer. For nonlinear networks the objective is nonconvex, so different initializations can produce different losses, reconstructions and code coordinates. Early stopping selects a point on an optimization trajectory using validation data; it is not proof of convergence or global optimality.
Report the optimizer, learning rates, batch size, epoch limit, stopping patience, checkpoint criterion, initialization and seed distribution. Multiple seeds should be treated as repeated candidate fits: selecting the best validation seed is model selection, and test results must not guide that selection.
There is no posterior inference. Encoding a new observation is a deterministic forward pass through \(f_{\hat\theta}\).




It is a direct nonlinear extension of bottleneck reconstruction with an explicit held-out objective.
A fixed feed-forward architecture is easy to state, train and compare with PCA.
Encoder and decoder maps permit deterministic out-of-sample application without rebuilding a graph.
Reconstruction residuals can be inspected in original feature units as well as transformed units.
Architecture, capacity and optimization can be stress-tested through matched controls and multiple seeds.
It provides a deliberately weak neural baseline before introducing probabilistic, temporal or generative claims.





Memorization: a flexible network can assign sample-specific codes and reconstruct training observations without learning reusable structure.
Overfitting: training loss decreases while validation or test loss worsens.
Identity shortcuts: overcomplete layers, skip connections or preprocessing leakage can permit trivial copying; this bounded method forbids bottleneck-bypassing skips.
Dead units: saturating or rectified activations can leave bottleneck or hidden units inactive over the data range.
Code collapse: optimization can map most observations to nearly identical codes, often yielding a mean-like reconstruction and poor retained variation.
Scale dependence: high-variance or poorly scaled features dominate MSE.
Outlier sensitivity: squared error can devote capacity to atypical observations.
Optimization instability: seeds, learning rates, batch order and stopping epochs can change the solution.
Distribution shift: accurate reconstruction on the training distribution need not generalize across subjects, sessions, conditions or acquisition systems.
Interpolation artifacts: decoder outputs between observed codes can be implausible even when training reconstructions are accurate.
Noninjective encoding: distinct inputs can share a code, preventing faithful recovery.
Unused capacity: some bottleneck coordinates can be constant or redundant; nominal width is not the number of independently used coordinates.
Nuisance preservation: MSE rewards reconstruction of artifacts and irrelevant variance as readily as scientific signal.
Evaluation leakage: fitting scaling, architecture, bottleneck, early stopping or seed selection with test observations makes performance optimistic.
Interpretive overreach: a visually organized code can be mistaken for manifold coordinates, dynamics, mechanism or causal variables.

Kramer explicitly notes the tradeoff between insufficient network capacity and overfitting in nonlinear auto-associative reconstruction (Kramer 1991). Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville likewise emphasize that copying objectives can learn little about the data distribution when model capacity is too great (Goodfellow et al. 2016, chap. 14).



Autoencoder parameters and codes are generally non-identifiable. If an invertible transformation
\[
r:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d
\]
and its inverse are representable by the chosen network classes on the relevant code set, then
\[
f'(u)=r(f(u)),
\qquad
g'(z')=g(r^{-1}(z'))
\]
produce the same composite reconstruction. The observed reconstruction objective cannot prefer one such coordinate system without additional constraints.
Finite networks also admit more specific symmetries:

hidden units can be permuted while compensating in adjacent weight matrices;
sign changes can be compensated for compatible odd or linear activations;
positive scalings can be moved across positively homogeneous layers such as ReLU layers;
redundant or dead units can change parameters without changing the realized map; and
equal-function parameterizations can arise from multiple optimization paths.

For a linear autoencoder, the encoder and decoder factors are nonunique even when the principal reconstruction subspace is uniquely determined (Baldi and Hornik 1989). For nonlinear autoencoders, the equivalence can extend beyond rotations and scalings to nonlinear bottleneck reparameterizations supported by the architecture.
Consequently, axis names, ordering and Euclidean distances in code space are not intrinsically identified. Alignment across seeds can aid comparison but does not establish unique biological coordinates.




Training mean: reconstruct every observation using the training mean. This is the \(d=0\) reference.
PCA: the required rank-\(d\) analytic linear reconstruction baseline using identical training preprocessing and MSE geometry.
Linear autoencoder: use the same bottleneck and comparable layer layout with identity activations. At a well-optimized global solution it should approach the PCA principal-subspace reconstruction, providing an implementation control.
Factor Analysis: a static probabilistic latent-variable comparison with a latent distribution, diagonal feature-specific residual covariance, likelihood and conditional latent inference. The deterministic autoencoder has none of these probabilistic quantities and should not inherit their interpretation.
Frozen random encoder: keep an architecture-matched random encoder fixed and train only a decoder, repeating over seeds. This tests whether learned encoding improves on generic nonlinear features.
Capacity-matched alternatives: compare declared widths, parameter counts, optimization budgets and regularization rather than attributing every gain to nonlinearity.

An autoencoder that only beats the mean but not PCA has not demonstrated useful nonlinear reconstruction. A nonlinear gain over PCA is evidence about held-out MSE under the tested architecture and distribution, not evidence for a manifold or mechanism.



A leakage-safe evaluation should include:

Independent split units: hold out complete trials, trajectories, subjects, sessions or conditions as appropriate. Adjacent time points from one trajectory should not be scattered across folds when dependence matters.
Training-only preprocessing: fit centering, scaling, imputation and feature selection inside the training split.
Validation-only selection: choose bottleneck, widths, activations, regularization, epoch and seed using validation data, preferably through nested evaluation when many candidates are explored.
Untouched test reconstruction: report \[
\operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{test}}
=
\frac{1}{|I_{\mathrm{test}}|}
\sum_{i\in I_{\mathrm{test}}}
\left\lVert
u_i-g_{\hat\phi}(f_{\hat\theta}(u_i))
\right\rVert_2^2,
\] along with per-feature and original-unit residual summaries.
Generalization gap: report training, validation and test losses rather than only the selected test score.
Seed stability: report the distribution across predeclared random seeds and distinguish best-validation selection from average performance.
Baselines and controls: compare the mean, rank-matched PCA, linear autoencoder, frozen-random encoder and capacity-matched variants.
Code diagnostics: report active-coordinate variance, duplicated/dead units and sensitivity to preprocessing. Code plots are diagnostic, not evidence by themselves.
Distribution shift: when scientifically relevant, perform subject-, session-, condition- or acquisition-held-out tests rather than only random within-distribution splits.
Secondary tasks: fit downstream predictors inside a nested training procedure. Decoding performance is a separate criterion and does not validate the reconstruction representation as a mechanism.

PCA and autoencoder losses must be computed in the same transformed metric. Factor Analysis should primarily be judged by held-out likelihood or predictive distribution; its conditional-mean reconstruction may be reported secondarily but is model-dependent and not directly equivalent to deterministic MSE training.



A future non-executable toy model should sample a scalar parameter \(s\) and generate observations in \(\mathbb R^3\) by
\[
x(s)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
s\\
s^2\\
0.3\sin(2s)
\end{pmatrix}
+
\varepsilon,
\]
with declared bounded \(s\) range and isotropic observation noise. The generation record should retain \(s\), but neither PCA nor the autoencoder may use it during fitting.
Compare a mean predictor, rank-one PCA, a rank-one linear autoencoder, a fixed small nonlinear autoencoder with one-dimensional bottleneck, and a frozen-random-encoder control. Select epochs and regularization using validation observations and evaluate held-out MSE on independently sampled \(s\) values. Record multiple seeds, dead-code frequency and code monotonicity with \(s\) only as a generation-side diagnostic.
Required negative controls are: independent full-dimensional Gaussian data, where a one-dimensional curved explanation is false; a high-capacity architecture trained on very few points to expose memorization; and a shifted test range of \(s\) to expose extrapolation failure. Even if the nonlinear autoencoder reconstructs the curved example better than PCA, the valid conclusion is limited to that simulator and loss. No data, code or results are created in this Method Object.



The bounded autoencoder is LDG’s canonical deterministic nonlinear reconstruction baseline. It asks whether finite nonlinear function classes improve held-out reconstruction before stronger claims about geometry, probability or dynamics are entertained.






WarningWhat this does NOT imply



Low reconstruction error or an appealing bottleneck visualization does not prove a manifold, establish intrinsic dimension, identify unique latent coordinates, discover dynamics, recover a mechanism, or support causal interpretation. A narrow code is an architecture choice; a nonlinear decoder image is a fitted function; neither is automatically the true state space of the system.




No modality-specific empirical claim is retained. A feed-forward autoencoder could reconstruct fixed trajectory summaries or windows, but it would ignore temporal succession and would not establish behavioral state, movement dynamics or mechanism.



No modality-specific empirical claim is retained. Gaze samples, event summaries and aligned windows define different reconstruction problems; an organized code would not identify oculomotor coordinates or causal control variables.



No modality-specific empirical claim is retained. Channel scaling, rereferencing, artifact handling, subject splits and sensor geometry would determine the loss; bottleneck coordinates would not automatically be neural sources.



No modality-specific empirical claim is retained. A deterministic reconstruction baseline can test nonlinear compression of declared sensor or unit features, but held-out units, trials, conditions and sessions are distinct generalization problems. Reconstruction alone does not establish a neural manifold or dynamics.





Bourlard and Kamp analyze multilayer perceptron auto-association and its connection to singular-value decomposition, supplying an early technical basis for bottleneck reconstruction (Bourlard and Kamp 1988).
Baldi and Hornik characterize the squared-error landscape of layered linear networks and show the auto-associative principal-subspace solution while noting encoder/decoder factor nonuniqueness (Baldi and Hornik 1989).
Kramer formulates nonlinear principal-component analysis using a feed-forward auto-associative bottleneck network and squared reconstruction error, while discussing architecture capacity and overfitting (Kramer 1991).





Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville provide an inspected authoritative synthesis of undercomplete and regularized autoencoders, encoder/decoder notation, reconstruction objectives, capacity and identity-copying failures (Goodfellow et al. 2016, chap. 14). Denoising, sparse, contractive and variational extensions discussed there are outside this bounded method.





Which architecture-matched control best separates nonlinear benefit from parameter-count and optimization effects?
How should latent-code stability be compared when nonlinear reparameterizations preserve reconstruction?
Which held-out split reflects the intended scientific use: trials, conditions, subjects, sessions or acquisition systems?

title: Bounded Autoencoder Baseline
text:
A bounded autoencoder learns a deterministic feed-forward map from an observation to a fixed-width bottleneck and back to the observation space. Its purpose in LDG is modest: test whether a prespecified finite nonlinear encoder–decoder architecture improves held-out reconstruction over linear baselines under the same preprocessing and loss.
The bounded method excludes variational autoencoders, stochastic latent-variable models, recurrent or sequence autoencoders, dynamical autoencoders, contrastive objectives, denoising training, sparse or contractive penalties, and broad generative-model claims. Those are related families with different objectives and assumptions, not silent extensions of this baseline.

title: Bounded Autoencoder Baseline
Bounded Autoencoder Baseline
text:
For a fitted parameter pair \((\hat\theta,\hat\phi)\), the method returns:

an encoder \[
f_{\hat\theta}:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^d;
\]
a bottleneck code \[
z=f_{\hat\theta}(u);
\]
a decoder \[
g_{\hat\phi}:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^p;
\]
a transformed-coordinate reconstruction \[
\widehat u=g_{\hat\phi}(f_{\hat\theta}(u));
\]
and an original-unit reconstruction \[
\widehat x=\mu+S\widehat u.
\]

The code \(z\) is a learned deterministic feature vector. Calling it “latent” describes its internal unobserved role in the network; it does not make it a posterior latent variable, unique hidden cause or dynamical state.

title: Bounded Autoencoder Baseline
text:
Train the composition
\[
h_{\theta,\phi}=g_\phi\circ f_\theta
\]
to approximate the identity map on the training distribution while forcing all information through an undercomplete bottleneck. Auto-associative networks and nonlinear principal-component constructions use this identity-target arrangement to learn compact internal representations (Bourlard and Kamp 1988; Kramer 1991).
Compression alone does not guarantee useful structure. A sufficiently expressive encoder and decoder can memorize a finite training set even through a narrow code, and an overcomplete or bypassed architecture can learn an identity map without meaningful reduction. Capacity, validation and explicit baselines are therefore part of the scientific method, not merely implementation details (Goodfellow et al. 2016, chap. 14).

title: Bounded Autoencoder Baseline
Bounded Autoencoder Baseline
text:
For a fixed feed-forward architecture with \(L_e\) encoder layers and \(L_d\) decoder layers, write schematically
\[
f_\theta(u)
=
\rho_{L_e}\!\left(
W^{(e)}_{L_e}
\rho_{L_e-1}(\cdots \rho_1(W^{(e)}_1u+b^{(e)}_1)\cdots)
+b^{(e)}_{L_e}
\right),
\]
and similarly
\[
g_\phi(z)
=
\eta_{L_d}\!\left(
W^{(d)}_{L_d}
\eta_{L_d-1}(\cdots \eta_1(W^{(d)}_1z+b^{(d)}_1)\cdots)
+b^{(d)}_{L_d}
\right).
\]
The bottleneck output dimension is exactly \(d\). Hidden activation functions and the output activation are fixed architecture choices. For unconstrained real-valued standardized features, a linear output layer is the ordinary MSE choice; bounded output activations change the representable range and should match declared preprocessing.



Let \(I_{\mathrm{tr}}\) index training observations. The bounded objective is
\[
\widehat R_{\mathrm{tr}}(\theta,\phi)
=
\frac{1}{|I_{\mathrm{tr}}|}
\sum_{i\in I_{\mathrm{tr}}}
\left\lVert
u_i-g_\phi(f_\theta(u_i))
\right\rVert_2^2
+
\lambda_e\Omega_e(\theta)
+
\lambda_d\Omega_d(\phi),
\]
where ordinary weight decay may be used through declared penalties \(\Omega_e,\Omega_d\); setting both coefficients to zero is allowed. Sparsity, denoising, contractive, adversarial, contrastive or probabilistic terms are outside this bounded objective.
Training returns an optimizer-dependent candidate rather than a guaranteed global minimizer. Validation loss selects the epoch and any architecture, bottleneck, regularization or optimization hyperparameters. The untouched test set is used once for final comparison.



If the encoder and decoder are linear, biases are handled consistently with centering, the bottleneck has width \(d\), and squared reconstruction error is optimized globally, the composite rank-\(d\) map recovers the principal PCA subspace under the ordinary centered equal-weight Euclidean formulation. The individual encoder and decoder matrices need not equal the PCA loading matrix and are not unique; it is the reconstructed subspace or composite map that has the PCA relationship (Bourlard and Kamp 1988; Baldi and Hornik 1989).
Nonlinear activations remove this closed-form equivalence and introduce nonconvex optimization. A nonlinear autoencoder should therefore be compared both with analytic PCA and with an architecture-matched linear autoencoder. Failure of the trained linear network to approach PCA performance is an implementation or optimization warning, not evidence against PCA.

title: Bounded Autoencoder Baseline
text:
The training procedure learns all declared encoder and decoder weights and biases, producing a composite reconstruction map and bottleneck codes for supplied observations. If validation selects among candidates, it also selects one epoch, seed or hyperparameter configuration under the declared rule.
It does not learn a probability distribution, intrinsic dimension, transition model, vector field, causal graph, physical measurement process or unique latent coordinate system.

title: Bounded Autoencoder Baseline
text:
The analyst fixes the observation and feature definitions, preprocessing family, split units, architecture search space or single architecture, bottleneck candidates, activations, loss, regularization family, optimizer family, seed count, training budget, early-stopping rule, selection metric and baselines. Validation may choose only among these predeclared candidates.
Parameter count is part of the method. Comparing a high-capacity nonlinear network with a linear baseline without reporting capacity and training budget confounds nonlinearity with flexibility and optimization effort.

title: Bounded Autoencoder Baseline
text:
The bounded autoencoder is order-blind. Permuting observation rows leaves the empirical objective unchanged, apart from stochastic minibatch order. If rows are time samples, the network sees a collection of feature vectors but no temporal succession, lag, derivative or transition relation.
Time may be encoded inside each input vector, for example through a fixed window, but then the autoencoder reconstructs that engineered window. It still does not learn dynamics. Recurrent, temporal-convolutional, predictive and sequence-to-sequence autoencoders are explicitly outside scope.

title: Bounded Autoencoder Baseline
text:
MSE imposes Euclidean squared reconstruction geometry after the declared scaling \(S\). Changing feature units or weights changes which discrepancies dominate. The decoder image
\[
\{g_{\hat\phi}(z):z\in\mathbb R^d\}
\]
can be curved, folded, self-intersecting or poorly constrained away from training codes. Neither low reconstruction error nor smooth interpolation proves that this image is a manifold, that the encoder is injective, or that Euclidean distance in code space corresponds to a scientifically meaningful metric.
The term “embedding” should therefore be used only as an algorithmic label unless injectivity and structural preservation are independently supported. A bottleneck map can send distinct observations to the same code and compensate only imperfectly through reconstruction.

title: Bounded Autoencoder Baseline
text:
No external class or behavioral label enters the core objective. The identity reconstruction target supplies a training target, so the method is often described as unsupervised or self-supervised depending on convention. Label-guided architecture selection, outcome-based component selection or downstream-task tuning adds supervision and must occur inside a leakage-safe validation protocol.
The absence of labels does not make the learned representation objective-free: MSE, architecture, preprocessing, bottleneck and sampling distribution provide strong inductive biases.

title: Bounded Autoencoder Baseline
text:
Training uses gradient-based empirical-risk minimization with a declared optimizer. For nonlinear networks the objective is nonconvex, so different initializations can produce different losses, reconstructions and code coordinates. Early stopping selects a point on an optimization trajectory using validation data; it is not proof of convergence or global optimality.
Report the optimizer, learning rates, batch size, epoch limit, stopping patience, checkpoint criterion, initialization and seed distribution. Multiple seeds should be treated as repeated candidate fits: selecting the best validation seed is model selection, and test results must not guide that selection.
There is no posterior inference. Encoding a new observation is a deterministic forward pass through \(f_{\hat\theta}\).

title: Bounded Autoencoder Baseline
text:
It is a direct nonlinear extension of bottleneck reconstruction with an explicit held-out objective.
A fixed feed-forward architecture is easy to state, train and compare with PCA.
Encoder and decoder maps permit deterministic out-of-sample application without rebuilding a graph.
Reconstruction residuals can be inspected in original feature units as well as transformed units.
Architecture, capacity and optimization can be stress-tested through matched controls and multiple seeds.
It provides a deliberately weak neural baseline before introducing probabilistic, temporal or generative claims.

title: Bounded Autoencoder Baseline
text:
Memorization: a flexible network can assign sample-specific codes and reconstruct training observations without learning reusable structure.
Overfitting: training loss decreases while validation or test loss worsens.
Identity shortcuts: overcomplete layers, skip connections or preprocessing leakage can permit trivial copying; this bounded method forbids bottleneck-bypassing skips.
Dead units: saturating or rectified activations can leave bottleneck or hidden units inactive over the data range.
Code collapse: optimization can map most observations to nearly identical codes, often yielding a mean-like reconstruction and poor retained variation.
Scale dependence: high-variance or poorly scaled features dominate MSE.
Outlier sensitivity: squared error can devote capacity to atypical observations.
Optimization instability: seeds, learning rates, batch order and stopping epochs can change the solution.
Distribution shift: accurate reconstruction on the training distribution need not generalize across subjects, sessions, conditions or acquisition systems.
Interpolation artifacts: decoder outputs between observed codes can be implausible even when training reconstructions are accurate.
Noninjective encoding: distinct inputs can share a code, preventing faithful recovery.
Unused capacity: some bottleneck coordinates can be constant or redundant; nominal width is not the number of independently used coordinates.
Nuisance preservation: MSE rewards reconstruction of artifacts and irrelevant variance as readily as scientific signal.
Evaluation leakage: fitting scaling, architecture, bottleneck, early stopping or seed selection with test observations makes performance optimistic.
Interpretive overreach: a visually organized code can be mistaken for manifold coordinates, dynamics, mechanism or causal variables.

Kramer explicitly notes the tradeoff between insufficient network capacity and overfitting in nonlinear auto-associative reconstruction (Kramer 1991). Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville likewise emphasize that copying objectives can learn little about the data distribution when model capacity is too great (Goodfellow et al. 2016, chap. 14).

title: Bounded Autoencoder Baseline
text:
Autoencoder parameters and codes are generally non-identifiable. If an invertible transformation
\[
r:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d
\]
and its inverse are representable by the chosen network classes on the relevant code set, then
\[
f'(u)=r(f(u)),
\qquad
g'(z')=g(r^{-1}(z'))
\]
produce the same composite reconstruction. The observed reconstruction objective cannot prefer one such coordinate system without additional constraints.
Finite networks also admit more specific symmetries:

hidden units can be permuted while compensating in adjacent weight matrices;
sign changes can be compensated for compatible odd or linear activations;
positive scalings can be moved across positively homogeneous layers such as ReLU layers;
redundant or dead units can change parameters without changing the realized map; and
equal-function parameterizations can arise from multiple optimization paths.

For a linear autoencoder, the encoder and decoder factors are nonunique even when the principal reconstruction subspace is uniquely determined (Baldi and Hornik 1989). For nonlinear autoencoders, the equivalence can extend beyond rotations and scalings to nonlinear bottleneck reparameterizations supported by the architecture.
Consequently, axis names, ordering and Euclidean distances in code space are not intrinsically identified. Alignment across seeds can aid comparison but does not establish unique biological coordinates.

title: Bounded Autoencoder Baseline
text:
Training mean: reconstruct every observation using the training mean. This is the \(d=0\) reference.
PCA: the required rank-\(d\) analytic linear reconstruction baseline using identical training preprocessing and MSE geometry.
Linear autoencoder: use the same bottleneck and comparable layer layout with identity activations. At a well-optimized global solution it should approach the PCA principal-subspace reconstruction, providing an implementation control.
Factor Analysis: a static probabilistic latent-variable comparison with a latent distribution, diagonal feature-specific residual covariance, likelihood and conditional latent inference. The deterministic autoencoder has none of these probabilistic quantities and should not inherit their interpretation.
Frozen random encoder: keep an architecture-matched random encoder fixed and train only a decoder, repeating over seeds. This tests whether learned encoding improves on generic nonlinear features.
Capacity-matched alternatives: compare declared widths, parameter counts, optimization budgets and regularization rather than attributing every gain to nonlinearity.

An autoencoder that only beats the mean but not PCA has not demonstrated useful nonlinear reconstruction. A nonlinear gain over PCA is evidence about held-out MSE under the tested architecture and distribution, not evidence for a manifold or mechanism.

title: Bounded Autoencoder Baseline
text:
A leakage-safe evaluation should include:

Independent split units: hold out complete trials, trajectories, subjects, sessions or conditions as appropriate. Adjacent time points from one trajectory should not be scattered across folds when dependence matters.
Training-only preprocessing: fit centering, scaling, imputation and feature selection inside the training split.
Validation-only selection: choose bottleneck, widths, activations, regularization, epoch and seed using validation data, preferably through nested evaluation when many candidates are explored.
Untouched test reconstruction: report \[
\operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{test}}
=
\frac{1}{|I_{\mathrm{test}}|}
\sum_{i\in I_{\mathrm{test}}}
\left\lVert
u_i-g_{\hat\phi}(f_{\hat\theta}(u_i))
\right\rVert_2^2,
\] along with per-feature and original-unit residual summaries.
Generalization gap: report training, validation and test losses rather than only the selected test score.
Seed stability: report the distribution across predeclared random seeds and distinguish best-validation selection from average performance.
Baselines and controls: compare the mean, rank-matched PCA, linear autoencoder, frozen-random encoder and capacity-matched variants.
Code diagnostics: report active-coordinate variance, duplicated/dead units and sensitivity to preprocessing. Code plots are diagnostic, not evidence by themselves.
Distribution shift: when scientifically relevant, perform subject-, session-, condition- or acquisition-held-out tests rather than only random within-distribution splits.
Secondary tasks: fit downstream predictors inside a nested training procedure. Decoding performance is a separate criterion and does not validate the reconstruction representation as a mechanism.

PCA and autoencoder losses must be computed in the same transformed metric. Factor Analysis should primarily be judged by held-out likelihood or predictive distribution; its conditional-mean reconstruction may be reported secondarily but is model-dependent and not directly equivalent to deterministic MSE training.

title: Bounded Autoencoder Baseline
text:
A future non-executable toy model should sample a scalar parameter \(s\) and generate observations in \(\mathbb R^3\) by
\[
x(s)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
s\\
s^2\\
0.3\sin(2s)
\end{pmatrix}
+
\varepsilon,
\]
with declared bounded \(s\) range and isotropic observation noise. The generation record should retain \(s\), but neither PCA nor the autoencoder may use it during fitting.
Compare a mean predictor, rank-one PCA, a rank-one linear autoencoder, a fixed small nonlinear autoencoder with one-dimensional bottleneck, and a frozen-random-encoder control. Select epochs and regularization using validation observations and evaluate held-out MSE on independently sampled \(s\) values. Record multiple seeds, dead-code frequency and code monotonicity with \(s\) only as a generation-side diagnostic.
Required negative controls are: independent full-dimensional Gaussian data, where a one-dimensional curved explanation is false; a high-capacity architecture trained on very few points to expose memorization; and a shifted test range of \(s\) to expose extrapolation failure. Even if the nonlinear autoencoder reconstructs the curved example better than PCA, the valid conclusion is limited to that simulator and loss. No data, code or results are created in this Method Object.

title: Bounded Autoencoder Baseline
text:
The bounded autoencoder is LDG’s canonical deterministic nonlinear reconstruction baseline. It asks whether finite nonlinear function classes improve held-out reconstruction before stronger claims about geometry, probability or dynamics are entertained.






WarningWhat this does NOT imply



Low reconstruction error or an appealing bottleneck visualization does not prove a manifold, establish intrinsic dimension, identify unique latent coordinates, discover dynamics, recover a mechanism, or support causal interpretation. A narrow code is an architecture choice; a nonlinear decoder image is a fitted function; neither is automatically the true state space of the system.




No modality-specific empirical claim is retained. A feed-forward autoencoder could reconstruct fixed trajectory summaries or windows, but it would ignore temporal succession and would not establish behavioral state, movement dynamics or mechanism.



No modality-specific empirical claim is retained. Gaze samples, event summaries and aligned windows define different reconstruction problems; an organized code would not identify oculomotor coordinates or causal control variables.



No modality-specific empirical claim is retained. Channel scaling, rereferencing, artifact handling, subject splits and sensor geometry would determine the loss; bottleneck coordinates would not automatically be neural sources.



No modality-specific empirical claim is retained. A deterministic reconstruction baseline can test nonlinear compression of declared sensor or unit features, but held-out units, trials, conditions and sessions are distinct generalization problems. Reconstruction alone does not establish a neural manifold or dynamics.

title: Bounded Autoencoder Baseline
text:
Bourlard and Kamp analyze multilayer perceptron auto-association and its connection to singular-value decomposition, supplying an early technical basis for bottleneck reconstruction (Bourlard and Kamp 1988).
Baldi and Hornik characterize the squared-error landscape of layered linear networks and show the auto-associative principal-subspace solution while noting encoder/decoder factor nonuniqueness (Baldi and Hornik 1989).
Kramer formulates nonlinear principal-component analysis using a feed-forward auto-associative bottleneck network and squared reconstruction error, while discussing architecture capacity and overfitting (Kramer 1991).

title: Bounded Autoencoder Baseline
text: Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville provide an inspected authoritative synthesis of undercomplete and regularized autoencoders, encoder/decoder notation, reconstruction objectives, capacity and identity-copying failures (Goodfellow et al. 2016, chap. 14). Denoising, sparse, contractive and variational extensions discussed there are outside this bounded method.

title: Diffusion Maps
text:
Diffusion Maps construct data-dependent spectral coordinates from a random walk on a weighted similarity graph. The method replaces direct ambient distance by diffusion distance: two sampled observations are close when their distributions over destinations after a declared number of graph-walk steps are similar. Truncated eigenvectors of the resulting Markov operator provide Euclidean coordinates that approximate this distance (Coifman and Lafon 2006).
The unit of analysis is a sampled observation or graph vertex. This object covers the finite-sample, symmetric-affinity, reversible construction. Directed affinities and nonreversible operators are discussed as a boundary, not silently treated as the same algorithm.
Assumed background: a similarity or affinity kernel is a nonnegative function used to weight pairs of observations, and a Markov operator maps a function or probability distribution through one step of a stochastic transition rule. These meanings are not supplied by knowledge/concepts/kernel.qmd: that repository object defines a temporal impulse-response/filter kernel and is not a prerequisite for Diffusion Maps.



Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) be observations and let \(\rho(x_i,x_j)\) be a declared dissimilarity, commonly a metric after fixed preprocessing. A reproducible analysis must specify:

the observational unit, selected sample, features, centering/scaling, missing-data treatment, and dependence structure;
the dissimilarity \(\rho\) and whether it is scientifically meaningful locally;
the affinity family and bandwidth convention;
whether the graph is fully connected, \(k\)-nearest-neighbor, mutual-neighbor, radius-truncated, or otherwise sparsified and symmetrized;
treatment of self-affinities, isolated vertices, duplicate observations, and connected components;
density-normalization exponent \(\alpha\);
diffusion time \(t\), retained coordinate count \(m\), and truncation rule; and
any out-of-sample extension and all parameters fitted from training data.

This object uses the Gaussian-style convention
\[
K_{ij}=\exp\!\left[-\frac{\rho(x_i,x_j)^2}{\varepsilon}\right],
\]
possibly followed by declared sparsification. Other conventions place \(2\sigma^2\) or \(4\varepsilon\) in the denominator, so a reported bandwidth value is meaningless without its formula.



For fixed choices, Diffusion Maps return:

a normalized affinity matrix \(K^{(\alpha)}\);
a row-stochastic Markov matrix \(P\) and, for a connected reversible graph, stationary weights \(\pi\);
eigenvalues and eigenvectors of \(P\) or its symmetric conjugate;
a diffusion distance \(D_t\) on, or in degenerate cases a pseudometric over, the training vertices; and
truncated coordinates

\[
\Phi_{t,m}(x_i)
=\bigl(\lambda_1^t\psi_1(i),\ldots,\lambda_m^t\psi_m(i)\bigr),
\]
excluding the trivial constant eigenvector. The output is initially transductive: it assigns coordinates to the fitted sample. A separate extension rule is needed for new observations.



A local affinity defines one-step connectivity. Row normalization turns that affinity into a random walk. Powers \(P^t\) aggregate all length-\(t\) paths, so comparing rows of \(P^t\) compares how similarly two starting vertices communicate with the rest of the graph. Spectral decomposition makes these comparisons computationally and geometrically explicit: modes with \(|\lambda_\ell|<1\) are attenuated by \(|\lambda_\ell|^t\), producing a family of scale-dependent embeddings (Coifman and Lafon 2006).
Here diffusion time \(t\) counts applications of the constructed Markov operator. It is an algorithmic scale parameter. It is not elapsed experimental time, a learned transition law for the observed system, or evidence of physical diffusion or biological dynamics.



Canonical Diffusion Maps are not a generative probability model for observations. Their operative assumptions and design commitments are:

the chosen dissimilarity and affinity encode useful local relationships;
graph connectivity at the selected bandwidth is scientifically meaningful rather than an artifact of units, nuisance variables, or sampling gaps;
the symmetric nonnegative affinity supports a reversible Markov construction;
finite-sample spectral modes are stable enough to summarize the target relationships; and
when a continuum or manifold interpretation is invoked, additional smoothness, sampling, boundary, bandwidth, and asymptotic conditions hold.

The last point is optional and demanding. The finite graph algorithm can be computed without assuming a manifold. Conversely, successful computation or an appealing embedding does not verify the assumptions needed for a Laplace–Beltrami limit.



Starting from symmetric \(K_{ij}\geq0\), define the kernel-density proxy
\[
q_i=\sum_{j=1}^n K_{ij}.
\]
For a declared \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), apply the anisotropic density normalization
\[
K^{(\alpha)}_{ij}
=\frac{K_{ij}}{q_i^\alpha q_j^\alpha},
\qquad
d_i^{(\alpha)}=\sum_{j=1}^n K^{(\alpha)}_{ij}.
\]
If every \(d_i^{(\alpha)}>0\), the row-stochastic matrix is
\[
P_{ij}=\frac{K^{(\alpha)}_{ij}}{d_i^{(\alpha)}},
\qquad
\sum_jP_{ij}=1.
\]
For a connected undirected graph this chain is reversible with
\[
\pi_i=\frac{d_i^{(\alpha)}}{\sum_jd_j^{(\alpha)}}
\]
and is similar to the real symmetric matrix
\[
S=(D^{(\alpha)})^{-1/2}K^{(\alpha)}(D^{(\alpha)})^{-1/2}.
\]
Thus one may compute a Euclidean-orthonormal eigendecomposition of \(S\) and transform it to right eigenvectors \(P\psi_\ell=\lambda_\ell\psi_\ell\). Here the right eigenvectors are scaled to be orthonormal in \(L^2(\pi)\),
\[
\sum_i \pi_i\psi_\ell(i)\psi_r(i)=\delta_{\ell r}.
\]
They are not generally orthogonal in the ordinary Euclidean inner product. With self-loops or another aperiodicity condition and a connected graph, \(\lambda_0=1\) is simple and \(|\lambda_\ell|<1\) for nontrivial modes (Coifman and Lafon 2006; Luxburg 2007).
For integer \(t\geq1\), define
\[
D_t(i,j)^2
=\sum_{k=1}^n
\frac{\left(P^t_{ik}-P^t_{jk}\right)^2}{\pi_k}.
\]
Under the reversible spectral normalization,
\[
D_t(i,j)^2
=\sum_{\ell\geq1}\lambda_\ell^{2t}
\left(\psi_\ell(i)-\psi_\ell(j)\right)^2.
\]
The full diffusion map is therefore an isometric representation of this graph-defined distance when the spectral assumptions separate vertices; truncating after \(m\) modes omits the corresponding tail. If distinct vertices have identical \(t\)-step transition profiles, \(D_t\) is only a pseudometric on vertex labels.
The role of \(\alpha\) must not be hidden. In the smooth-manifold, independent-sampling, large-\(n\), small-bandwidth regime studied by Coifman and Lafon, \(\alpha=0\) retains sampling-density influence, while \(\alpha=1\) removes the leading density drift and targets a Laplace–Beltrami operator. This is an asymptotic, assumption-dependent result—not a finite-data guarantee that density, geometry, or a manifold has been recovered (Coifman and Lafon 2006, sec. 3). Singer’s convergence analysis further exposes a bias–variance tradeoff: shrinking bandwidth reduces one approximation error while increasing sampling variance unless sample size grows appropriately (Singer 2006).



From the fitted sample, the method learns a graph-dependent empirical Markov operator, its spectrum, diffusion distances, and coordinate values on training vertices. “Learns” here means data-adaptive construction and eigendecomposition; it does not mean estimating the physical transition mechanism that generated the observations.
The identifiable output is best viewed as eigenspaces and diffusion distances under fixed graph choices. Individual eigenvector signs, bases inside repeated eigenspaces, and coordinates across independently fitted samples require alignment conventions.



The analyst fixes the sample and representation, dissimilarity, affinity form, bandwidth, graph construction, symmetrization, \(\alpha\), self-loop policy, diffusion time, coordinate count, spectral ordering, numerical solver, and out-of-sample rule. Data may determine numerical values of \(q_i\), \(P\), and the eigenpairs, but it does not make the preceding design choices model-free.
If hyperparameters are selected using an outcome or evaluation set, that selection is supervision and must be nested inside the training procedure.



Ordinary Diffusion Maps are order-blind with respect to the input rows. Permuting observations and applying the same permutation to the graph changes no fitted relation. The symbol \(t\) denotes random-walk steps on the constructed affinity graph, not sample timestamps. A temporal sequence can influence the method only if time, lag, or transition information is explicitly encoded in the representation or affinity; doing so defines a different, application-specific operator.
Smooth trajectories in diffusion coordinates can arise from local similarity and spectral smoothing alone. They do not establish temporal dynamics, a vector field, process noise, or a state-space model.



Diffusion geometry is defined by the complete pipeline
\[
\text{representation}\to\rho\to K\to K^{(\alpha)}\to P\to(P^t,D_t).
\]
It reflects multistep graph connectivity rather than direct ambient distance or single shortest paths. Changing feature units, bandwidth, neighborhood rule, density normalization, or \(t\) changes the geometry.
Under additional continuum assumptions, normalized graph operators can approximate differential operators on a smooth sampled manifold (Coifman and Lafon 2006; Singer 2006). The finite embedding itself, however, does not prove a manifold, recover topology, identify a Riemannian metric, estimate intrinsic dimension without a criterion, or show that the chosen ambient metric corresponds to scientific similarity.



The canonical construction is unsupervised: labels and outcomes do not enter the affinity or eigendecomposition. It becomes supervised or task-adaptive if labels choose features, distances, bandwidths, edges, \(\alpha\), \(t\), or retained modes. Such choices may be legitimate, but the resulting embedding is no longer evidence from a label-free method.



The main computation is a sparse or dense eigenproblem, not likelihood maximization and not latent posterior inference. A common implementation diagonalizes the symmetric conjugate \(S\), whose eigenvectors can be Euclidean-orthonormal, then maps and rescales them to right eigenvectors of \(P\) that are orthonormal in the \(\pi\)-weighted inner product. Approximate nearest-neighbor graphs, sparse eigensolvers, randomized methods, and convergence tolerances introduce additional numerical error.
For the canonical reversible operator, eigenvalues are real, \(S\) has a real Euclidean-orthogonal eigenbasis, and \(P\) has the corresponding real \(\pi\)-weighted-orthogonal right eigenbasis. Sparsification can yield negative eigenvalues; their signs affect odd-\(t\) coordinates even though diffusion distance uses \(\lambda_\ell^{2t}\). If a directed or asymmetric affinity produces a nonreversible \(P\), eigenvalues and eigenvectors can be complex or defective, the reversible weighted-orthogonality formula need not hold, and a singular-vector, Schur, or explicitly real representation must be specified. A nonreversible result must not be reported using the canonical formulas without this qualification.




It converts local similarities into a multiscale connectivity distance that aggregates multiple paths.
The relationship between the Markov operator, diffusion distance, and spectral coordinates is explicit.
The \(\alpha\) family exposes rather than hides one choice about sampling-density influence.
Sparse graphs and partial eigensolvers can make leading-coordinate computation practical.
It provides a structured nonlinear comparison to PCA without requiring a decoder or generative observation model.





Bandwidth too small: the graph fragments, creates isolated vertices, or yields unstable local degrees and repeated unit eigenvalues.
Bandwidth too large: affinities become nearly uniform, local structure is washed out, and nontrivial eigenvalues collapse.
Sampling-density confounding: dense regions dominate degrees and transitions unless the chosen normalization and its assumptions are appropriate.
Disconnected graph: each component contributes a stationary mode; a unique global stationary distribution and ordinary between-component interpretation fail.
Near-disconnection: small graph changes can rotate a cluster of nearly repeated eigenvectors, even when the invariant subspace is more stable.
Metric or feature failure: nuisance variables, scaling, artifacts, or mixed data types can define the wrong neighborhoods before spectral analysis begins.
Boundary and finite-sample effects: continuum approximations can be biased near boundaries or under sparse, nonuniform, dependent, or noisy sampling.
Spectral truncation: omitting slowly decaying modes distorts diffusion distance; retaining tiny modes can amplify numerical and out-of-sample instability.
Large diffusion time: on a connected ergodic graph, \(P^t\) approaches stationarity and all diffusion distances collapse toward zero.
Leakage: constructing the graph on training plus test observations makes a nominally held-out evaluation transductive.
Interpretive overreach: visually smooth coordinates can be mistaken for intrinsic coordinates, topology, dynamics, or mechanism.




For a simple real eigenvalue, \(\psi_\ell\) and \(-\psi_\ell\) are equivalent coordinate conventions. If an eigenvalue has multiplicity greater than one, any orthogonal basis of its eigenspace is valid; the stable target is the eigenspace and the diffusion distance contribution, not named individual axes. Close eigenvalues create a practical version of this instability under sampling or numerical perturbations (Luxburg 2007, sec. 7).
Disconnected components make \(\lambda=1\) multiple, and no unique global stationary vector is selected without component weights or another convention. Negative eigenvalues introduce parity-dependent coordinate signs. Nonreversible operators may have complex eigenpairs and nonorthogonal modes, so phase, scaling, ordering, and even diagonalizability require explicit treatment.
The coordinate count \(m\) is not identified as an intrinsic dimension. It depends on \(t\), truncation tolerance, eigengaps, sample size, bandwidth, normalization, and the purpose of the representation.




PCA: a global linear Euclidean baseline. Compare at matched coordinate count using training-only preprocessing. Improvement on a chosen neighborhood or prediction criterion supports the nonlinear graph representation, not a manifold claim.
Raw affinity and graph diagnostics: before embedding, inspect connected components, isolated vertices, degree distribution, stationary mass, neighborhood examples, and spectra. If these are pathological, coordinates cannot repair the graph.
Laplacian eigenmaps / normalized spectral coordinates: use closely related graph eigenvectors but differ in normalization, eigenvalue weighting, and objective interpretation. They test whether the diffusion-time scaling \(\lambda_\ell^t\) and diffusion-distance target add value.
Isomap: uses graph shortest-path distances and classical scaling, whereas Diffusion Maps aggregate transition probabilities across many paths. Neither is uniformly superior; both depend on graph construction.
Unembedded diffusion distance: if the task only needs pairwise distances, using \(D_t\) directly separates the value of the distance from the additional truncation choice.




Evaluation must match the intended use and include graph diagnostics before downstream scores:

report connectivity, isolated vertices, degree/stationary-mass distributions, leading eigenvalues, eigengaps, and sensitivity to bandwidth, graph rule, \(\alpha\), \(t\), and \(m\);
quantify the truncated-coordinate error relative to the full or higher-rank diffusion distance on the fitted graph;
compare eigenspaces across resamples or folds using principal angles rather than unaligned eigenvectors when signs or multiplicities are ambiguous;
compare with PCA and declared spectral/graph baselines at matched dimension and without test-set graph leakage;
if new-point deployment is intended, evaluate a training-fitted extension on held-out dependence units and compare it with a full refit after alignment; and
when synthetic ground truth is available, separately assess operator/eigenspace recovery, diffusion-distance recovery, neighborhood behavior, and downstream task performance.

No universal reconstruction objective is part of Diffusion Maps. Classification, regression, clustering, or visualization scores are application-specific and must be predeclared. Subjects, sessions, trajectories, or trials should be split as whole units when within-unit observations are dependent.
For a fixed training operator, a Nyström/eigenfunction extension can evaluate a new point by its normalized affinities to training points and divide by the relevant retained nonzero eigenvalue. A zero mode is not defined by that formula; very small nonzero modes are unstable. The extension is approximate, can also fail for poorly connected new points, and need not equal recomputing the graph and spectrum with the point included (Bengio et al. 2003).



A future non-executable toy contract would sample points at known angles on a circle embedded in \(\mathbb R^2\), with both uniform and deliberately nonuniform angular densities. It would:

construct Gaussian affinities over a bandwidth grid with explicitly retained self-loops;
compare \(\alpha=0\) and \(\alpha=1\), several integer diffusion times, and rank-two coordinates;
compare with rank-two PCA and unscaled normalized-Laplacian coordinates;
align the first nontrivial two-dimensional eigenspace to the known span of \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\), recognizing that the repeated continuum eigenvalue permits arbitrary rotation;
score graph connectivity, operator/eigenspace error, diffusion-distance truncation error, resampling stability, and held-out Nyström error; and
add negative controls consisting of a disconnected two-arc sample, a bandwidth that nearly completes the graph, and an asymmetric affinity requiring a nonreversible treatment.

The contract would test how density, bandwidth, connectivity, spectral multiplicity, and extension error affect recovery. It would not treat a circular visualization as proof of topology, manifold structure, or intrinsic dimension. No data, code, result, or benchmark is produced in this Method Object.



Diffusion Maps are LDG’s canonical affinity-operator embedding method. They make a useful distinction between ambient distance, local similarity, graph connectivity, an algorithmic diffusion scale, and spectral coordinates. That distinction is necessary before asking whether a representation reflects merely a chosen graph operator or supports stronger geometric or dynamical claims.






WarningWhat this does NOT imply



A stable Diffusion Maps embedding does not prove that the data lie on a manifold, recover topology or a Riemannian metric, determine model-free intrinsic dimension, identify physical time, learn system dynamics, or reveal a biological mechanism. Diffusion time is a graph-scale parameter, and density correction is conditional on explicit asymptotic assumptions.




Diffusion Maps can organize declared trajectory features or time samples by affinity, but the canonical method ignores temporal order. Whole animals or trajectories should be held out when dependence requires it. No modality-specific empirical result is retained here.



The method can embed eye-position, velocity, event, or window features after a scientifically justified metric is declared. Sampling rate, event imbalance, filtering, and repeated observations can dominate local density. No modality-specific empirical result is retained here.



Sensor, spectral, covariance, or trial features require different metrics and preprocessing. A smooth diffusion coordinate is not automatically a neural source, temporal process, or disease axis. No modality-specific empirical result is retained here.



Diffusion Maps may provide a nonlinear affinity baseline for population-state representations, but neuron/sensor scaling, trial dependence, condition imbalance, and graph leakage must be controlled. No modality-specific empirical result is retained here.

title: Diffusion Maps
text:
Diffusion Maps construct data-dependent spectral coordinates from a random walk on a weighted similarity graph. The method replaces direct ambient distance by diffusion distance: two sampled observations are close when their distributions over destinations after a declared number of graph-walk steps are similar. Truncated eigenvectors of the resulting Markov operator provide Euclidean coordinates that approximate this distance (Coifman and Lafon 2006).
The unit of analysis is a sampled observation or graph vertex. This object covers the finite-sample, symmetric-affinity, reversible construction. Directed affinities and nonreversible operators are discussed as a boundary, not silently treated as the same algorithm.
Assumed background: a similarity or affinity kernel is a nonnegative function used to weight pairs of observations, and a Markov operator maps a function or probability distribution through one step of a stochastic transition rule. These meanings are not supplied by knowledge/concepts/kernel.qmd: that repository object defines a temporal impulse-response/filter kernel and is not a prerequisite for Diffusion Maps.

title: Diffusion Maps
Diffusion Maps
text:
For fixed choices, Diffusion Maps return:

a normalized affinity matrix \(K^{(\alpha)}\);
a row-stochastic Markov matrix \(P\) and, for a connected reversible graph, stationary weights \(\pi\);
eigenvalues and eigenvectors of \(P\) or its symmetric conjugate;
a diffusion distance \(D_t\) on, or in degenerate cases a pseudometric over, the training vertices; and
truncated coordinates

\[
\Phi_{t,m}(x_i)
=\bigl(\lambda_1^t\psi_1(i),\ldots,\lambda_m^t\psi_m(i)\bigr),
\]
excluding the trivial constant eigenvector. The output is initially transductive: it assigns coordinates to the fitted sample. A separate extension rule is needed for new observations.

title: Diffusion Maps
text:
A local affinity defines one-step connectivity. Row normalization turns that affinity into a random walk. Powers \(P^t\) aggregate all length-\(t\) paths, so comparing rows of \(P^t\) compares how similarly two starting vertices communicate with the rest of the graph. Spectral decomposition makes these comparisons computationally and geometrically explicit: modes with \(|\lambda_\ell|<1\) are attenuated by \(|\lambda_\ell|^t\), producing a family of scale-dependent embeddings (Coifman and Lafon 2006).
Here diffusion time \(t\) counts applications of the constructed Markov operator. It is an algorithmic scale parameter. It is not elapsed experimental time, a learned transition law for the observed system, or evidence of physical diffusion or biological dynamics.

title: Diffusion Maps
Diffusion Maps
text:
Starting from symmetric \(K_{ij}\geq0\), define the kernel-density proxy
\[
q_i=\sum_{j=1}^n K_{ij}.
\]
For a declared \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), apply the anisotropic density normalization
\[
K^{(\alpha)}_{ij}
=\frac{K_{ij}}{q_i^\alpha q_j^\alpha},
\qquad
d_i^{(\alpha)}=\sum_{j=1}^n K^{(\alpha)}_{ij}.
\]
If every \(d_i^{(\alpha)}>0\), the row-stochastic matrix is
\[
P_{ij}=\frac{K^{(\alpha)}_{ij}}{d_i^{(\alpha)}},
\qquad
\sum_jP_{ij}=1.
\]
For a connected undirected graph this chain is reversible with
\[
\pi_i=\frac{d_i^{(\alpha)}}{\sum_jd_j^{(\alpha)}}
\]
and is similar to the real symmetric matrix
\[
S=(D^{(\alpha)})^{-1/2}K^{(\alpha)}(D^{(\alpha)})^{-1/2}.
\]
Thus one may compute a Euclidean-orthonormal eigendecomposition of \(S\) and transform it to right eigenvectors \(P\psi_\ell=\lambda_\ell\psi_\ell\). Here the right eigenvectors are scaled to be orthonormal in \(L^2(\pi)\),
\[
\sum_i \pi_i\psi_\ell(i)\psi_r(i)=\delta_{\ell r}.
\]
They are not generally orthogonal in the ordinary Euclidean inner product. With self-loops or another aperiodicity condition and a connected graph, \(\lambda_0=1\) is simple and \(|\lambda_\ell|<1\) for nontrivial modes (Coifman and Lafon 2006; Luxburg 2007).
For integer \(t\geq1\), define
\[
D_t(i,j)^2
=\sum_{k=1}^n
\frac{\left(P^t_{ik}-P^t_{jk}\right)^2}{\pi_k}.
\]
Under the reversible spectral normalization,
\[
D_t(i,j)^2
=\sum_{\ell\geq1}\lambda_\ell^{2t}
\left(\psi_\ell(i)-\psi_\ell(j)\right)^2.
\]
The full diffusion map is therefore an isometric representation of this graph-defined distance when the spectral assumptions separate vertices; truncating after \(m\) modes omits the corresponding tail. If distinct vertices have identical \(t\)-step transition profiles, \(D_t\) is only a pseudometric on vertex labels.
The role of \(\alpha\) must not be hidden. In the smooth-manifold, independent-sampling, large-\(n\), small-bandwidth regime studied by Coifman and Lafon, \(\alpha=0\) retains sampling-density influence, while \(\alpha=1\) removes the leading density drift and targets a Laplace–Beltrami operator. This is an asymptotic, assumption-dependent result—not a finite-data guarantee that density, geometry, or a manifold has been recovered (Coifman and Lafon 2006, sec. 3). Singer’s convergence analysis further exposes a bias–variance tradeoff: shrinking bandwidth reduces one approximation error while increasing sampling variance unless sample size grows appropriately (Singer 2006).

title: Diffusion Maps
text:
From the fitted sample, the method learns a graph-dependent empirical Markov operator, its spectrum, diffusion distances, and coordinate values on training vertices. “Learns” here means data-adaptive construction and eigendecomposition; it does not mean estimating the physical transition mechanism that generated the observations.
The identifiable output is best viewed as eigenspaces and diffusion distances under fixed graph choices. Individual eigenvector signs, bases inside repeated eigenspaces, and coordinates across independently fitted samples require alignment conventions.

title: Diffusion Maps
text:
The analyst fixes the sample and representation, dissimilarity, affinity form, bandwidth, graph construction, symmetrization, \(\alpha\), self-loop policy, diffusion time, coordinate count, spectral ordering, numerical solver, and out-of-sample rule. Data may determine numerical values of \(q_i\), \(P\), and the eigenpairs, but it does not make the preceding design choices model-free.
If hyperparameters are selected using an outcome or evaluation set, that selection is supervision and must be nested inside the training procedure.

title: Diffusion Maps
text:
Ordinary Diffusion Maps are order-blind with respect to the input rows. Permuting observations and applying the same permutation to the graph changes no fitted relation. The symbol \(t\) denotes random-walk steps on the constructed affinity graph, not sample timestamps. A temporal sequence can influence the method only if time, lag, or transition information is explicitly encoded in the representation or affinity; doing so defines a different, application-specific operator.
Smooth trajectories in diffusion coordinates can arise from local similarity and spectral smoothing alone. They do not establish temporal dynamics, a vector field, process noise, or a state-space model.

title: Diffusion Maps
text:
Diffusion geometry is defined by the complete pipeline
\[
\text{representation}\to\rho\to K\to K^{(\alpha)}\to P\to(P^t,D_t).
\]
It reflects multistep graph connectivity rather than direct ambient distance or single shortest paths. Changing feature units, bandwidth, neighborhood rule, density normalization, or \(t\) changes the geometry.
Under additional continuum assumptions, normalized graph operators can approximate differential operators on a smooth sampled manifold (Coifman and Lafon 2006; Singer 2006). The finite embedding itself, however, does not prove a manifold, recover topology, identify a Riemannian metric, estimate intrinsic dimension without a criterion, or show that the chosen ambient metric corresponds to scientific similarity.

title: Diffusion Maps
text: The canonical construction is unsupervised: labels and outcomes do not enter the affinity or eigendecomposition. It becomes supervised or task-adaptive if labels choose features, distances, bandwidths, edges, \(\alpha\), \(t\), or retained modes. Such choices may be legitimate, but the resulting embedding is no longer evidence from a label-free method.

title: Diffusion Maps
text:
The main computation is a sparse or dense eigenproblem, not likelihood maximization and not latent posterior inference. A common implementation diagonalizes the symmetric conjugate \(S\), whose eigenvectors can be Euclidean-orthonormal, then maps and rescales them to right eigenvectors of \(P\) that are orthonormal in the \(\pi\)-weighted inner product. Approximate nearest-neighbor graphs, sparse eigensolvers, randomized methods, and convergence tolerances introduce additional numerical error.
For the canonical reversible operator, eigenvalues are real, \(S\) has a real Euclidean-orthogonal eigenbasis, and \(P\) has the corresponding real \(\pi\)-weighted-orthogonal right eigenbasis. Sparsification can yield negative eigenvalues; their signs affect odd-\(t\) coordinates even though diffusion distance uses \(\lambda_\ell^{2t}\). If a directed or asymmetric affinity produces a nonreversible \(P\), eigenvalues and eigenvectors can be complex or defective, the reversible weighted-orthogonality formula need not hold, and a singular-vector, Schur, or explicitly real representation must be specified. A nonreversible result must not be reported using the canonical formulas without this qualification.

title: Diffusion Maps
text:
It converts local similarities into a multiscale connectivity distance that aggregates multiple paths.
The relationship between the Markov operator, diffusion distance, and spectral coordinates is explicit.
The \(\alpha\) family exposes rather than hides one choice about sampling-density influence.
Sparse graphs and partial eigensolvers can make leading-coordinate computation practical.
It provides a structured nonlinear comparison to PCA without requiring a decoder or generative observation model.

title: Gaussian-Process Factor Analysis
text:
Gaussian-process factor analysis (GPFA) infers smooth, low-dimensional latent trajectories from high-dimensional time series by combining a factor-analysis-style linear Gaussian observation model with Gaussian-process priors over latent coordinates. In its canonical neural application, the observations are transformed binned spike counts from simultaneously recorded units, and each trial receives a full-interval posterior distribution over its latent path (Yu et al. 2009).
The bounded method solves a retrospective probabilistic smoothing and dimensionality-reduction problem:

Under a declared linear Gaussian observation model and declared covariance functions over within-trial time, what posterior distribution over latent trajectories is supported by the complete observed sequence?

GPFA does not learn a state-transition equation. Its temporal structure is specified through covariance kernels that directly encode correlations among latent values at different times. Smooth posterior means are therefore partly consequences of the selected prior family, timescales, and observation model rather than direct observations of a uniquely existing path.
Assumed background: Gaussian processes and symmetric positive-semidefinite covariance kernels. A Gaussian-process covariance kernel \(k(t,t')\) specifies covariance between random function values and must generate positive-semidefinite Gram matrices on every finite time grid (Rasmussen and Williams 2006). The existing Kernel Concept uses kernel for a temporal impulse-response/filter weighting function. It is not a prerequisite for, and must not be confused with, the positive-semidefinite covariance kernels used here.



For trial \(n=1,\ldots,N\), let
\[
Y^{(n)}=
\begin{bmatrix}
y^{(n)}_1&\cdots&y^{(n)}_{T_n}
\end{bmatrix}
\in\mathbb R^{p\times T_n},
\]
where \(p\) is the number of observed channels and \(t^{(n)}_1,\ldots,t^{(n)}_{T_n}\) is that trial’s declared time grid. In the canonical neural formulation, \(y^{(n)}_t\) contains nonoverlapping binned spike counts after a square-root transformation; unlike a two-stage smoother followed by static dimensionality reduction, the transformed counts are not presmoothed before GPFA (Yu et al. 2009).
A reproducible analysis must declare:

the experimental unit, recording population, simultaneous-versus-pseudo-population status, inclusion rules, and trial/sequence boundaries;
bin width, time grid, event alignment, analyzed interval, count transformation, and handling of unequal trial lengths;
whether an across-condition or trial-specific mean has been removed, represented in \(d\), or modeled separately;
candidate latent dimension \(q\) and its selection rule;
covariance-kernel family, signal variance convention, timescale constraints, and any latent nugget/noise term;
observation covariance structure and whether diagonal \(R\) is scientifically defensible;
parameter initialization, optimization, restarts, convergence checks, and regularization;
missing-observation and censoring rules; and
training, validation, and test split units.

The canonical multi-trial model treats trials as conditionally independent given shared parameters. It does not require equal \(T_n\), but it does assume that all trials use the same loading matrix, observation offset, residual covariance, and kernel-hyperparameter family. Alignment resets within-trial time and does not create continuity between trial endpoints.



For a selected latent dimension \(q\), fitted GPFA returns:

a loading matrix \(C\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}\);
an observation offset \(d\in\mathbb R^p\);
a diagonal observation-residual covariance \(R\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}\);
one covariance kernel and fitted hyperparameters for each latent coordinate;
a marginal Gaussian distribution over every observed trial;
a joint Gaussian posterior over the complete latent path for each trial; and
posterior means, marginal covariances, cross-time covariances, samples, or posterior predictions derived from that path distribution.

The posterior mean is one trajectory summary. It is not the latent trajectory random element itself, a measured state path, or a trajectory with parameter uncertainty integrated out. If parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood and then held fixed, reported posterior covariance is conditional on those plug-in parameters.



Static factor analysis applies the same low-rank-plus-diagonal Gaussian observation model independently to each observation vector. GPFA retains that observation layer but couples latent values across time using a GP prior. Nearby latent states can be strongly correlated when the covariance function has a long timescale, producing smooth posterior paths; a short timescale or large latent nugget permits faster or less smooth variation.
Yu et al. describe GPFA as one factor analyzer per time point with shared observation parameters, linked in latent space by GP priors (Yu et al. 2009). The complete finite-grid model is multivariate Gaussian, so the latent path can be integrated out to obtain an exact marginal likelihood and conditioned on the full trial to obtain an exact Gaussian posterior. Exactness is conditional on the Gaussian model and finite matrix computations; it is not evidence that transformed spike counts or neural activity truly follow that model.



For time \(t\) in one trial, the observation model is
\[
y_t=Cx_t+d+\epsilon_t,
\qquad
\epsilon_t\sim\mathcal N(0,R),
\]
where \(x_t\in\mathbb R^q\) and
\[
R=\operatorname{diag}(r_1,\ldots,r_p),
\qquad r_i>0.
\]
Observation residuals are independent across channels conditional on \(x_t\) because \(R\) is diagonal, and they are ordinarily assumed independent across time and trials. The latent functions are independent a priori across coordinates:
\[
x_j^{(n)}(\cdot)\sim\mathcal{GP}(0,k_j),
