text:
The state carries the information needed for the next-step transition, while observations are noisy linear views of that state. The Markov factorization converts one high-dimensional trajectory distribution into an initial-state law, local transition laws, and local observation laws. Gaussian closure makes the relevant conditional and marginal distributions Gaussian, permitting exact finite-horizon inference when parameters are known (Särkkä 2013, chs. 4, 8).
The method’s value is not merely that its inferred mean trajectory looks smooth. It is that a declared stochastic temporal model yields testable predictive distributions and separates uncertainty introduced at the transition from uncertainty introduced at measurement.

title: Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
text:
The canonical input-driven model is
\[
z_1\sim\mathcal N(m_1,P_1),
\]
\[
z_{t+1}=Az_t+Bu_t+w_t,
\qquad
w_t\sim\mathcal N(0,Q),
\]
\[
x_t=Cz_t+Du_t+v_t,
\qquad
v_t\sim\mathcal N(0,R).
\]
The no-input core is recovered by omitting \(u_t\), \(B\), and \(D\). Unless explicitly generalized, the model assumes:

\(P_1,Q\succeq0\) and \(R\succ0\);
\(z_1\), every \(w_t\), and every \(v_s\) are mutually independent;
process and observation noises are independent across time;
\(A,B,C,D,Q,R\) are constant over the sequence;
the latent transition is first-order Markov;
observations are conditionally independent across time given the state path and inputs; and
inputs are fixed in advance or externally supplied without depending on contemporaneous or future observations, so they are valid conditioning variables rather than unexplained stochastic causes.

Gaussianity is stronger than specifying only means and covariances. Correlated process and observation noise, colored noise, heteroscedasticity, time-varying matrices, or history-dependent measurements require an explicit modified model rather than an informal reinterpretation of \(Q\) or \(R\).

title: Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
text:
For a fixed open-loop input path, the joint law factorizes as
\[
p_\theta(z_{1:T},x_{1:T}\mid u_{1:T})
=p_\theta(z_1)
\prod_{t=1}^{T-1}p_\theta(z_{t+1}\mid z_t,u_t)
\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_\theta(x_t\mid z_t,u_t),
\]
where
\[
p_\theta(z_{t+1}\mid z_t,u_t)
=\mathcal N(Az_t+Bu_t,Q),
\]
\[
p_\theta(x_t\mid z_t,u_t)
=\mathcal N(Cz_t+Du_t,R).
\]
This factorization defines several different conditional targets. The future input values appearing below must be known scenario values rather than controls that encode future observations:
\[
\text{forecasting:}\quad
p(z_{t+h},x_{t+h}\mid x_{1:t},u_{1:t+h}),
\]
\[
\text{filtering:}\quad
p(z_t\mid x_{1:t},u_{1:t}),
\]
\[
\text{smoothing:}\quad
p(z_t\mid x_{1:T},u_{1:T}),\quad T>t,
\]
or the full path posterior \(p(z_{1:T}\mid x_{1:T},u_{1:T})\). Kalman explicitly distinguishes smoothing, filtering, and prediction by whether the estimated state time is earlier than, equal to, or later than the final conditioning observation (Kalman 1960). The exact recursions are deliberately deferred to separate filtering and smoothing Method Objects.
The marginal likelihood is
\[
p_\theta(x_{1:T}\mid u_{1:T})
=\int p_\theta(z_{1:T},x_{1:T}\mid u_{1:T})\,dz_{1:T}.
\]
It can be factorized into one-step predictive densities,
\[
p_\theta(x_{1:T}\mid u_{1:T})
=\prod_{t=1}^{T}
p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{1:t-1},u_{1:t}),
\]
which separates sequence scoring from state-point estimation (Särkkä 2013, sec. 12.1).
Feedback-controlled data require a separate timing and policy model. A valid control \(u_t\) must be measurable from information available before the transition it drives and, when \(D\ne0\), before the contemporaneous observation \(x_t\); using \(x_t\) itself in \(u_t\) creates an algebraic loop. If future controls depend on future observations, conditioning on the realized \(u_{1:T}\) can leak future information. Policy-aware likelihoods and forecasts must instead state the nonanticipating policy and integrate or simulate controls not yet known.

title: Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
text:
Depending on the protocol, parameter learning may estimate some or all of \(m_1,P_1,A,B,C,D,Q,R\) and select \(q\). Given fitted parameters, state inference determines conditional distributions over latent states; it does not relearn the model parameters unless an explicitly joint or online-learning procedure is used.
Maximum-likelihood learning targets the observable sequence distribution after integrating over latent states. EM instead alternates between model-conditional expectations of latent sufficient statistics and parameter updates that increase the same marginal likelihood under exact steps (Ghahramani and Hinton 1996). The inferred state path is therefore an intermediate uncertain quantity, not observed training data.

title: Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
text:
The analyst fixes the state dimension or its selection search, sequence boundaries, time step, input definition, matrix structure and parameter sharing, Gaussian and independence assumptions, covariance constraints, initial-state treatment, missing-data mechanism, learning criterion, regularization or priors, and evaluation target.
When some matrices come from physical modeling, the fixed-versus-estimated partition must be explicit. Calling \(A\) “the dynamics” does not establish that it is a physical law if \(C\), \(Q\), \(R\), state coordinates, or inputs are learned phenomenologically.

title: Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
text:
Time is discrete and ordered. Permuting observations generally changes the likelihood. The first-order Markov assumption states that, conditional on \(z_t\) and the known input, \(z_{t+1}\) does not depend on earlier states. It does not imply that the observed sequence is first-order Markov.
Stability and stationarity are distinct. For the time-invariant no-input mean dynamics, \(\rho(A)<1\) is the usual Schur-stability condition under which deterministic perturbations decay. With zero mean, constant \(Q\), and suitable finite covariance, a stable \(A\) supports a stationary state covariance \(\Sigma\) satisfying
\[
\Sigma=A\Sigma A^\top+Q.
\]
The process is stationary only when its initialization and inputs are also compatible with the stationary law. A stable model initialized away from that law has a transient; a unit-root or unstable finite-horizon model can still define valid distributions without being stationary. Time-varying inputs can make means nonstationary even when \(A\) is stable.
Irregular sampling cannot be handled by silently treating every index gap as equal. It requires gap-dependent transitions, an underlying continuous-time model and discretization, or another explicit variant.

title: Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
text:
The latent state is represented in a finite-dimensional vector space. \(A\) is linear in the chosen state coordinates, while \(Q\) and \(R\) define coordinate-dependent Mahalanobis uncertainty. Euclidean distances between posterior state means have no invariant scientific meaning unless a metric and coordinate convention are justified.
The model does not posit a nonlinear manifold or Riemannian geometry. A low-dimensional linear latent state is a modeling choice, not proof of intrinsic dimension or a unique state space.

title: Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
text:
Likelihood-based fitting from observation sequences is unsupervised with respect to external labels. Fixed open-loop inputs condition the transition and observation laws; their presence is not automatically “supervision” in the prediction-label sense. Labels, outcomes, or interventions used to design states, constrain matrices, select hyperparameters, or score models introduce task dependence and must be declared.
An observational input correlated with unmodeled disturbances is not automatically exogenous. Including \(u_t\) does not identify the causal effect represented by \(B\) or \(D\). Feedback-dependent inputs require the policy-aware extension delimited above rather than the open-loop conditional factorization used here.

title: Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
text:
For known parameters, finite-horizon linear-Gaussian forecasting, filtering, and smoothing are exact Gaussian conditioning problems. They differ only in target and information set, but require distinct computations. Filtering uses data through the current time; fixed-interval smoothing uses future observations within the declared interval (Särkkä 2013, chs. 4, 8).
Parameter learning is a separate optimization or Bayesian inference problem. Direct maximum-likelihood optimization can use the predictive-density factorization. In EM, the E-step requires smoothed expectations such as \(\mathbb E[z_t]\), \(\mathbb E[z_tz_t^\top]\), and \(\mathbb E[z_tz_{t-1}^\top]\) under the current parameters; the M-step updates model parameters from those expectations (Ghahramani and Hinton 1996). Thus an EM implementation may internally call filtering and smoothing, but the learned model, filtering posterior, smoothing posterior, and optimizer are not interchangeable objects.
The likelihood is generally nonconvex in a free latent parameterization. Initializations, covariance constraints, regularization, stopping criteria, multiple starts, and numerical factorizations must be reported. An increasing EM objective does not prove global optimality or scientific validity.

title: Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
text:
It defines a coherent joint distribution over ordered latent and observed sequences.
Process and observation uncertainty are represented separately through \(Q\) and \(R\).
Exact Gaussian forecasts and state posteriors are available when parameters are fixed.
Marginal likelihood supports sequence-level predictive comparison and parameter learning.
Inputs can be incorporated without abandoning linear-Gaussian tractability.
It is a transparent temporal baseline before nonlinear or non-Gaussian latent models.

title: Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
text:
Wrong latent dimension or structure: omitted modes leave temporal residual structure; redundant modes create weakly identified or unused states.
Noise tradeoff: short, weakly observed sequences may not distinguish process variation from observation variation, so \(Q\), \(R\), \(C\), and the state path can compensate for one another.
Unmodeled dependence: colored, correlated, heteroscedastic, or state-dependent noise invalidates the white independent Gaussian assumptions.
Nonlinearity or regime changes: one global \(A\) and \(C\) cannot represent switching, saturation, curved observation maps, or abrupt interventions.
Instability or near-unit roots: forecasts can diverge or become highly uncertain, and parameter estimates can be sensitive in short records.
Unobservable modes: latent directions that do not affect available observations cannot be recovered from those observations.
Weak excitation: inputs or process noise may fail to explore directions needed to estimate transition effects.
Missingness or censoring: treating informative missing observations as ignorable can bias learning and state inference.
Boundary covariance estimates: nearly singular \(Q\), \(R\), or \(P_1\) can create numerical failure or degenerate likelihood behavior.
Local optimization: different initializations can converge to different representatives or local optima.
Leakage: smoothing future data into an online forecast, fitting preprocessing on test sequences, or splitting adjacent time points across train and test yields optimistic evaluation.
Mechanistic overreach: a predictive \(A\) can summarize conditional evolution without identifying a biological mechanism or causal transition law.

title: Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
text:
For any invertible \(T\in\mathbb R^{q\times q}\), define \(z'_t=Tz_t\). The transformed parameters
\[
A'=TAT^{-1},\quad B'=TB,\quad C'=CT^{-1},
\]
\[
m'_1=Tm_1,\quad P'_1=TP_1T^\top,\quad Q'=TQT^\top
\]
with unchanged \(D\) and \(R\) generate the same observation distribution. Sign changes, permutations, rotations, and state-coordinate scalings are special cases. Therefore individual latent axes and matrix entries are not identified without a coordinate convention; invariant predictions, transfer behavior under declared inputs, or similarity classes may be the defensible targets.
Similarity transformation is not always the only ambiguity. Nonminimal realizations can contain unobservable or unreachable states; unknown \(C,Q,R,P_1\), restricted input coverage, singular covariances, or finite sequence length can create stronger structural or practical nonidentifiability. A good optimizer cannot recover a unique parameter outside what the observation design identifies.
For deterministic pairs, observability of \((A,C)\) asks whether states can in principle be distinguished from an output history, while controllability of \((A,B)\) asks whether inputs can reach state directions. In stochastic estimation, excitation through \(Q\) and detectability/stabilizability conditions introduce related but distinct boundaries. These properties are not automatic consequences of writing an LGSSM, and they do not by themselves prove causal or physical meaning.

title: Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
text:
Training mean or independent Gaussian: ignores both latent structure and temporal dependence. The LGSSM should improve held-out predictive likelihood or calibrated forecasts before its temporal complexity is credited.
PCA: a deterministic, static, order-blind linear representation. It provides no process/observation noise split or temporal likelihood.
Factor Analysis: a static probabilistic low-rank observation model. With independent factors at each time and no state persistence, it tests whether the transition layer is needed. FA remains the canonical static probabilistic comparison.
Observation-space autoregression or persistence: predicts measurements directly without a separate latent observation map. It is often a stronger temporal baseline than a static method and tests whether latent states add value.
Known-parameter model: separates state-inference performance from errors introduced by parameter learning. Simulation studies should report both known-parameter and learned-parameter cases.

title: Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
text:
Consider the scalar no-input model
\[
z_{t+1}=az_t+w_t,
\qquad
x_t=z_t+v_t,
\]
with \(w_t\sim\mathcal N(0,q)\) and \(v_t\sim\mathcal N(0,r)\). If \(|a|<1\) and
\[
z_1\sim\mathcal N\!\left(0,\frac{q}{1-a^2}\right),
\]
then the latent process is stationary with
\[
\operatorname{Var}(z_t)=\frac{q}{1-a^2},
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(x_t,x_{t+h})
=a^h\frac{q}{1-a^2}\quad(h>0),
\]
and \(\operatorname{Var}(x_t)=q/(1-a^2)+r\). This separates temporal persistence \(a\), process variation \(q\), and measurement variation \(r\). Setting \(a=0\) produces temporally independent latent variables; setting \(a=1\) removes the stationary covariance formula even though a finite-horizon random-walk model remains well defined.
A future non-executable toy contract would generate multiple independent sequences with known \(a,q,r\); compare the training mean, static FA, observation-space AR(1), known-parameter LGSSM, and learned-parameter LGSSM; evaluate blocked predictive likelihood, multi-step calibration, innovation autocorrelation, filtered versus smoothed information sets, and similarity-aligned state recovery. Negative controls would include a unit root, correlated \(w_t\) and \(v_t\), informative missingness, and an unobservable augmented state. No data, code, fitted result, or benchmark is produced in this Method Object.

title: Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
text:
The discrete-time LGSSM is LDG’s canonical probabilistic temporal latent baseline. It connects a factor-analysis-style observation layer to an explicit stochastic transition while preserving clear distinctions among model structure, state inference, forecasting, and parameter learning. It is the prerequisite model class for later Kalman filtering and smoothing Methods.






WarningWhat this does NOT imply



A well-predicting LGSSM does not prove that latent coordinates are unique, that \(A\) is a biological mechanism or causal law, that inferred trajectories are directly observed, or that data lie on a manifold with a discovered intrinsic dimension. Stability is not stationarity, smooth posterior means can be model-imposed, and exact inference is exact only conditional on the declared linear-Gaussian model and fixed parameters.




An LGSSM can model ordered kinematic observations and known task inputs, but alignment, variable sampling intervals, animal-level dependence, nonlinear biomechanics, and interventions must be declared. No modality-specific empirical result is retained here.



The model can separate a latent temporal state from measurement variability in declared gaze or oculomotor features. Saccades, censoring, event-dependent noise, and irregular samples can violate one global linear-Gaussian model. No modality-specific empirical result is retained here.



Sensor sequences may be modeled through latent linear dynamics, but rereferencing, spatial mixing, artifacts, colored noise, and nonstationarity challenge \(C\), \(Q\), and \(R\). Latent states are not automatically neural sources. No modality-specific empirical result is retained here.



The method provides a baseline for population recordings with ordered trials or time bins. Unit scaling, condition averaging, trial dependence, input definitions, and observation distributions must be explicit. No modality-specific empirical result is retained here.

title: Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
text:
Kalman develops the state-transition and random-excitation approach to linear filtering and prediction, and explicitly separates smoothing, filtering, and prediction by their conditioning time (Kalman 1960). His inspected formulation is not used here as the sole source for the separate additive observation-noise equation.
Ghahramani and Hinton specify the discrete-time linear-Gaussian transition, observation, initial-state, \(Q/R\) covariance model and derive EM parameter updates from smoothed latent sufficient statistics (Ghahramani and Hinton 1996).

title: Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
text:
Särkkä gives an authoritative Bayesian treatment of probabilistic state-space models, linear-Gaussian filtering and smoothing targets, predictive-density likelihood factorization, and parameter estimation (Särkkä 2013).
Roweis and Ghahramani review factor analysis, PCA, and linear-Gaussian dynamic models in a common generative framework and distinguish static from ordered dynamic data (Roweis and Ghahramani 1999).

title: Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
text:
Which state-dimension and covariance constraints remain reliable for short, dependent, high-dimensional LDG sequences?
Which interventions or observation designs break scientifically important similarity and noise-allocation ambiguities?
When is an observation-space autoregression sufficient, making a latent state unnecessary?
How should irregular sampling, informative missingness, and correlated process/observation noise be introduced without obscuring the canonical baseline?

title: Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
text:
Schema-complete Method Object at L2/review.
Initial state, input-driven transition, observation law, Gaussian \(Q/R\), and independence assumptions specified.
Model specification, forecasting, filtering, smoothing, marginal likelihood, and parameter learning distinguished.
Filtering and smoothing algorithms deferred to later units.

Similarity-transform ambiguity and stronger nonidentifiability stated.
Learned/fixed, geometry, supervision, failure modes, baselines, leakage-safe evaluation, and analytic/prose toy contract included.
No causal, mechanism, manifold, or model-free intrinsic-dimension claim made.

title: First-Order Autonomous Dynamical System
text:
The six Cycle 1 Concepts distinguish a state, its state space, a trajectory, an initial condition, a vector field, and a flow. This Math Object connects those roles in one reusable continuous-time formulation:
\[
\frac{dx}{dt}=f(x),
\qquad
x(t_0)=x_0.
\]
The differential equation is not merely a compact description of a plotted curve. It is a constraint on an unknown differentiable state trajectory. Existence, uniqueness, continuation, and finite-time flow statements require separate hypotheses. Making those hypotheses explicit is necessary before later LDG work can use an autonomous ODE as a generative model or recovery target.
The scope is deliberately narrow: \(\mathcal{X}\) is an open subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), time is continuous, and the rule is deterministic and autonomous. Discrete-time, stochastic, input-driven, explicitly time-dependent, and non-Euclidean systems are outside this object.




State: the state value carried by the model at a time.
State Space: the admissible values of that state.
Trajectory: one time-parameterized evolution.
Initial Condition: the assignment \(x(t_0)=x_0\).
Vector Field: the instantaneous state-change rule.
Flow: finite-time evolution across supported initial states.

Assumed background: elementary sets, functions, Euclidean vectors, single-variable differentiation and integration, the chain rule, and composition of functions.





Let
\[
\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n
\]
be open, and let
\[
f:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
The equation
\[
\dot{x}=f(x)
\]
is a first-order autonomous ordinary differential equation. It is first-order because the highest derivative is \(\dot{x}\), and autonomous because the right-hand side depends on the current state \(x\) but not explicitly on clock time \(t\).
A solution on an interval \(I\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) is a differentiable curve
\[
x:I\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
\]
such that, for every \(t\in I\),
\[
\dot{x}(t)=f\bigl(x(t)\bigr).
\]
Thus \(x(t)\) is a state value in \(\mathcal{X}\), while both \(\dot{x}(t)\) and \(f(x(t))\) are vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^n\). The equation requires the trajectory to be tangent to the vector assigned by \(f\) at every visited state.



For a reference time \(t_0\) and initial state \(x_0\in\mathcal{X}\), the initial-value problem (IVP) is
\[
\dot{x}=f(x),
\qquad
x(t_0)=x_0.
\]
A solution of the IVP must satisfy both the differential equation and the initial condition. The rule \(f\) describes possible instantaneous evolution across its domain; the initial condition selects the solution or set of solutions that pass through \(x_0\) at \(t_0\).




A local solution is defined on an open interval \(I\) containing \(t_0\).
A solution is maximal if it cannot be extended to a strictly larger interval while remaining a solution in \(\mathcal{X}\). If the IVP admits a unique local solution—that is, local solutions exist and any two compatible local solutions agree on their common domain—those local pieces assemble into one unique maximal solution on an open maximal interval
\[
I_{t_0,x_0}=(T_-(t_0,x_0),T_+(t_0,x_0)).
\]
A global solution in this object’s all-time setting is defined for every \(t\in\mathbb{R}\), so its maximal interval is \(\mathbb{R}\).

Local existence and uniqueness do not imply global existence. Under the same local solvability assumptions, if a maximal solution has a finite forward endpoint \(T_+\), then as \(t\uparrow T_+\) it eventually leaves every compact subset of \(\mathcal{X}\). When \(\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}^n\), this means \(\|x(t)\|\to\infty\). On a proper open domain, the trajectory can instead remain bounded while approaching the complement of \(\mathcal{X}\); it need not converge to one particular boundary point. The analogous statements hold at a finite backward endpoint. Teschl separates local solvability from maximal continuation and states this compact-set criterion explicitly (Teschl 2012, secs. 2.2, 2.6).



It is useful to measure time from the initial condition. Write
\[
\tau=t-t_0
\]
for elapsed time. For each \(x\in\mathcal{X}\), suppose a unique maximal solution through \(x\) at elapsed time \(0\) is defined on an interval \(I_x\) containing \(0\). Define
\[
W=\{(\tau,x)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathcal{X}:\tau\in I_x\}.
\]
The set \(W\) records which elapsed-time/state pairs are supported. It need not equal \(\mathbb{R}\times\mathcal{X}\): a state can support only a finite interval of forward or backward evolution. For fixed elapsed time \(\tau\), the finite-time map has the typed domain
\[
\operatorname{dom}(\phi_\tau)
=
\{x\in\mathcal{X}:(\tau,x)\in W\}.
\]


Under local existence and uniqueness, the maximal solutions define a single-valued map
\[
\Phi:W\rightarrow\mathcal{X},
\qquad
(\tau,x)\mapsto\Phi(\tau,x)=\phi_\tau(x).
\]
This local evolution family satisfies
\[
\phi_0(x)=x
\]
and, whenever the terms are defined,
\[
\phi_{\tau+s}(x)=\phi_\tau\bigl(\phi_s(x)\bigr).
\]
More explicitly, if \(s\in I_x\) and \(\tau\in I_{\phi_s(x)}\), then \(s+\tau\in I_x\) and evolving first for \(s\) and then for \(\tau\) agrees with evolving for the combined elapsed time \(s+\tau\). These algebraic properties follow from autonomy and uniqueness. They do not by themselves assert joint continuity or differentiability in \((\tau,x)\).
When \(f\) is locally Lipschitz, it is continuous, so each individual curve \(\tau\mapsto\phi_\tau(x)\) is \(C^1\) in elapsed time and satisfies
\[
\frac{d}{d\tau}\phi_\tau(x)
=
f\bigl(\phi_\tau(x)\bigr).
\]
In particular,
\[
\left.\frac{d}{d\tau}\phi_\tau(x)\right|_{\tau=0}
=
f(x).
\]
This is differentiability along one trajectory in \(\tau\); it is not yet a claim of differentiability with respect to the initial state \(x\).



If \(f\in C^1(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}^n)\), Teschl’s smooth-dependence result gives that \(W\) is open and the joint map
\[
\Phi:W\rightarrow\mathcal{X},
\qquad
(\tau,x)\mapsto\Phi(\tau,x)=\phi_\tau(x),
\]
is \(C^1\) jointly in elapsed time and initial state. Under the adopted LDG convention, this jointly \(C^1\) map, together with the identity and composition laws above, is the local flow generated by \(f\). More generally, \(f\in C^k\) with \(k\geq1\) gives a joint \(C^k\) local-flow map (Teschl 2012, sec. 6.2).












Symbol
Role




\(\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\)
Open Euclidean state-space domain.


\(x\in\mathcal{X}\)
One admissible state value.


\(x(t)\)
State value along one trajectory at clock time \(t\).


\(t_0\)
Reference clock time for the IVP.


\(x_0\)
Initial state satisfying \(x(t_0)=x_0\).


\(f:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^n\)
Autonomous vector field.


\(\dot{x}(t)\)
Instantaneous derivative of the trajectory.


\(I_{t_0,x_0}\)
Maximal clock-time interval for the solution through \((t_0,x_0)\).


\(\tau=t-t_0\)
Elapsed time relative to the reference time.


\(I_x\)
Maximal elapsed-time interval for the solution through \(x\) at \(\tau=0\).


\(W\)
Supported elapsed-time/state pairs \((\tau,x)\).


\(\operatorname{dom}(\phi_\tau)\)
States \(x\) for which \((\tau,x)\in W\).


\(\Phi(\tau,x)=\phi_\tau(x)\)
Single-valued local finite-time evolution; jointly \(C^1\) when \(f\in C^1\).



Clock time \(t\) locates a state on a particular trajectory. Elapsed time \(\tau\) indexes how far the autonomous rule advances an initial state. Autonomy is what permits the same one-parameter notation \(\phi_\tau\) to be used independently of the numerical value of \(t_0\).





The formula \(\dot{x}=f(x)\) alone does not settle whether solutions exist, are unique, or persist globally. For the open Euclidean domain above, the following sufficient conditions form a useful ladder.








Assumption on \(f\)
Consequence used here
What is not obtained automatically




\(f\) is an arbitrary map
The expression assigns a candidate instantaneous vector to each state.
Even local existence is not guaranteed.


\(f\) is continuous
For every \((t_0,x_0)\), at least one local solution exists by the autonomous form of Peano’s theorem. Because \(\dot{x}=f(x)\) is then continuous along a solution, each classical solution is \(C^1\) (Teschl 2012, sec. 2.7).
The solution need not be unique.


\(f\) is locally Lipschitz
Local Lipschitz continuity implies continuity. Picard–Lindelöf therefore gives local existence and uniqueness, and the compatible local pieces assemble into a unique maximal solution. The maximal solutions define single-valued local finite-time evolution with identity and composition where defined (Teschl 2012, secs. 2.2, 2.6).
Global existence and joint differentiability with respect to the initial state are not implied.


\(f\in C^k(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}^n)\), \(k\geq1\)
The unique solution curves are \(C^{k+1}\) in time. The supported set \(W\) is open, and the joint local-flow map \(\Phi:W\to\mathcal{X}\) is \(C^k\) in \((\tau,x)\) (Teschl 2012, secs. 2.2, 6.2).
Even smoothness does not prevent finite-time blow-up or exit from a proper open domain.



Here locally Lipschitz means that every \(x\in\mathcal{X}\) has a neighborhood \(U\subseteq\mathcal{X}\) and a finite constant \(L_U\) such that
\[
\|f(y)-f(z)\|\leq L_U\|y-z\|
\qquad
\text{for all }y,z\in U.
\]
This ladder gives sufficient, not logically necessary, conditions. Some continuous non-Lipschitz fields still have unique solutions, and some less regular settings admit other existence or uniqueness theorems. The scoped conclusion is only that continuity and local Lipschitz continuity cleanly separate basic existence from basic uniqueness.



Existence asks:

Is there at least one differentiable curve through \((t_0,x_0)\) satisfying the equation?

Uniqueness asks:

If two such curves pass through the same initial state at the same reference time, must they coincide on their common domain?

A theorem can answer the first question without answering the second. This distinction matters for flow notation: \(\phi_\tau(x_0)\) is a single state only when the evolution from \(x_0\) is single-valued under the active assumptions or an additional selection rule has been declared.



Now assume \(f\) is continuous and \(x:I\to\mathcal{X}\) is a classical solution of the IVP. Then \(f\circ x\) is continuous, so \(\dot{x}=f\circ x\) is continuous and \(x\in C^1(I,\mathcal{X})\). The fundamental theorem of calculus therefore gives
\[
x(t)-x_0
=
\int_{t_0}^{t}\dot{x}(s)\,ds
=
\int_{t_0}^{t}f\bigl(x(s)\bigr)\,ds.
\]
Hence every solution satisfies
\[
x(t)=x_0+\int_{t_0}^{t}f\bigl(x(s)\bigr)\,ds.
\]
Conversely, let \(f\) be continuous and let a continuous curve \(x:I\to\mathcal{X}\) satisfy this integral equation for every \(t\in I\). Then \(s\mapsto f(x(s))\) is continuous. The integral on the right is therefore \(C^1\), so \(x\) is \(C^1\) and differentiation gives \(\dot{x}(t)=f(x(t))\); setting \(t=t_0\) gives \(x(t_0)=x_0\). Thus the differential and integral formulations are equivalent in this continuous-\(f\) classical-solution setting. Picard iteration uses the integral equation as a fixed-point problem under the stronger local Lipschitz hypothesis (Teschl 2012, sec. 2.2).



Assume local existence and uniqueness. For an initial state \(x_0\), let \(x(\cdot;t_0,x_0)\) denote its maximal solution. Autonomy permits the finite-time map
\[
\phi_\tau(x_0)
=
x(t_0+\tau;t_0,x_0),
\]
whenever \(t_0+\tau\) lies in the maximal interval. The result does not depend on the numerical choice of \(t_0\): shifting clock time shifts an autonomous solution without changing the elapsed-time evolution rule.
For one fixed \(x_0\),
\[
t\mapsto x(t)=\phi_{t-t_0}(x_0)
\]
is one trajectory. By contrast, the flow varies both elapsed time and initial state:
\[
(\tau,x_0)\mapsto\phi_\tau(x_0).
\]
The identity relation follows because no elapsed time has passed. The composition relation follows from autonomy and uniqueness: as functions of a new elapsed-time variable, both continuations start at the intermediate state \(\phi_s(x)\) and solve the same IVP, so they agree wherever both are defined. No differentiability with respect to \(x_0\) is required for these identities.



For locally Lipschitz \(f\), the individual curve \(\tau\mapsto\phi_\tau(x)\) is \(C^1\) and its instantaneous generator is
\[
f(x)
=
\left.\frac{d}{d\tau}\phi_\tau(x)\right|_{\tau=0}.
\]
This derivative is only with respect to elapsed time. If \(f\in C^1\), the stronger conclusion is that \(\Phi(\tau,x)\) is jointly \(C^1\) in both \(\tau\) and \(x\). Conversely, a jointly differentiable local flow satisfying identity and composition generates an autonomous vector field through the derivative-at-zero relation, and its flow curves satisfy the corresponding ODE (Teschl 2012, sec. 6.2, problem 6.5). Thus instantaneous and finite-time descriptions are linked without conflating time differentiability of one trajectory with differentiable dependence on initial state.




The central logical chain is:

Choose the admissible states. Declare an open domain \(\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
Assign instantaneous change. Specify \(f:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^n\).
Constrain a curve. Require a differentiable \(x:I\to\mathcal{X}\) to satisfy \(\dot{x}(t)=f(x(t))\).
Anchor the curve. Add \(x(t_0)=x_0\) to form an IVP.
Invoke the relevant regularity result. Continuity supplies at least one local solution; local Lipschitz continuity supplies local uniqueness as well.
Continue as far as possible. Because local existence and uniqueness both hold at the locally Lipschitz rung, compatible local pieces combine into one unique maximal solution on \(I_{t_0,x_0}\).
Re-index by elapsed time. Set \(\tau=t-t_0\) and define \(\phi_\tau(x_0)=x(t_0+\tau;t_0,x_0)\) where supported.
Use uniqueness to compose. Evolving from \(x\) for \(s\) reaches \(\phi_s(x)\). Starting there and evolving for \(\tau\) solves the same IVP as evolving from \(x\) for \(s+\tau\), so
\[
\phi_{\tau+s}(x)=\phi_\tau(\phi_s(x)).
\]
Differentiate at zero elapsed time. Since locally Lipschitz \(f\) is continuous, each solution curve is \(C^1\) in \(\tau\), and its local slope recovers the instantaneous rule:
\[
\left.\frac{d}{d\tau}\phi_\tau(x)\right|_{\tau=0}=f(x).
\]
This is a derivative along the elapsed-time coordinate. Joint \(C^1\) dependence on \((\tau,x)\) is asserted only at the stronger \(f\in C^1\) rung.

No step in this chain turns local existence into global existence. For example, the smooth field \(f(x)=x^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) has the solution
\[
x(t)=\frac{x_0}{1-x_0(t-t_0)}
\]
for \(x_0>0\). Its maximal interval is
\[
(-\infty,t_0+1/x_0),
\]
because the solution diverges as \(t\uparrow t_0+1/x_0\). Smoothness gives local uniqueness and a smooth local flow, not a global flow on \(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}\) (Teschl 2012, secs. 1.3, 6.2).



At each \(x\in\mathcal{X}\), the vector \(f(x)\) is a local arrow with units of state per unit time. A compatible trajectory is tangent to the arrow at every state it visits:
\[
\text{trajectory tangent at }x(t)
=
\dot{x}(t)
=
f(x(t)).
\]
The flow asks a different question. Rather than showing only the arrow at one point, \(\phi_\tau\) transports every supported initial point through a finite elapsed time \(\tau\). Fixing the point gives one trajectory; fixing the elapsed time gives one state-to-state map.
This picture is intuition, not evidence that measured data possess a vector field or flow. Arrows fitted to samples and curves displayed in a projection inherit the assumptions of the state definition, sampling process, and fitted model.



Consider the scalar IVP
\[
\frac{dx}{dt}=a x,
\qquad
x(t_0)=x_0,
\]
where \(a\in\mathbb{R}\) is fixed.


Multiply the state by the integrating factor \(e^{-a(t-t_0)}\). By the product rule,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dt}\left(e^{-a(t-t_0)}x(t)\right)
&=
-a e^{-a(t-t_0)}x(t)
+e^{-a(t-t_0)}\dot{x}(t)\\
&=
e^{-a(t-t_0)}\bigl(\dot{x}(t)-a x(t)\bigr)\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore \(e^{-a(t-t_0)}x(t)\) is constant in \(t\). Evaluating that constant at \(t=t_0\) gives
\[
e^{-a(t_0-t_0)}x(t_0)=x_0.
\]
Hence
\[
x(t)=x_0e^{a(t-t_0)}.
\]
This derivation also covers \(x_0=0\) without dividing by the state.



Differentiate the proposed solution:
\[
\dot{x}(t)
=
a x_0e^{a(t-t_0)}
=
a x(t).
\]
At the reference time,
\[
x(t_0)=x_0e^0=x_0.
\]
It therefore satisfies both the ODE and the initial condition.




State space: \(\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}\).
State value: \(x(t)\in\mathbb{R}\).
Vector field: \(f(x)=ax\).
Initial state: \(x_0\) at reference time \(t_0\).
Trajectory: \(t\mapsto x_0e^{a(t-t_0)}\) for the chosen \(x_0\).
Elapsed-time flow:
\[
\phi_\tau(x)=xe^{a\tau}.
\]

The field is globally Lipschitz because
\[
|f(x)-f(y)|=|a|\,|x-y|.
\]
The solution is finite for every real \(t\), so this example has a global flow.



Identity:
\[
\phi_0(x)=xe^{a\cdot0}=x.
\]
Composition:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\phi_\tau\bigl(\phi_s(x)\bigr)
&=\phi_\tau(xe^{as})\\
&=(xe^{as})e^{a\tau}\\
&=xe^{a(\tau+s)}\\
&=\phi_{\tau+s}(x).
\end{aligned}
\]
Generator:
\[
\left.\frac{d}{d\tau}\phi_\tau(x)\right|_{\tau=0}
=
\left.a xe^{a\tau}\right|_{\tau=0}
=
ax
=
f(x).
\]
The example makes the three levels explicit: \(f(x)=ax\) gives instantaneous change, \(\phi_\tau(x)=xe^{a\tau}\) gives finite-time evolution across initial states, and choosing one \(x_0\) yields one trajectory.



For a bounded two-dimensional example, let the state be
\[
z(t)=
\begin{pmatrix}
x(t)\\
y(t)
\end{pmatrix}
\in\mathbb{R}^2
\]
and fix parameters \(a,\omega\in\mathbb{R}\). Consider the autonomous IVP
\[
\dot z=Az,
\qquad
A=
\begin{pmatrix}
a & -\omega\\
\omega & a
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
z(t_0)=z_0.
\]
Define the planar rotation matrix
\[
R(\theta)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\cos\theta & -\sin\theta\\
\sin\theta & \cos\theta
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
With elapsed time \(\tau=t-t_0\), propose
\[
z(t_0+\tau)
=
e^{a\tau}R(\omega\tau)z_0.
\]
When \(\omega\neq0\), the rotation changes the angular position while the factor \(e^{a\tau}\) changes the radius: \(a<0\) gives inward spirals, \(a=0\) gives constant-radius rotation, and \(a>0\) gives outward spirals. These descriptions concern this declared system only; they do not infer spiral dynamics from a plotted trajectory.


At zero elapsed time, \(e^{a\cdot0}=1\) and \(R(0)=I\), so
\[
z(t_0)=e^0R(0)z_0=z_0.
\]
Let
\[
J=
\begin{pmatrix}
0 & -1\\
1 & 0
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
A=aI+\omega J.
\]
Direct differentiation of the sine and cosine entries gives
\[
\frac{d}{d\tau}R(\omega\tau)
=
\omega J R(\omega\tau).
\]
Because \(d\tau/dt=1\), the product rule yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\dot z(t_0+\tau)
&=
e^{a\tau}
\left[aI+\omega J\right]
R(\omega\tau)z_0\\
&=
A\left[e^{a\tau}R(\omega\tau)z_0\right]\\
&=Az(t_0+\tau).
\end{aligned}
\]
The proposed curve therefore satisfies both the ODE and the initial condition.




State space: \(\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}^2\).
State value: \(z(t)=(x(t),y(t))^T\in\mathbb{R}^2\).
Vector field: \(f(z)=Az\).
Initial condition: \(z(t_0)=z_0\).
Trajectory: \(t\mapsto e^{a(t-t_0)}R(\omega(t-t_0))z_0\) for the chosen \(z_0\).
Elapsed-time flow:
\[
\phi_\tau(z)=e^{a\tau}R(\omega\tau)z.
\]




The identity law follows immediately:
\[
\phi_0(z)=e^0R(0)z=z.
\]
Using \(e^{a\tau}e^{as}=e^{a(\tau+s)}\) and the planar rotation law \(R(\alpha)R(\beta)=R(\alpha+\beta)\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\phi_\tau\bigl(\phi_s(z)\bigr)
&=
e^{a\tau}R(\omega\tau)
e^{as}R(\omega s)z\\
&=
e^{a(\tau+s)}R\bigl(\omega(\tau+s)\bigr)z\\
&=
\phi_{\tau+s}(z).
\end{aligned}
\]
The field is globally Lipschitz on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) because, for the Euclidean norm and its induced matrix norm,
\[
\|f(z)-f(w)\|
=
\|A(z-w)\|
\leq
\|A\|\,\|z-w\|.
\]
The explicit formula is finite for every \(z\in\mathbb{R}^2\) and every finite \(\tau\in\mathbb{R}\). Hence the supported domain is
\[
W=\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^2,
\]
so this system has a global two-sided flow. Each \(\phi_\tau\) is a globally defined bijection with inverse \(\phi_{-\tau}\). Outward growth when \(a>0\) is unbounded as \(\tau\to\infty\), but it does not cause finite-time blow-up.




Now consider
\[
\dot{x}=\sqrt{|x|},
\qquad
x(0)=0,
\qquad
\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}.
\]
The vector field \(f(x)=\sqrt{|x|}\) is continuous, so Peano’s theorem guarantees at least one local solution through \((0,0)\). It is not locally Lipschitz at \(0\), because for \(x\neq0\),
\[
\frac{|f(x)-f(0)|}{|x-0|}
=
\frac{\sqrt{|x|}}{|x|}
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{|x|}},
\]
which is unbounded as \(x\to0\).
One solution is
\[
x(t)=0.
\]
For every waiting time \(c\geq0\), another solution is
\[
x_c(t)=
\begin{cases}
0, & t\leq c,\\
\dfrac{(t-c)^2}{4}, & t\geq c.
\end{cases}
\]
For \(t<c\), both \(\dot{x}_c(t)\) and \(\sqrt{|x_c(t)|}\) are zero. For \(t>c\),
\[
\dot{x}_c(t)=\frac{t-c}{2}
=
\sqrt{\frac{(t-c)^2}{4}}
=
\sqrt{|x_c(t)|}.
\]
At \(t=c\), the left and right derivatives are both zero, so \(x_c\) is differentiable there. Since \(c\geq0\), every such curve also satisfies \(x_c(0)=0\). The same IVP therefore has infinitely many solutions. This is the standard nonuniqueness mechanism illustrated by Teschl’s square-root example (Teschl 2012, sec. 1.3).
The lesson is precise: continuity supports existence here, but the failed local Lipschitz condition removes the basic uniqueness guarantee. Consequently, the ODE and initial state alone do not determine a unique value \(\phi_\tau(0)\) after positive elapsed time and therefore do not induce one uniquely determined single-valued flow.





Treating the equation as a curve rather than a constraint. The expression \(\dot{x}=f(x)\) specifies which differentiable curves qualify as solutions; it is not itself one trajectory.
Equating existence with uniqueness. A continuous field can admit solutions without selecting exactly one solution from an initial state.
Equating local with global. Local Lipschitz continuity gives local existence and uniqueness and hence a unique maximal continuation, not an all-time solution.
Ignoring the declared domain. A solution must remain in \(\mathcal{X}\). Reaching its boundary can end the maximal solution even when the coordinate values stay bounded.
Using \(t\) and \(\tau\) interchangeably. Clock time labels a trajectory relative to \(t_0\); elapsed time indexes autonomous evolution maps.
Calling one trajectory a flow. One fixed \(x_0\) gives one trajectory. A flow organizes evolution across multiple initial states and must satisfy identity and composition where defined.
Assuming every vector field has a global flow. Even a smooth vector field can have finite-time blow-up.
Inferring a field from a display. A plotted curve or fitted arrow field is not by itself evidence for a unique autonomous mechanism.

This formalism also does not imply that:

every observed time series is a dynamical-system trajectory;
every time-varying latent representation admits a valid autonomous vector field;
one observed trajectory uniquely determines a vector field, either away from or along incompletely sampled states;
multiple similar trajectories prove one shared flow;
predictive success establishes mechanistic correctness;
an inferred latent state is the uniquely true physical state;
all systems are autonomous or continuous-time;
all scientifically relevant state spaces are Euclidean; or
all vector fields generate global flows.




Given a declared \(f\), \(x_0\), and \(t_0\), a numerical ODE solver approximates one solution trajectory over a requested time interval. Step size, error control, stiffness, domain boundaries, and finite-time divergence affect whether the computation is reliable. Numerical output does not replace the analytical questions addressed here: whether a solution exists, whether it is unique, and whether the requested interval lies inside its maximal domain.
The flow viewpoint corresponds computationally to solving the same ODE for many initial states and elapsed times. A finite grid of simulations samples a proposed flow; it is not the complete map \(\Phi:W\to\mathcal{X}\). Likewise, estimating \(f\) from data is a separate Method problem involving sampling, observation, noise, identifiability, and baselines. It is not part of this mathematical definition.



This object formalizes, rather than replaces, the six Cycle 1 Concepts:



Concept
Formal role in the autonomous IVP




State
\(x(t)\) is the state value carried at clock time \(t\).


State Space
\(x(t)\in\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).


Initial Condition
\(x(t_0)=x_0\) anchors the evolution at a reference time.


Vector Field
\(f:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^n\) assigns instantaneous change.


Trajectory
\(t\mapsto x(t)\) is one solution selected by an initial condition when uniqueness holds.


Flow
\((\tau,x_0)\mapsto\phi_\tau(x_0)\) organizes finite-time evolution across supported initial states.



For LDG, the main methodological boundary is that mathematical coherence inside a declared ODE model is not empirical evidence that measured neural, behavioral, or latent variables obey that model. A later toy model may use this object to specify known ground truth. Real-data claims would additionally require a justified state description, observation model, estimation procedure, simpler baselines, and tests that distinguish an autonomous shared rule from inputs, nonstationarity, omitted state, and measurement artifacts.




Existence, uniqueness, smoothness, integral form, and continuation of IVP solutions: (Teschl 2012, ch. 2).
Scalar autonomous examples demonstrating global evolution, finite-time blow-up, and nonuniqueness: (Teschl 2012, sec. 1.3).
Maximal integral curves, the supported domain \(W\), local-flow composition, and the infinitesimal generator: (Teschl 2012, sec. 6.2).





Uses the six stable Cycle 1 Concepts as canonical prerequisites.
States the autonomous Euclidean IVP with well-typed domains and codomains.
Separates continuity, local Lipschitz continuity, and stronger smoothness.
Distinguishes existence from uniqueness and local from maximal and global solutions.
Defines the supported local-flow domain and states identity and composition only where defined.
Relates the differentiable local flow to its vector field through the derivative at zero.
Includes and verifies the complete \(\dot{x}=ax\) trajectory and flow derivation.
Includes an analytically checked two-dimensional rotation–dilation trajectory and global flow.
Includes a checked nonuniqueness example and a bounded finite-time blow-up boundary.
States empirical and modeling non-implications without entering excluded downstream topics.
Completed one internal mathematical consistency / Red-Team pass.
Applied the bounded corrections from the independent L2 mathematical review.
Independent focused re-review confirmed the revised statements; the owner approved L2 / stable promotion on 2026-08-18.

title: First-Order Autonomous Dynamical System
text:
The six Cycle 1 Concepts distinguish a state, its state space, a trajectory, an initial condition, a vector field, and a flow. This Math Object connects those roles in one reusable continuous-time formulation:
\[
\frac{dx}{dt}=f(x),
\qquad
x(t_0)=x_0.
\]
The differential equation is not merely a compact description of a plotted curve. It is a constraint on an unknown differentiable state trajectory. Existence, uniqueness, continuation, and finite-time flow statements require separate hypotheses. Making those hypotheses explicit is necessary before later LDG work can use an autonomous ODE as a generative model or recovery target.
The scope is deliberately narrow: \(\mathcal{X}\) is an open subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), time is continuous, and the rule is deterministic and autonomous. Discrete-time, stochastic, input-driven, explicitly time-dependent, and non-Euclidean systems are outside this object.

title: First-Order Autonomous Dynamical System
text:
State: the state value carried by the model at a time.
State Space: the admissible values of that state.
Trajectory: one time-parameterized evolution.
Initial Condition: the assignment \(x(t_0)=x_0\).
Vector Field: the instantaneous state-change rule.
Flow: finite-time evolution across supported initial states.

Assumed background: elementary sets, functions, Euclidean vectors, single-variable differentiation and integration, the chain rule, and composition of functions.

title: First-Order Autonomous Dynamical System
text:
Let
\[
\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n
\]
be open, and let
\[
f:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
The equation
\[
\dot{x}=f(x)
\]
is a first-order autonomous ordinary differential equation. It is first-order because the highest derivative is \(\dot{x}\), and autonomous because the right-hand side depends on the current state \(x\) but not explicitly on clock time \(t\).
A solution on an interval \(I\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) is a differentiable curve
\[
x:I\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
\]
such that, for every \(t\in I\),
\[
\dot{x}(t)=f\bigl(x(t)\bigr).
\]
Thus \(x(t)\) is a state value in \(\mathcal{X}\), while both \(\dot{x}(t)\) and \(f(x(t))\) are vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^n\). The equation requires the trajectory to be tangent to the vector assigned by \(f\) at every visited state.



For a reference time \(t_0\) and initial state \(x_0\in\mathcal{X}\), the initial-value problem (IVP) is
\[
\dot{x}=f(x),
\qquad
x(t_0)=x_0.
\]
A solution of the IVP must satisfy both the differential equation and the initial condition. The rule \(f\) describes possible instantaneous evolution across its domain; the initial condition selects the solution or set of solutions that pass through \(x_0\) at \(t_0\).




A local solution is defined on an open interval \(I\) containing \(t_0\).
A solution is maximal if it cannot be extended to a strictly larger interval while remaining a solution in \(\mathcal{X}\). If the IVP admits a unique local solution—that is, local solutions exist and any two compatible local solutions agree on their common domain—those local pieces assemble into one unique maximal solution on an open maximal interval
\[
I_{t_0,x_0}=(T_-(t_0,x_0),T_+(t_0,x_0)).
\]
A global solution in this object’s all-time setting is defined for every \(t\in\mathbb{R}\), so its maximal interval is \(\mathbb{R}\).

Local existence and uniqueness do not imply global existence. Under the same local solvability assumptions, if a maximal solution has a finite forward endpoint \(T_+\), then as \(t\uparrow T_+\) it eventually leaves every compact subset of \(\mathcal{X}\). When \(\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}^n\), this means \(\|x(t)\|\to\infty\). On a proper open domain, the trajectory can instead remain bounded while approaching the complement of \(\mathcal{X}\); it need not converge to one particular boundary point. The analogous statements hold at a finite backward endpoint. Teschl separates local solvability from maximal continuation and states this compact-set criterion explicitly (Teschl 2012, secs. 2.2, 2.6).



It is useful to measure time from the initial condition. Write
\[
\tau=t-t_0
\]
for elapsed time. For each \(x\in\mathcal{X}\), suppose a unique maximal solution through \(x\) at elapsed time \(0\) is defined on an interval \(I_x\) containing \(0\). Define
\[
W=\{(\tau,x)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathcal{X}:\tau\in I_x\}.
\]
The set \(W\) records which elapsed-time/state pairs are supported. It need not equal \(\mathbb{R}\times\mathcal{X}\): a state can support only a finite interval of forward or backward evolution. For fixed elapsed time \(\tau\), the finite-time map has the typed domain
\[
\operatorname{dom}(\phi_\tau)
=
\{x\in\mathcal{X}:(\tau,x)\in W\}.
\]


Under local existence and uniqueness, the maximal solutions define a single-valued map
\[
\Phi:W\rightarrow\mathcal{X},
\qquad
(\tau,x)\mapsto\Phi(\tau,x)=\phi_\tau(x).
\]
This local evolution family satisfies
\[
\phi_0(x)=x
\]
and, whenever the terms are defined,
\[
\phi_{\tau+s}(x)=\phi_\tau\bigl(\phi_s(x)\bigr).
\]
More explicitly, if \(s\in I_x\) and \(\tau\in I_{\phi_s(x)}\), then \(s+\tau\in I_x\) and evolving first for \(s\) and then for \(\tau\) agrees with evolving for the combined elapsed time \(s+\tau\). These algebraic properties follow from autonomy and uniqueness. They do not by themselves assert joint continuity or differentiability in \((\tau,x)\).
When \(f\) is locally Lipschitz, it is continuous, so each individual curve \(\tau\mapsto\phi_\tau(x)\) is \(C^1\) in elapsed time and satisfies
\[
\frac{d}{d\tau}\phi_\tau(x)
=
f\bigl(\phi_\tau(x)\bigr).
\]
In particular,
\[
\left.\frac{d}{d\tau}\phi_\tau(x)\right|_{\tau=0}
=
f(x).
\]
This is differentiability along one trajectory in \(\tau\); it is not yet a claim of differentiability with respect to the initial state \(x\).



If \(f\in C^1(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}^n)\), Teschl’s smooth-dependence result gives that \(W\) is open and the joint map
\[
\Phi:W\rightarrow\mathcal{X},
\qquad
(\tau,x)\mapsto\Phi(\tau,x)=\phi_\tau(x),
\]
is \(C^1\) jointly in elapsed time and initial state. Under the adopted LDG convention, this jointly \(C^1\) map, together with the identity and composition laws above, is the local flow generated by \(f\). More generally, \(f\in C^k\) with \(k\geq1\) gives a joint \(C^k\) local-flow map (Teschl 2012, sec. 6.2).

title: First-Order Autonomous Dynamical System
text:
Symbol
Role




\(\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\)
Open Euclidean state-space domain.


\(x\in\mathcal{X}\)
One admissible state value.


\(x(t)\)
State value along one trajectory at clock time \(t\).


\(t_0\)
Reference clock time for the IVP.


\(x_0\)
Initial state satisfying \(x(t_0)=x_0\).


\(f:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^n\)
Autonomous vector field.


\(\dot{x}(t)\)
Instantaneous derivative of the trajectory.


\(I_{t_0,x_0}\)
Maximal clock-time interval for the solution through \((t_0,x_0)\).


\(\tau=t-t_0\)
Elapsed time relative to the reference time.


\(I_x\)
Maximal elapsed-time interval for the solution through \(x\) at \(\tau=0\).


\(W\)
Supported elapsed-time/state pairs \((\tau,x)\).


\(\operatorname{dom}(\phi_\tau)\)
States \(x\) for which \((\tau,x)\in W\).


\(\Phi(\tau,x)=\phi_\tau(x)\)
Single-valued local finite-time evolution; jointly \(C^1\) when \(f\in C^1\).



Clock time \(t\) locates a state on a particular trajectory. Elapsed time \(\tau\) indexes how far the autonomous rule advances an initial state. Autonomy is what permits the same one-parameter notation \(\phi_\tau\) to be used independently of the numerical value of \(t_0\).

title: First-Order Autonomous Dynamical System
text:
The formula \(\dot{x}=f(x)\) alone does not settle whether solutions exist, are unique, or persist globally. For the open Euclidean domain above, the following sufficient conditions form a useful ladder.








Assumption on \(f\)
Consequence used here
What is not obtained automatically




\(f\) is an arbitrary map
The expression assigns a candidate instantaneous vector to each state.
Even local existence is not guaranteed.


\(f\) is continuous
For every \((t_0,x_0)\), at least one local solution exists by the autonomous form of Peano’s theorem. Because \(\dot{x}=f(x)\) is then continuous along a solution, each classical solution is \(C^1\) (Teschl 2012, sec. 2.7).
The solution need not be unique.


\(f\) is locally Lipschitz
Local Lipschitz continuity implies continuity. Picard–Lindelöf therefore gives local existence and uniqueness, and the compatible local pieces assemble into a unique maximal solution. The maximal solutions define single-valued local finite-time evolution with identity and composition where defined (Teschl 2012, secs. 2.2, 2.6).
Global existence and joint differentiability with respect to the initial state are not implied.


\(f\in C^k(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}^n)\), \(k\geq1\)
The unique solution curves are \(C^{k+1}\) in time. The supported set \(W\) is open, and the joint local-flow map \(\Phi:W\to\mathcal{X}\) is \(C^k\) in \((\tau,x)\) (Teschl 2012, secs. 2.2, 6.2).
Even smoothness does not prevent finite-time blow-up or exit from a proper open domain.



Here locally Lipschitz means that every \(x\in\mathcal{X}\) has a neighborhood \(U\subseteq\mathcal{X}\) and a finite constant \(L_U\) such that
\[
\|f(y)-f(z)\|\leq L_U\|y-z\|
\qquad
\text{for all }y,z\in U.
\]
This ladder gives sufficient, not logically necessary, conditions. Some continuous non-Lipschitz fields still have unique solutions, and some less regular settings admit other existence or uniqueness theorems. The scoped conclusion is only that continuity and local Lipschitz continuity cleanly separate basic existence from basic uniqueness.



Existence asks:

Is there at least one differentiable curve through \((t_0,x_0)\) satisfying the equation?

Uniqueness asks:

If two such curves pass through the same initial state at the same reference time, must they coincide on their common domain?

A theorem can answer the first question without answering the second. This distinction matters for flow notation: \(\phi_\tau(x_0)\) is a single state only when the evolution from \(x_0\) is single-valued under the active assumptions or an additional selection rule has been declared.



Now assume \(f\) is continuous and \(x:I\to\mathcal{X}\) is a classical solution of the IVP. Then \(f\circ x\) is continuous, so \(\dot{x}=f\circ x\) is continuous and \(x\in C^1(I,\mathcal{X})\). The fundamental theorem of calculus therefore gives
\[
x(t)-x_0
=
\int_{t_0}^{t}\dot{x}(s)\,ds
=
\int_{t_0}^{t}f\bigl(x(s)\bigr)\,ds.
\]
Hence every solution satisfies
\[
x(t)=x_0+\int_{t_0}^{t}f\bigl(x(s)\bigr)\,ds.
\]
Conversely, let \(f\) be continuous and let a continuous curve \(x:I\to\mathcal{X}\) satisfy this integral equation for every \(t\in I\). Then \(s\mapsto f(x(s))\) is continuous. The integral on the right is therefore \(C^1\), so \(x\) is \(C^1\) and differentiation gives \(\dot{x}(t)=f(x(t))\); setting \(t=t_0\) gives \(x(t_0)=x_0\). Thus the differential and integral formulations are equivalent in this continuous-\(f\) classical-solution setting. Picard iteration uses the integral equation as a fixed-point problem under the stronger local Lipschitz hypothesis (Teschl 2012, sec. 2.2).



Assume local existence and uniqueness. For an initial state \(x_0\), let \(x(\cdot;t_0,x_0)\) denote its maximal solution. Autonomy permits the finite-time map
\[
\phi_\tau(x_0)
=
x(t_0+\tau;t_0,x_0),
\]
whenever \(t_0+\tau\) lies in the maximal interval. The result does not depend on the numerical choice of \(t_0\): shifting clock time shifts an autonomous solution without changing the elapsed-time evolution rule.
For one fixed \(x_0\),
\[
t\mapsto x(t)=\phi_{t-t_0}(x_0)
\]
is one trajectory. By contrast, the flow varies both elapsed time and initial state:
\[
(\tau,x_0)\mapsto\phi_\tau(x_0).
\]
The identity relation follows because no elapsed time has passed. The composition relation follows from autonomy and uniqueness: as functions of a new elapsed-time variable, both continuations start at the intermediate state \(\phi_s(x)\) and solve the same IVP, so they agree wherever both are defined. No differentiability with respect to \(x_0\) is required for these identities.



For locally Lipschitz \(f\), the individual curve \(\tau\mapsto\phi_\tau(x)\) is \(C^1\) and its instantaneous generator is
\[
f(x)
=
\left.\frac{d}{d\tau}\phi_\tau(x)\right|_{\tau=0}.
\]
This derivative is only with respect to elapsed time. If \(f\in C^1\), the stronger conclusion is that \(\Phi(\tau,x)\) is jointly \(C^1\) in both \(\tau\) and \(x\). Conversely, a jointly differentiable local flow satisfying identity and composition generates an autonomous vector field through the derivative-at-zero relation, and its flow curves satisfy the corresponding ODE (Teschl 2012, sec. 6.2, problem 6.5). Thus instantaneous and finite-time descriptions are linked without conflating time differentiability of one trajectory with differentiable dependence on initial state.

title: First-Order Autonomous Dynamical System
text:
The central logical chain is:

Choose the admissible states. Declare an open domain \(\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
Assign instantaneous change. Specify \(f:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^n\).
Constrain a curve. Require a differentiable \(x:I\to\mathcal{X}\) to satisfy \(\dot{x}(t)=f(x(t))\).
Anchor the curve. Add \(x(t_0)=x_0\) to form an IVP.
Invoke the relevant regularity result. Continuity supplies at least one local solution; local Lipschitz continuity supplies local uniqueness as well.
Continue as far as possible. Because local existence and uniqueness both hold at the locally Lipschitz rung, compatible local pieces combine into one unique maximal solution on \(I_{t_0,x_0}\).
Re-index by elapsed time. Set \(\tau=t-t_0\) and define \(\phi_\tau(x_0)=x(t_0+\tau;t_0,x_0)\) where supported.
Use uniqueness to compose. Evolving from \(x\) for \(s\) reaches \(\phi_s(x)\). Starting there and evolving for \(\tau\) solves the same IVP as evolving from \(x\) for \(s+\tau\), so
\[
\phi_{\tau+s}(x)=\phi_\tau(\phi_s(x)).
\]
Differentiate at zero elapsed time. Since locally Lipschitz \(f\) is continuous, each solution curve is \(C^1\) in \(\tau\), and its local slope recovers the instantaneous rule:
\[
\left.\frac{d}{d\tau}\phi_\tau(x)\right|_{\tau=0}=f(x).
\]
This is a derivative along the elapsed-time coordinate. Joint \(C^1\) dependence on \((\tau,x)\) is asserted only at the stronger \(f\in C^1\) rung.

No step in this chain turns local existence into global existence. For example, the smooth field \(f(x)=x^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) has the solution
\[
x(t)=\frac{x_0}{1-x_0(t-t_0)}
\]
for \(x_0>0\). Its maximal interval is
\[
(-\infty,t_0+1/x_0),
\]
because the solution diverges as \(t\uparrow t_0+1/x_0\). Smoothness gives local uniqueness and a smooth local flow, not a global flow on \(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}\) (Teschl 2012, secs. 1.3, 6.2).

title: First-Order Autonomous Dynamical System
text:
At each \(x\in\mathcal{X}\), the vector \(f(x)\) is a local arrow with units of state per unit time. A compatible trajectory is tangent to the arrow at every state it visits:
\[
\text{trajectory tangent at }x(t)
=
\dot{x}(t)
=
f(x(t)).
\]
The flow asks a different question. Rather than showing only the arrow at one point, \(\phi_\tau\) transports every supported initial point through a finite elapsed time \(\tau\). Fixing the point gives one trajectory; fixing the elapsed time gives one state-to-state map.
This picture is intuition, not evidence that measured data possess a vector field or flow. Arrows fitted to samples and curves displayed in a projection inherit the assumptions of the state definition, sampling process, and fitted model.

title: First-Order Autonomous Dynamical System
text:
Consider the scalar IVP
\[
\frac{dx}{dt}=a x,
\qquad
x(t_0)=x_0,
\]
where \(a\in\mathbb{R}\) is fixed.


Multiply the state by the integrating factor \(e^{-a(t-t_0)}\). By the product rule,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dt}\left(e^{-a(t-t_0)}x(t)\right)
&=
-a e^{-a(t-t_0)}x(t)
+e^{-a(t-t_0)}\dot{x}(t)\\
&=
e^{-a(t-t_0)}\bigl(\dot{x}(t)-a x(t)\bigr)\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore \(e^{-a(t-t_0)}x(t)\) is constant in \(t\). Evaluating that constant at \(t=t_0\) gives
\[
e^{-a(t_0-t_0)}x(t_0)=x_0.
\]
Hence
\[
x(t)=x_0e^{a(t-t_0)}.
\]
This derivation also covers \(x_0=0\) without dividing by the state.



Differentiate the proposed solution:
\[
\dot{x}(t)
=
a x_0e^{a(t-t_0)}
=
a x(t).
\]
At the reference time,
\[
x(t_0)=x_0e^0=x_0.
\]
It therefore satisfies both the ODE and the initial condition.




State space: \(\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}\).
State value: \(x(t)\in\mathbb{R}\).
Vector field: \(f(x)=ax\).
Initial state: \(x_0\) at reference time \(t_0\).
Trajectory: \(t\mapsto x_0e^{a(t-t_0)}\) for the chosen \(x_0\).
Elapsed-time flow:
\[
\phi_\tau(x)=xe^{a\tau}.
\]

The field is globally Lipschitz because
\[
|f(x)-f(y)|=|a|\,|x-y|.
\]
The solution is finite for every real \(t\), so this example has a global flow.



Identity:
\[
\phi_0(x)=xe^{a\cdot0}=x.
\]
Composition:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\phi_\tau\bigl(\phi_s(x)\bigr)
&=\phi_\tau(xe^{as})\\
&=(xe^{as})e^{a\tau}\\
&=xe^{a(\tau+s)}\\
&=\phi_{\tau+s}(x).
\end{aligned}
\]
Generator:
\[
\left.\frac{d}{d\tau}\phi_\tau(x)\right|_{\tau=0}
=
\left.a xe^{a\tau}\right|_{\tau=0}
=
ax
=
f(x).
\]
The example makes the three levels explicit: \(f(x)=ax\) gives instantaneous change, \(\phi_\tau(x)=xe^{a\tau}\) gives finite-time evolution across initial states, and choosing one \(x_0\) yields one trajectory.



For a bounded two-dimensional example, let the state be
\[
z(t)=
\begin{pmatrix}
x(t)\\
y(t)
\end{pmatrix}
\in\mathbb{R}^2
\]
and fix parameters \(a,\omega\in\mathbb{R}\). Consider the autonomous IVP
\[
\dot z=Az,
\qquad
A=
\begin{pmatrix}
a & -\omega\\
\omega & a
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
z(t_0)=z_0.
\]
Define the planar rotation matrix
\[
R(\theta)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\cos\theta & -\sin\theta\\
\sin\theta & \cos\theta
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
With elapsed time \(\tau=t-t_0\), propose
\[
z(t_0+\tau)
=
e^{a\tau}R(\omega\tau)z_0.
\]
When \(\omega\neq0\), the rotation changes the angular position while the factor \(e^{a\tau}\) changes the radius: \(a<0\) gives inward spirals, \(a=0\) gives constant-radius rotation, and \(a>0\) gives outward spirals. These descriptions concern this declared system only; they do not infer spiral dynamics from a plotted trajectory.


At zero elapsed time, \(e^{a\cdot0}=1\) and \(R(0)=I\), so
\[
z(t_0)=e^0R(0)z_0=z_0.
\]
Let
\[
J=
\begin{pmatrix}
0 & -1\\
1 & 0
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
A=aI+\omega J.
\]
Direct differentiation of the sine and cosine entries gives
\[
\frac{d}{d\tau}R(\omega\tau)
=
\omega J R(\omega\tau).
\]
Because \(d\tau/dt=1\), the product rule yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\dot z(t_0+\tau)
&=
e^{a\tau}
\left[aI+\omega J\right]
R(\omega\tau)z_0\\
&=
A\left[e^{a\tau}R(\omega\tau)z_0\right]\\
&=Az(t_0+\tau).
\end{aligned}
\]
The proposed curve therefore satisfies both the ODE and the initial condition.




State space: \(\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}^2\).
State value: \(z(t)=(x(t),y(t))^T\in\mathbb{R}^2\).
Vector field: \(f(z)=Az\).
Initial condition: \(z(t_0)=z_0\).
Trajectory: \(t\mapsto e^{a(t-t_0)}R(\omega(t-t_0))z_0\) for the chosen \(z_0\).
Elapsed-time flow:
\[
\phi_\tau(z)=e^{a\tau}R(\omega\tau)z.
\]




The identity law follows immediately:
\[
\phi_0(z)=e^0R(0)z=z.
\]
Using \(e^{a\tau}e^{as}=e^{a(\tau+s)}\) and the planar rotation law \(R(\alpha)R(\beta)=R(\alpha+\beta)\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\phi_\tau\bigl(\phi_s(z)\bigr)
&=
e^{a\tau}R(\omega\tau)
e^{as}R(\omega s)z\\
&=
e^{a(\tau+s)}R\bigl(\omega(\tau+s)\bigr)z\\
&=
\phi_{\tau+s}(z).
\end{aligned}
\]
The field is globally Lipschitz on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) because, for the Euclidean norm and its induced matrix norm,
\[
\|f(z)-f(w)\|
=
\|A(z-w)\|
\leq
\|A\|\,\|z-w\|.
\]
The explicit formula is finite for every \(z\in\mathbb{R}^2\) and every finite \(\tau\in\mathbb{R}\). Hence the supported domain is
\[
W=\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^2,
\]
so this system has a global two-sided flow. Each \(\phi_\tau\) is a globally defined bijection with inverse \(\phi_{-\tau}\). Outward growth when \(a>0\) is unbounded as \(\tau\to\infty\), but it does not cause finite-time blow-up.




Now consider
\[
\dot{x}=\sqrt{|x|},
\qquad
x(0)=0,
\qquad
\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}.
\]
The vector field \(f(x)=\sqrt{|x|}\) is continuous, so Peano’s theorem guarantees at least one local solution through \((0,0)\). It is not locally Lipschitz at \(0\), because for \(x\neq0\),
\[
\frac{|f(x)-f(0)|}{|x-0|}
=
\frac{\sqrt{|x|}}{|x|}
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{|x|}},
\]
which is unbounded as \(x\to0\).
One solution is
\[
x(t)=0.
\]
For every waiting time \(c\geq0\), another solution is
\[
x_c(t)=
\begin{cases}
0, & t\leq c,\\
\dfrac{(t-c)^2}{4}, & t\geq c.
\end{cases}
\]
For \(t<c\), both \(\dot{x}_c(t)\) and \(\sqrt{|x_c(t)|}\) are zero. For \(t>c\),
\[
\dot{x}_c(t)=\frac{t-c}{2}
=
\sqrt{\frac{(t-c)^2}{4}}
=
\sqrt{|x_c(t)|}.
\]
At \(t=c\), the left and right derivatives are both zero, so \(x_c\) is differentiable there. Since \(c\geq0\), every such curve also satisfies \(x_c(0)=0\). The same IVP therefore has infinitely many solutions. This is the standard nonuniqueness mechanism illustrated by Teschl’s square-root example (Teschl 2012, sec. 1.3).
The lesson is precise: continuity supports existence here, but the failed local Lipschitz condition removes the basic uniqueness guarantee. Consequently, the ODE and initial state alone do not determine a unique value \(\phi_\tau(0)\) after positive elapsed time and therefore do not induce one uniquely determined single-valued flow.

title: First-Order Autonomous Dynamical System
First-Order Autonomous Dynamical System
text:
Given a declared \(f\), \(x_0\), and \(t_0\), a numerical ODE solver approximates one solution trajectory over a requested time interval. Step size, error control, stiffness, domain boundaries, and finite-time divergence affect whether the computation is reliable. Numerical output does not replace the analytical questions addressed here: whether a solution exists, whether it is unique, and whether the requested interval lies inside its maximal domain.
The flow viewpoint corresponds computationally to solving the same ODE for many initial states and elapsed times. A finite grid of simulations samples a proposed flow; it is not the complete map \(\Phi:W\to\mathcal{X}\). Likewise, estimating \(f\) from data is a separate Method problem involving sampling, observation, noise, identifiability, and baselines. It is not part of this mathematical definition.

title: First-Order Autonomous Dynamical System
text:
This object formalizes, rather than replaces, the six Cycle 1 Concepts:



Concept
Formal role in the autonomous IVP




State
\(x(t)\) is the state value carried at clock time \(t\).


State Space
\(x(t)\in\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).


Initial Condition
\(x(t_0)=x_0\) anchors the evolution at a reference time.


Vector Field
\(f:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^n\) assigns instantaneous change.


Trajectory
\(t\mapsto x(t)\) is one solution selected by an initial condition when uniqueness holds.


Flow
\((\tau,x_0)\mapsto\phi_\tau(x_0)\) organizes finite-time evolution across supported initial states.



For LDG, the main methodological boundary is that mathematical coherence inside a declared ODE model is not empirical evidence that measured neural, behavioral, or latent variables obey that model. A later toy model may use this object to specify known ground truth. Real-data claims would additionally require a justified state description, observation model, estimation procedure, simpler baselines, and tests that distinguish an autonomous shared rule from inputs, nonstationarity, omitted state, and measurement artifacts.

text:
Existence, uniqueness, smoothness, integral form, and continuation of IVP solutions: (Teschl 2012, ch. 2).
Scalar autonomous examples demonstrating global evolution, finite-time blow-up, and nonuniqueness: (Teschl 2012, sec. 1.3).
Maximal integral curves, the supported domain \(W\), local-flow composition, and the infinitesimal generator: (Teschl 2012, sec. 6.2).

title: First-Order Autonomous Dynamical System
text:
Uses the six stable Cycle 1 Concepts as canonical prerequisites.
States the autonomous Euclidean IVP with well-typed domains and codomains.
Separates continuity, local Lipschitz continuity, and stronger smoothness.
Distinguishes existence from uniqueness and local from maximal and global solutions.
Defines the supported local-flow domain and states identity and composition only where defined.
Relates the differentiable local flow to its vector field through the derivative at zero.
Includes and verifies the complete \(\dot{x}=ax\) trajectory and flow derivation.
Includes an analytically checked two-dimensional rotation–dilation trajectory and global flow.
Includes a checked nonuniqueness example and a bounded finite-time blow-up boundary.
States empirical and modeling non-implications without entering excluded downstream topics.
Completed one internal mathematical consistency / Red-Team pass.

title: Covariance-Prior Trajectories
text:
This L1/stable Candidate F Toy Model compares static, two-stage, Gaussian-process, and first-order Markov priors for retrospective latent-path inference. It asks what is gained by a shared temporal covariance prior, and how that gain fails under incorrect kernels, observation laws, alignment, residual covariance, or missingness. Numerical values are deterministic outputs under master seed 20260819; they are conditional on this simulator, masks, plug-in parameters, and declared covariance families.
Assumed background: multivariate Gaussian conditioning, factor analysis, covariance kernels, Cholesky solves, linear-Gaussian smoothing, and independent train/validation/test trials.


For multiple independent trials generated by two latent Gaussian processes with different timescales and observed through one known factor-analysis layer:

does an exact known-parameter GPFA posterior recover latent paths and calibrated uncertainty;
can a finite train-plus-validation timescale grid recover a useful plug-in prior without test or latent-truth leakage;
how much do temporal coupling, cross-channel sharing, and the observation layer contribute to masked prediction;
how does a one-lag-matched LGSSM/RTS approximation differ from the non-Markov squared-exponential prior; and
how do changepoints, residual correlation, low counts, equal kernels, alignment error, informative missingness, and wrong covariance families break the interpretation?

A smooth posterior mean is a conditional expectation under a selected covariance prior and observation model. It is retrospective, parameter-conditional, and not a discovered transition equation, vector field, intrinsic trajectory, or mechanism (Yu et al. 2009; Cunningham and Yu 2014).





The latent dimension is \(q=2\), the observed dimension is \(p=6\), and every trial contains \(T=24\) samples on
\[
t_m=\frac{m}{23},
\qquad m=0,\ldots,23.
\]
Whole trials are independent draws. Split sizes are:

No path continuity, prior covariance, filtering state, or smoother state crosses a trial boundary.



For trial \(n\) and latent coordinate \(j\),
\[
x_j^{(n)}(\cdot)\sim\mathcal{GP}(0,k_j),
\]
independently across \(j\) and \(n\). The true characteristic timescales are
\[
(\tau_1,\tau_2)=(0.08,0.30).
\]
The latent nugget variance is fixed at
\[
\nu^2=0.02,
\]
and marginal variance is fixed at one:
\[
k_j(t,t')
=
(1-\nu^2)
\exp\left[-\frac{(t-t')^2}{2\tau_j^2}\right]
+\nu^2\mathbf 1[t=t'].
\]
Thus \(k_j(t,t)=1\). The smooth signal variance is \(0.98\) and the independent sampled-time latent nugget variance is \(0.02\). The nugget is not observation noise, LGSSM process noise, or parameter uncertainty. Fixing the latent variance removes loading/latent scale ambiguity while retaining sign and permutation ambiguity (Yu et al. 2009).
Every finite Gram matrix is assembled directly on the declared grid and sampled by a deterministic Cholesky factor. Latent draws and observation residuals use independent seed streams.



For each trial and time,
\[
y_t=Cx_t+d+\epsilon_t,
\qquad
\epsilon_t\sim\mathcal N(0,R),
\]
with
\[
C=
\begin{pmatrix}
1.00&0.25\\
0.70&-0.45\\
0.30&0.90\\
-0.65&0.40\\
0.80&0.55\\
-0.25&-0.75
\end{pmatrix},
\]
\[
d=(0.30,-0.20,0.15,0.05,-0.10,0.25)^\top,
\]
and
\[
R=\operatorname{diag}(0.10,0.16,0.22,0.30,0.38,0.48).
\]
The implementation verifies that \(C\) has rank two, records its singular values and condition number, and retains the exact loading subspace \(\operatorname{col}(C)\). Ground-truth latent paths, kernels, and observation parameters enter fitting only for methods explicitly labelled known-parameter oracle.




For each split and trial:

independently draw each latent path from its finite-grid GP covariance;
independently draw Gaussian observation residuals;
generate the complete \(24\times6\) observation array;
freeze the complete array and latent truth;
create evaluation masks as separate views of selected test trials; and
expose hidden observations and latent truth only to final scoring and implementation oracles.

The master seed is 20260819. Random streams use Generator(PCG64(SeedSequence(words))) with explicit stage, split, trial, latent, residual, mask, stress, and baseline codes stored in the manifest.
Generation, observation-layer fitting, timescale selection, posterior inference, masking, alignment, and scoring are separate functions. Parameter selection receives complete train and validation observations, but no test values, test masks, or latent arrays.





The known observation layer \(C,d,R\) is frozen. The selected-timescale GPFA baseline evaluates the nine ordered pairs
\[
\tau_1\in\{0.06,0.08,0.14\},
\qquad
\tau_2\in\{0.18,0.30,0.45\}.
\]
The true pair is included. For each pair, compute total train-plus-validation observation marginal negative log likelihood under independent trials. Select the minimum total NLL; break exact ties lexicographically by \((\tau_1,\tau_2)\). Test observations and every latent truth array are excluded.
This is a finite plug-in covariance-prior selection baseline. It is not unrestricted maximum-likelihood GPFA, does not learn \(C,d,R\), and does not integrate hyperparameter uncertainty. Rasmussen and Williams describe marginal-likelihood hyperparameter learning and its possible ridges or local alternatives; this finite grid deliberately avoids claiming a general optimizer (Rasmussen and Williams 2006, ch. 5).
